author: SLEVALL4868
title: Existential Sci-Fi with a Clone's Heart
text:
Review of Mickey 17 Rating: 8/10

Mickey 17 is a bold and cerebral sci-fi film directed by Bong Joon-ho, known for blending sharp social commentary with genre storytelling. Based on Edward Ashton's novel, the movie offers a visually rich and thought-provoking exploration of identity, mortality, and purpose.

Plot

Set in a dystopian future, the story follows Mickey Barnes - a disposable "expendable" assigned to a dangerous planetary colonization mission. Each time he dies, a new clone with most of his memories is created to continue the work. But when Mickey 17 realizes that his replacements aren't supposed to exist at the same time, things spiral into existential crisis and rebellion.

Performances

Robert Pattinson gives a layered and compelling performance as Mickey, bringing both vulnerability and dry wit to a character who constantly dies and comes back to life. The supporting cast also adds depth, though Mickey's internal struggle is the heart of the story.

Strengths and Weaknesses

The film's world-building is imaginative and immersive, and Bong's direction offers both emotional weight and philosophical depth. Visually, it's stunning - with stylish cinematography and futuristic design. However, the pacing occasionally falters, and some narrative threads remain vague or underdeveloped, possibly leaving casual viewers confused.

Overall Impressions

Mickey 17 is a smart and visually striking sci-fi journey that poses big questions about humanity and purpose. While it may not be for everyone due to its abstract layers and slower pace, it's a must-watch for fans of intelligent science fiction and fans of Bong Joon-ho's unique storytelling.

author: mark-67214-52993
title: A Star Turn for Robert Pattinson; An Exercise in Self-Indulgence for Bong Joon Ho
text:
Director/Co-Writer Bong Joon Ho's last film, "Parasite," deservedly won the Oscar for Best Picture in 2020. "Mickey 17," unfortunately, comes nowhere close to the high standard set by Bong's previous film.
It's 2054. Mickey Barnes (Robert Pattinson) and his friend Timo (Steven Yeun) are convinced that macarons will become as popular as hamburgers. So of course they borrow money from a loan shark to set up a macaron store. The store fails and Mickey needs to leave the planet in order to avoid the debt collectors. He agrees to become an "expendable" on a space mission to the ice planet Niflheim. Without reading the fine print, Mickey has signed up to die over and over again as the arriving colony explores the atmosphere, discovers vaccines for local diseases and figures out how to coexist with the "creepers," indigenous creatures that look like giant slugs in velour warm-up suits. The good news is that every time Mickey dies, he is simply "reprinted." (Scientists have made a record of all his biometrics and his memories, so a new Mickey is extruded from a machine that looks like an MRI after each death.) When Mickey 17 falls through the ice while exploring the new planet, staff assume the worst and simply generate Mickey 18. But wait. Mickey 17 has survived. His girlfriend Nasha (an excellent Naomi Ackie) seems very pleased to now be dating two very different Mickeys. But "multiples" are illegal. Dramatic conflict abounds.
Bong uses this story to re-examine many familiar themes: the excesses of capitalism, class inequality, the risks of authoritarianism, the reality that humans are making the earth irretrievably uninhabitable. The scenes with the creepers give a glancing blow to issues around immigration and colonialism. As with Bong's previous films, these themes are more palatable because they are wrapped in dark comedy. Unfortunately, there are so many topics floating around Niflheim that none really receive the thoughtful treatment delivered in "Parasite," which was more focused, less self-indulgent.
This film is fabulous vehicle for Robert Pattinson to show off his acting versatility. While Mickey 17 is quiet and kind, Mickey 18 is brash, aggressive and grating. Pattinson does an excellent job changing his posture, voice and manner to effectively inhabit these two very different roles.
What doesn't work - at all - is the "development" of other characters in this piece. Mark Ruffalo plays Kenneth Marshall, a failed politician who is in charge of the mission to Niflheim. Toni Collette is his wife, Ylfa. Kenneth and Ylfa are preening idiots whose main feature is their irrationally high self-regard. They're caricatures, not characters. Their shallow buffoonery stands in stark contrast to the better drawn, more interesting characters, particularly the kind, gentle, fatalistic Mickey 17. For me, these tonal shifts were a deal-breaker.
While Bong's political commentary around Kenneth is quite overt and heavy-handed, he pays no meaningful attention to other promising topics. For example, as an "expendable," Mickey is the lowest member of the colony's caste system. Yet he is entrusted with one of humanity's central existential secrets: what happens when we die? It's a tantalizing irony left completely unexplored.
Hopefully, Bong's next film will show a little more focus and a lot more self-discipline.

author: Movie_Rating_n_Ranking
title: A promising story that loses steam halfway through.
text:
Perhaps it's easy to agree with the general opinion. Mickey 17 doesn't live up to expectations, but come on, making something similar to Parasites is like winning the lottery twice in a row.
Bong Joon Ho's latest offering isn't a bad film. It's an entertaining political satire with characters that are instantly recognizable. It's not only a critique of the classist system, but also a way of exposing the world to the consequences of giving the reins to eccentric characters with dubious leadership skills, yet still possessing great selfishness and ambition. On a personal note, I don't really know if comedy is the best ally to develop a script that had every intention of being more complex, but it's enough to hook us as an audience to the screen and watch the clearly lukewarm outcome of a long-delayed story.
The performances fill the shoes of any satire with exaggerated overtones and loudly shouted dialogue. Among the most valuable technical aspects is the editing and montage, which takes you on a non-linear journey through the chronology of the ill-fated Mickey.
In short, this is a feature film that shines in a year that started off rather poorly for cinema. Recommended? Obviously. It's still a Bong Joon Ho film. Watch it.

author: likemoviesverymuch
title: very refreshing
text:
This is one of those rare films that reminds you why you love going to the movies. It's sharp, unexpected, and full of energy-but what really makes it stand out is how refreshingly different it feels. In a time where so many films follow the same formula, *Mickey 17* takes its own path. It's bold, creative, and completely unafraid to be strange in the best possible way.
What struck me most, though, wasn't just the unique tone or the visual style-it was Robert Pattinson. He continues to prove that he's one of the most interesting and versatile actors working today. Every time you think you know what to expect from him, he switches it up. In *Mickey 17*, he brings something completely new to the table yet again. It's not just a great performance-it's a reminder of how far he's come and how much range he has.
Watching Pattinson in this role is like watching someone completely in their element. He's not afraid to be weird, funny, emotional, or completely out there-and somehow he balances it all without ever feeling forced. There's a sense of playfulness in his acting here that's so rare to see in big films. He seems to have a deep understanding of the kind of movie he's in, and he leans into it fully, making the entire experience more engaging and fun to watch.
What makes it even more impressive is how natural he is with the tone of the film. *Mickey 17* shifts between comedy, drama, and subtle moments of emotion, and Pattinson moves through all of it effortlessly. That kind of balance is hard to pull off, but he makes it look easy. He carries the movie with a kind of quiet confidence that keeps your attention from beginning to end.
This film also reminds us just how fearless he is as an actor. He's not chasing safe roles or typical leading man parts-he's choosing projects that challenge him, that offer something different. Whether it's an indie drama, a gritty thriller, or a surreal sci-fi movie like this, he throws himself into every character fully. It's exciting to watch, and it's exactly what keeps him so compelling.
Aside from Pattinson himself, the movie as a whole just feels like a breath of fresh air. It's quirky without trying too hard, clever without being overly complicated, and confident in its own weirdness. It doesn't follow trends-it makes its own. That kind of bold creative energy is something we don't get enough of, and it's what makes *Mickey 17* such a standout experience.
It's also worth saying how nice it is to watch a film that trusts its audience. It doesn't spoon-feed anything or over-explain. It just puts you into this world and lets you enjoy the ride. That confidence, paired with Pattinson's layered performance, makes for a film that sticks with you.
At the end of the day, *Mickey 17* is more than just another movie-it's proof that originality still has a place in big cinema. And more than that, it's a showcase for Robert Pattinson's incredible talent. He's not just a good actor-he's a great one, and this film is another reminder of just how much he can do.
If you're looking for something that feels fresh and different, *Mickey 17* is 100% worth your time. And if you're already a fan of Pattinson, this will only make you respect him more.

Instead, what I got was a movie that feels like it was assembled from the spare parts of better sci-fi stories. The premise is intriguing: a disposable human clone sent on deadly missions, only to be regenerated after each death. But instead of diving into the emotional or ethical weight of that, the movie just... coasts.
The pacing drags, the characters (including Mickey himself) feel undercooked, and despite all the futuristic tech, the world-building somehow feels small. The attempts at humor fall flat more often than not, and by the third act, I found myself rooting for Mickey to stay dead-permanently.
Visually, it has moments. But if you're looking for thoughtful sci-fi, this one's all flash and no depth. A disappointing clone of a movie that had so much potential.
4/10 stars. Watch something else and spare yourself the existential crisis of wasting 2 hours.

author: Wanaja
title: A semi-interesting sci-fi, an uninspired social satire
text:
The premise is interesting but gets a bit sidelined by competing thematic threads and a muddled narrative, resulting in an unfocused film. Watching it in early 2025, the real-life political parallels, especially, draw too much focus. I wondered throughout how much was specifically meant to be a satire of current events and how much was just casually referencing them. I read that this was filmed in 2022-2023, so perhaps the timing of its release makes the parallels seem more pertinent. That it's so heavy-handed and cartoonish doesn't help - it kind of reminded me of the ridiculous escalation of Don't Look Up, which also felt very pandering. It also slightly overshadows the other interesting themes of the film - the ethics of human cloning, colonisation, worker oppression, class society, personal and social identity, and overcoming trauma - which are somewhat disparate threads and a lot to deal with on their own. Sadly, none of them are fully explored.
Robert Pattinson was excellent and really commits to the role - I especially liked what he did with his voice and accent. The relationship dynamic between Mickey and Nasha is interesting to follow, although it feels a bit inconsistent at times. The creature design was ok and adds a touch of originality to the film, even though the heavy CGI doesn't really do it for me. Steven Yeun was underutilised, while we see too much of Mark Ruffalo and Toni Colette (I can't help but wonder whether they decided to include more of them while editing with everything that's happened since the US presidential election). The pacing feels a bit off with it taking a long time for things to start moving and then making it hard to tell what the main events are and what the film is building towards. There is one romantic subplot (if you can even call it that) that could have easily been edited out.
It's definitely more Okja than Parasite, and I was hoping for a more interesting and refined follow up. I feel like 7 is being generous, but I'll give that final point for originality.

author: PlushieCinemaBuddies
title: Mickey 17 - A Dazzling, Thought-Provoking Sci-Fi Masterpiece
text:
Mickey 17 is nothing short of a sci-fi triumph. Directed by the brilliant Bong Joon-ho, this film seamlessly blends cutting-edge visuals, a gripping narrative, and thought-provoking themes into a truly unforgettable experience. Based on Edward Ashton's novel Mickey 7, it takes viewers on a wild ride that explores the nature of identity, humanity, and the ethical dilemmas posed by technology-particularly through the lens of cloning.
The premise is both fascinating and deeply unsettling: Mickey Barnes (Robert Pattinson), a member of a team tasked with colonizing a harsh alien planet, is repeatedly sent on the most dangerous missions, only to die and be resurrected in a new body with most of his memories intact. While this seems like an advantage at first, the psychological toll it takes on Mickey is explored with surprising depth, raising important questions about what it means to be human and the morality of treating life and death as mere plot points.
Pattinson delivers a powerhouse performance, capturing the internal conflict of a man who is constantly reborn but slowly losing his sense of self. His portrayal of Mickey is nothing short of mesmerizing, showcasing a nuanced portrayal of existential crisis, vulnerability, and resilience. The supporting cast, including Naomi Ackie, Mark Ruffalo, and Toni Collette, all bring a unique energy that enhances the film, whether through moments of dark humor or sheer emotional depth. Each actor plays a pivotal role in making the world feel rich and alive.
Visually, Mickey 17 is a masterpiece. The special effects are stunning, especially in terms of creating the alien planet Niflheim-an unforgiving and beautiful world that feels alive in every frame. Bong Joon-ho's direction excels in balancing tension, humor, and philosophical depth, keeping the audience engaged while exploring complex issues. The pacing is tight, ensuring that every scene is purposeful and drives the story forward.
The film also cleverly mixes moments of dark comedy with serious social commentary, particularly in its critique of corporate greed and exploitation. It's a theme that feels timely and relevant, but Bong manages to explore it with a fresh perspective, making it more than just a typical sci-fi trope. The satire never feels forced, instead blending seamlessly into the narrative and adding to its emotional and intellectual impact.
Though there are a few moments where the film could have gone deeper into some of its philosophical concepts, and some characters might have benefited from a bit more development, Mickey 17 is an incredibly satisfying film that punches above its weight in both entertainment and substance. It's a rare blend of action, humor, and existential pondering that will leave audiences thinking long after the credits roll.
Final Thoughts: Mickey 17 is an exceptional sci-fi epic that delivers on multiple fronts. It's visually stunning, narratively ambitious, and emotionally resonant. While some may find its tone a bit unpredictable, those who are open to its blend of dark humor, social critique, and deep philosophical inquiry will find themselves captivated. A must-see for anyone who appreciates bold, innovative cinema, this film is destined to be remembered as one of the standout sci-fi films of the decade.

author: ebayman-69397
title: Interesting premise devolves and disappoints
text:
Mickey 17 opens with a compelling and original concept: a "disposable" clone who dies repeatedly in service to a colonization mission, only to be resurrected each time with his memories intact. It's the kind of premise sci-fi dreams are made of-one that begs for philosophical depth, emotional introspection, and social critique. For a moment, it seems like the film might deliver.
But instead of embracing its rich narrative possibilities, Mickey 17 quickly abandons its own premise in favor of a shallow and heavy-handed political allegory. The film trades existential questions for lazy comparisons to real-world political movements-most notably MAGA populism-which are not only clumsy but often fallacious. The story's futuristic setting feels awkwardly grafted onto 21st-century talking points, as if the filmmakers didn't trust the power of their own story and had to fall back on moral grandstanding to make a point.
To make matters worse, almost no character in Mickey 17 is likable or even remotely redeemable. The Mickeys are different, but each is frustratingly stagnant. Supporting characters are either cold, arrogant, or one-dimensional. There's little in the way of emotional growth, meaningful relationships, or genuine transformation. The result is a film populated by people who seem designed more to represent ideas than to feel real or relatable. As viewers, we're left with no one to root for, no one to care about, and ultimately no reason to stay invested.
That lack of character development might have been forgiven if the film had followed through on its high-concept promise. But instead, the script sidesteps the deeper ethical dilemmas of clone labor, the psychological horror of disposable humanity, and the hierarchy between originals and copies. These rich themes are introduced only to be abandoned in favor of on-the-nose political messaging and surface-level plot mechanics.
Mickey 17 had the raw material to become a sci-fi classic, but it wastes that potential on hollow allegory and unearned moralizing. In the end, it doesn't trust its audience-or its own story-enough to aim for anything more than ideological signaling wrapped in a futuristic aesthetic.

author: kareems-00
title: VERY HUGE potential that is horribly wasted
text:
Big budget, amazing cast, and a truly fruitful idea-sounds like the recipe for something unique and powerful. And to be fair, Mickey 17 starts off strong. But as the story unfolds, every bit of potential the movie opens up gets wasted-and I'll tell you how, and why it hurt to watch.

The movie kicks off with real promise. The buildup is great-seeing Mickey die, feeling his pain and fear. There's this raw, organic wave of emotion. But not only does no one try to understand his suffering, they treat it like a joke-like he's just a lab rat.

Wasted Potential #1 & #2: First, Mickey's repeated deaths start off impactful, but very quickly become "normal"-and not in the good, thought-provoking way. The movie could have explored how Mickey acts like it's normal, but deep down it's breaking him. They teased that idea, but never committed.

Second, the scientists. There was a massive opportunity here to show their dark, cold detachment from humanity-villainous, but still very human in their drive for progress. We could've seen inner conflict, guilt, rationalization. Maybe one of them forms a connection with Mickey. But instead, they're treated like disposable side characters with zero soul or relevance. Wasted.

Wasted Potential #3: Mickey's backstory-his decision to take on the mission-is weak. It leads nowhere. But then they hit us with something deeper: a childhood memory where he feels responsible for his mother's death. That had real emotional weight. That could've been a thread tying all his pain and acceptance of death together. But it was abandoned completely.

Wasted Potential #4: Timo-great actor, poorly written role. He could have been a real emotional anchor for Mickey. A friend. A brother. Someone who mattered. Instead, he's barely part of the story, and when he is, it feels shallow.

Wasted Potential #5 & #6: The clone consciousness dilemma... this should've been the heart of the movie. It's such a rich concept-identity, mortality, the soul. They touch on it when Mickey meets his clone, but it's rushed and undercooked.

The backstory about clone multiplication becoming a crime? Brilliant. Dark, realistic, and one of the few flawless moments. But they don't build on it. They stop at Clone 18, when they could've dived deep into identity fragmentation, conflicting personalities, and existential horror.

And yes, some clones had different personalities-that could've been gold. Exploring how copies deviate, how traits change, how they aren't really the same person. It's such a huge narrative playground... but again, wasted.

Wasted Potential #7: Kai-kind-hearted, in love with him, the only one who seems to care about his endless suffering. She could've been the moral compass of the film, the emotional thread pulling Mickey out of numbness. She had the power to shape his choices, to give meaning to his pain. But the film does almost nothing with her.

Wasted Potential #8: Nasha... honestly, I didn't even understand why she loved him so much. I was expecting some deeper reveal-like maybe she was planted in his life to stabilize him or keep him sane. That would've made sense and worked so well with the tone the movie was setting up. But instead, we got a weird, unnecessary love triangle that added nothing and took away from what the story could have been.

It's just frustrating. This wasn't a bad idea, or a bad cast, or even a bad setup. It just needed a different approach-one that actually followed through with its themes, characters, and emotional core.

I want this movie. I want this cast. I want this idea.

But I want it done differently. This could've easily been an Oscar-worthy masterpiece.

author: mattdamonlover69
text:
What a great day for lovers of Robert Pattinson and Bong Joon Ho! One-of-a-kind movie! Weirdly existential, weirdly funny, weirdly weird. And that's the point. You're tossed into a world that shouldn't make sense, and yet it does, because the film knows how to guide you through its madness. The humour isn't an afterthought; it's integrated into the script perfectly. Even the serious bits have a kind of dry, wink-at-the-camera undertone that keeps things from ever taking themselves too seriously. A perfect satire!
Now, why did this work so well? One word: Direction. Let's be real. With Bong Joon Ho at the helm, expectations were high. But somehow, he still overdelivered! This guy doesn't just make movies, he curates experiences. Wonderful ones at that! This movie so brilliantly balances comedy with plot that through the laughs you can grasp the intellectual points it presents. You can feel Joon Ho's fingerprints in every frame, from the tonal shifts that feel like genre-jumps to the absurdist dialogue that somehow still lands with emotional weight. Right down to Rob Pattinson tripping on a staircase!
Technically? Stunning. The cinematography is sleek but intimate, with an aesthetic truly sci-fi. It's textured, atmospheric, occasionally claustrophobic, but never visually overwhelming. And the music? Class!! But not in the way you'd expect. It's deep. Too deep, almost. There's this elegant, emotional undercurrent in the score that totally contrasts the film's comedic top layer. That depth gives the satire weight, it's like you're laughing, but also wondering if you're supposed to be sad. The dramatic classical alongside the rest of the sound really gives this film a lot more than you'd expect.
As for the script; it's sharp and witty in the most offbeat way. Dialogue that bounces between philosophical musings and absolute nonsense, which honestly makes it feel more human than most "realistic" sci-fi films. And the background details? Insanely peculiar. They didn't just worldbuild, they built a cult. You could probably watch it three times and still catch new absurd little things in the margins. From the backstory of the macaron store to the sauce jokes, hilaaaarious details.
It's satire, but like... satire that actually works. Not just haha-funny, but big time funny. A perfect satire, I'd say, one that laughs at itself, its genre, its audience, and somehow still feels like it has heart.
Now, the only reason it's not a full 9+ for me? The ending. Not bad, just... slightly undercooked. Compared to the rest of the movie, which was dancing circles around expectations, the final stretch felt like it took the safer route. Wrapped up a bit too neatly. Like the film had so much fun playing, but then remembered it had to clean up before the credits rolled. Still satisfying, just not as bold as the setup deserved. Absurd, but alright, nothing special.
8.8/10.
Would 100% rewatch and still laugh at the exact same scenes. Also, someone called this movie a romcom, which (alongside the sheer uniqueness of the plot, which I will never shut up about) boosted the rating by about 0.3 because I absolutely agree.

author: enderozd
title: A Missed Opportunity That Left Me Disappointed
text:
When I first saw the poster for Mickey 17, I was instantly sold. "This is it," I thought-a film with a lead character being copied, a premise brimming with endless possibilities. My mind buzzed with anticipation: a story that could explore identity, morality, and the human condition in wildly inventive ways. But after watching the movie, I was floored-and not in a good way. The harsh reality hit me: my own imagination had conjured up something far more entertaining than what the film delivered. To me, it feels like the filmmakers took a golden opportunity and pushed it away with both hands. Add to that the bizarre portrayals of characters by Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette, and you've got a recipe for a letdown that stings more than I'd like to admit.
A Promising Premise That Falls Flat
The concept of Mickey 17 is a filmmaker's dream. A character who can be duplicated? That's a narrative goldmine. I pictured a movie where each copy could wrestle with its own purpose, where the boundaries between original and replica dissolve into a gripping psychological maze. Maybe the lead would confront his duplicates in a battle of wills, or perhaps the story would spiral into a haunting meditation on what it means to be human. The possibilities felt infinite. Yet, what I got was a film that played it safe, sticking to a predictable, almost mundane storyline. Instead of diving into the deep end of creativity, it wades in the shallows, offering little more than a surface-level plot that left me wanting. It's frustrating because the foundation was there-they just didn't build anything remarkable on it.
A Wasted Chance for Cinematic Greatness
What really gets under my skin is the
overwhelming sense of a missed opportunity. This could have been a playground for bold, innovative storytelling-a chance to push boundaries and leave audiences talking for years. Instead, Mickey 17 feels like it's content to coast by on its intriguing premise without ever taking a risk. It's as if the filmmakers had a blank canvas and a box of vibrant paints but chose to sketch a stick figure in pencil. There are moments that hint at something bigger-brief flashes of potential-but they're quickly swept aside for a formulaic approach that feels more like a checklist than a vision. I couldn't shake the feeling that I'd been promised an adventure and handed a pamphlet instead.
Ruffalo and Collette: Talent Oddly Misplaced
Then there's the matter of Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette, two actors I admire immensely. I went in expecting performances that would elevate the film, given their track records. But their characters? Utterly strange and out of sync. Ruffalo's role feels like a jumble of eccentricities that never quite gel into something meaningful-like he's trying to play a caricature but isn't sure why. Collette's character is marginally better, but even her talent can't rescue a part that seems detached from the story's heart. It's as if the script didn't know what to do with them, leaving these powerhouse performers stranded in roles that lack depth or relevance. For actors of their caliber, it's a baffling misstep that only amplifies the film's shortcomings.
Final Thoughts: A Dream Unfulfilled
In the end, Mickey 17 is a film that hooked me with its promise but lost me with its execution. My excitement from that first glance at the poster has been replaced by a lingering disappointment, a sense that what I'd dreamed up in my head outshone the reality on screen. It's not a total disaster-there are glimmers of what could have been-but it's nowhere near the bold, thought-provoking experience I'd hoped for. I can't help but wonder what might have happened if the filmmakers had taken a chance, fleshed out those intriguing copies, and given Ruffalo and Collette characters worthy of their skills. As it stands, Mickey 17 is a reminder that even the best ideas need vision to soar-and this one barely gets off the ground.

author: CinemaClown
title: Not As Incisive As Bong Joon-Ho's Best Films
text:
From the writer-director of Snowpiercer & Okja comes his third English-language feature film, a biting social critique of our increasingly dehumanising world that's sidelining ethics, morality & compassion for profit & exploitation yet lacking the incisive quality of his best-known efforts. Led by a committed showcase from Robert Pattinson, Mickey 17 is fun, amusing & entertaining but far from memorable.
Written & directed by Bong Joon-ho (Memories of Murder & Parasite), the story follows a man's odyssey through death & rebirth as a disposable worker who gets cloned every time he dies for research purposes. Bong's ability to juggle several genre elements at once & sudden tonal shifts makes this sci-fi comedy an enjoyable ride with a fascinating concept but the picture is lacking in execution and isn't as neatly structured.
The story is at its most gripping when exploring the cloning idea & its implications but loses its tenacity when indulging in other aspects. The futuristic setting, sharp camerawork, impressive visual effects & fab performances help keep the interest alive but the long-winded narration & diminished satire undermine its impact. Pattinson is arresting throughout and aptly articulates the wide spectrum of emotions his character(s) goes through.
Overall, Mickey 17 is skilfully crafted & finely layered but it tries to do too many things at once instead of focusing on a singular subplot & deeply examining it. My expectation going into the film weren't high considering that Bong's Hollywood projects are rather weak compared to his Korean productions but I still hoped to be surprised. Arguably the weakest entry in his filmography, Bong's latest is still worth viewing for Pattinson's playful act alone.

author: isocano
title: Comedy Overshadows Everything Else
text:
A relatively plausible sci-fi world set in the not-too-distant future sets up a dystopia that quickly lays down a few foundation pieces for a story with clear potential... which it blatantly chooses not to explore, instead focusing on a style of humor that doesn't quite land-or at least, not for me.
The production value is solid. Nothing groundbreaking, but it works: spaceships, creatures, blood... It's not the film's strength, but it doesn't detract either.
A particularly wasted opportunity lies in how it handles death. Many films fail by refusing to kill off characters, but when you have the perfect excuse to do so, you need to capitalize on it. Here, it's barely touched on. While a couple of deaths are creative, they mostly feel like trailer bait.
The cast is fine, but I don't think any of them were given the script or direction needed to truly shine, especially considering the levels they've reached in other works.
All in all, I walked away a bit disappointed. It's an entertaining film with a few interesting ideas, but the bad aftertaste and humor that doesn't match my taste keep it at a soft six out of ten.

text:

author: KompetenterMedic
title: Not quite eternal, but still entertaining
text:
Mickey 17 is a visually compelling and thematically intriguing film that doesn't quite live up to the lofty expectations that come with the name Bong Joon Ho. While there are flashes of brilliance and plenty to enjoy, the final result lands somewhere between engaging and slightly underwhelming-particularly for those anticipating another genre-defining masterpiece.

Robert Pattinson once again proves his incredible range as an actor. His performance as Mickey is layered, subtle, and deeply compelling. He brings a quiet intensity to the role, managing to balance the existential weight of his character's situation with moments of dry humor and vulnerability. Pattinson's ability to portray emotional depth with minimal dialogue makes him the absolute centerpiece of the film, anchoring the story even when other elements falter.

On the flip side, Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette turn in performances that are hard to love-but in the best way possible. Their characters are aggressively unlikeable, and both actors lean into that discomfort with impressive commitment. It's a credit to the writing and their performances that they are so effective in being grating and unsettling, serving as excellent foils to Pattinson's more grounded and humane presence.

The costume design is one of the film's strongest and clearest visual storytellers. Every wardrobe choice is loaded with meaning. From her meticulously maintained nails to his sharp, intentional piercing, each detail helps build the world and reflect the characters' priorities and status. These seemingly small touches help paint a larger picture of vanity, control, and rebellion within this dystopian setting. The makeup department deserves equal praise-every character's look is carefully crafted to align with their inner psychology. Whether it's subtle skin blemishes, aged eyes, or pristine, polished perfection, the makeup work ensures each character's design supports who they are at their core.

Visually, the film is beautiful. There are several scenes and compositions that would be right at home in a sci-fi artbook. However, while the aesthetic is strong, the cinematography doesn't quite match the ambition of Bong Joon Ho's earlier works. Instead of the dynamic and inventive camera movements seen in films like Parasite or Snowpiercer, Mickey 17 feels more observational. The camera often seems content to simply document the action, rather than actively participate in the storytelling. As a result, it lacks the immersive, artful quality that fans have come to expect from Bong's direction.

The score also leaves something to be desired. While it's serviceable and never distracts, it doesn't elevate the film or carve out an identity of its own. For a director known for marrying sound and image with precision, this aspect feels surprisingly muted.

All in all, Mickey 17 is an okay film-certainly not bad, and in many ways enjoyable-but perhaps a little disappointing given the pedigree behind it. It's a fun and sometimes thought-provoking ride, bolstered by excellent performances and strong design elements. However, it never fully breaks through into the realm of greatness. If anything, it might suffer most from the burden of expectation. Still, for sci-fi fans and admirers of Pattinson's work, there's enough here to make the journey worthwhile.

author: evanston_dad
title: Surprisingly Dour and Un-Entertaining
text:
Even when I don't love Bong Joon Ho's movies (though I have loved most of them), I usually find them energetic and lively. So disappointing, then, to find that "Mickey 17" is such a dour slog. This movie isn't fun at all, and any commentary it makes on our current world is cartoonish and heavy-handed, and has already been said anyway, even in other Bong Joon Ho movies.
Robert Pattinson gives a valiant performance in the title role, but he's undermined by the execution. Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette, normally terrific actors, are saddled with the villain roles in this movie, and Ruffalo especially is directed to give an appalling performance that damn near ruins the entire thing.
What maybe would have felt like exaggerated satire of the world as we know it at some other period in time just feels too much like the way the world actually is, and who needs that for entertainment?
Grade: C+

author: SweetDanger69
title: Mickey 17: Wild Weird and Worth It
text:
Alright, Mickey 17 is a total blast from Bong Joon Ho, a sci-fi flick that's equal parts funny, weird, and out there. Robert Pattinson is Mickey, this unlucky dude who keeps dying and getting reprinted as a disposable colonist on a frozen planet called Niflheim. He's a riot, flipping between Mickey 17 and his surprise twin Mickey 18 with this goofy charm that totally steals the show. The whole setups wild, imagine waking up as a new you every time you bite it, but still kinda remembering the mess you left behind.

Naomi Ackies awesome as Nasha, Mickeys tough but sweet girlfriend, while Mark Ruffalo hams it up as the colony's smug big shot, Kenneth. Toni Collettes in there too, being her usual quirky self as Kenneth's wife, and its a vibe. The planet looks dope, super snowy with these freaky little critters called creepers that are honestly kinda cute but also a little creepy. Bongs got his classic mix of dark laughs and big ideas, though sometimes it feels like hes yelling "colonialism bad" a bit too loud.

Its not perfect, the starts kinda slow with a lot of setup, and the end goes full bonkers in a way that's almost too much. Plus, its a tad long, and some side stuff doesn't really go anywhere. But man, its never boring. Pattinson keeps you glued, and the whole things got this oddball energy that's just fun. It's not Parasite level tight, but if you're into weird sci-fi or Bongs style, Mickey 17s a good time. Definitely worth catching on the big screen!

author: simmans
title: Rinse, Repeat
text:
So, Bong made Snowpiercer again, and he spliced Okja into it.

That's the whole thing.

The people in charge get the best sauce, and the people down below are fed a strict ration of mystery proteins. Winter and class struggles! Tilda Swinton wasn't available, so there's Toni Collette.

Actually, it's Toni's husband, Mark Ruffalo in the true Tilda role -- as a fascist clown caricature -- and he even wears Tilda's bizarre Snowpiercer teeth!

The social commentary is so ham-handed that Snowpiercer looks subtle in retrospect. At some point Mark even shouts about breeding a "white, pure" colony, even though his diverse crew would certainly feed him to the Creepers for suggesting that (?).

Steve Yeun plays an absolute dirtbag, a villain, but when he survives the conclusion, it's presented as a hero moment.

Bong just thinks differently, I guess.

Sure, it's all played for absurdist comedy, but the myriad plot conveniences are one too many, even for a film like this.

"Hey, we just built a translator to talk to these mysterious Creepers. Why not try it out? It'll probably help save the day!"

Later on comes a "clever" twist, when we find out the Creepers were bluffing about a specific defense strategy. Problem is, they made the bluff to exactly one guy, who in no way appeared to be in charge of the attack. (Good thing he had that prototype translator box, though.) After making their bluff/threat, to that one ineffectual person, the Creepers began yodeling and screaming, thereby assuring he was unable to pass on the bluff/threat up the chain anyway.

At the happy end, when the "good" colonizers share the land with the Creepers, the Creepers freely admit that their bluff was just that. (Instead of, you know, keeping that card close to the chest, just in case.) But it doesn't matter anyway, 'cause they only told the one guy, and he's an imbecile.

Also, there are two characters named Mickey, but it hardly seems to matter.

Sadly, this movie was pretty good until the halfway mark. Ho hum.

author: anraelnow
title: Mickey 17 A Masterclass in Cinematic Futility
text:
"Mickey 17" is a film that manages the improbable feat of being both interminably long and utterly forgettable. What could have been an exploration of ambitious sci-fi concepts devolves into a tedious, poorly constructed slog, marred by inept execution and a staggering lack of vision.
Acting: A Void of Emotion
The performances here are so lifeless they border on parody. The lead actor delivers lines with all the enthusiasm of a placeholder reading a grocery list, their emotional range confined to variations of blank stares. Supporting cast members fare no better, reciting dialogue with the robotic cadence of actors who either disowned the material or were directed to prioritize monotony over nuance. Even the most pivotal scenes-ostensibly charged with tension or drama-feel like rehearsals for a high school play, devoid of stakes or authenticity.
Plot: A Nonsensical Chore
The narrative is a labyrinth of half-baked ideas, strung together with neither coherence nor purpose. What begins as a vague attempt at existential sci-fi quickly unravels into a meandering mess, punctuated by plot holes so vast they swallow any semblance of logic. Themes of identity and sacrifice are hinted at but never explored, leaving the audience to wonder if the screenplay was assembled via a game of Mad Libs. The film's "twists" elicit less shock than bewilderment, as if the writers themselves lost interest mid-draft.
Production: Aesthetic Bankruptcy
The film's cheapness is palpable. Sets resemble recycled plastic dioramas, CGI effects evoke early-2000s screensaver graphics, and costumes look scavenged from a discount Halloween store. The cinematography compounds these flaws, relying on murky lighting and repetitive framing to mask budgetary constraints. Even the score feels like a stock library track, looping ad nauseam to remind viewers that yes, they're still watching.
Pacing: A Test of Endurance
At a glacial runtime of over two hours, Mickey 17 transforms cinema into a form of passive punishment. Scenes drag interminably, with dialogue that circles nothing and action sequences devoid of tension. The editing seems allergic to momentum, lingering on inconsequential details while glossing over moments that might-in a competently made film-warrant emotional investment. By the third act, the theater feels less like a venue and more like a purgatory.
Conclusion: A Pointless Exercise
Mickey 17 is a film without purpose. It offers no insights, evokes no emotions, and leaves no impression beyond regret for the time squandered. Its existence feels less like a creative endeavor and more like a contractual obligation, a hollow product churned out with cynical indifference. For those seeking a cinematic experience, look elsewhere; this is a sinking ship masquerading as art.
Verdict:
Avoid at all costs. Mickey 17 isn't just bad-it's an affront to the very idea of storytelling.

author: gamegamer-12329
title: Funny and Stupid
text:
Bong Joon-ho once again delivers a cinematic gem with Mickey 17, a film that brilliantly fuses science fiction, dark humor, and existential tragedy into an unforgettable experience.

At its core, Mickey 17 is a deeply philosophical take on cloning and identity, exploring what it means to be "expendable" in a futuristic society where human life can be easily replaced. The film follows Mickey Barnes, played by the ever-versatile Robert Pattinson, a man assigned the dangerous task of being an "expendable" worker on the icy colony of Niflheim. Every time he dies, a clone replaces him, complete with the memories of his previous self-leading to an increasingly surreal and tragic cycle of self-awareness, rebellion, and darkly comedic existential dread.

author: MaxWhy
title: Sci-Fi or Slapstick Disaster? The Wasted Potential of Mickey 17
text:
The plot of Mickey 17 had so much potential but ultimately fell flat. The premise is fantastic: a guy who dies and is reborn, opening up endless possibilities for creative storytelling. You'd expect to see him die in hilarious ways, encounter various aliens, and constantly put himself in interesting dangers. The trailer made it seem like these aspects would be explored. It's a concept reminiscent of Groundhog Day, which is a great foundation for a movie. However, the film fails to deliver on this promise. Despite its intriguing premise, it leads to a disappointing conclusion, resulting in a lackluster story.

The film had a very powerful premise in the beginning, one that was profound and made you think about the meaning of life. But then, it turned into a complete joke, just for laughs. The main character (Mickey 17) became increasingly dumber, and it shifted into a slapstick comedy. It's disappointing for sci-fi fans because the movie had so much potential with its great premise. Instead, it devolved into a stupid slapstick comedy with some sexual jokes that felt meh. True sci-fi fans would agree that this type of movie was just nonsense. We were left thinking, "What the hell did I just watch?" It made no sense, and they wasted the potential. They could have made a cool story with interesting characters and aliens, but instead, we got this dumb politician couple who were terrible at acting-clearly cartoonish characters that weren't realistic at all.

Yes, the story began quite well, with Mickey narrating his own life in a way that was both funny and thought-provoking. He met a woman and ended up in a situation that led him back to the base, where he encountered a doppelgänger of himself. From that point, the plot became increasingly ridiculous and made less and less sense. There wasn't enough humor to make it solely a comedy, but as a sci-fi fantasy movie, it turned into a disaster. The plot got thinner rather than thicker, and the characters became ridiculous people that made no sense. I found myself wondering what was going on and when it would end. It was a mess.

Lastly, Mark Ruffalo's impression of Trump in his character as the politician was obvious. You could tell he was trying to mock Trump, with the way he held his mouth and tried to talk like him. He made him seem completely crazy, stupid, full of himself, and a liar. You could tell Ruffalo hated the person he was impersonating. But that's when impressions fail-if you're just mocking someone, it's not a good impression. You're not actually embodying them; you're just making fun of them, like, "I'm so stupid." A real impression should capture the person, meaning you have to think like them and try to be them. Ruffalo's character was awful. It felt like he was just mocking someone rather than playing a character with his own thoughts, and that ruined the performance.

author: benferns411
title: Save your time!
text: Mickey 17 ultimately proves to be a disappointing cinematic experience. The narrative felt disjointed, struggling to weave its various threads into a cohesive whole. The central premise of an alien threat also lacked any real conviction, particularly as the supposed extraterrestrial danger clearly presented as benign. Unfortunately, the attempts at humour fell flat, consistently delivering bland jokes devoid of any discernible punchlines. Furthermore, the backstory provided for the protagonist, Mickey, felt tired and cliché, offering little in the way of originality. This film represents a significant missed opportunity; despite visually appealing set design, there was a distinct lack of character investment and emotional connection to the unfolding events. Ultimately, on the strength of its weak narrative and unengaging characters, Mickey 17 is not a film I would recommend.

author: annadens
title: Awesome Concept...That Was Immediately Tossed Aside to Focus on Mocking Trump Instead
text:
I was super excited for this movie because the concept was so great. But then, the concept that is so original (reprinting a human so that they can use the human for jobs that would kill him) gets thrown away basically the moment the movie starts and then becomes a movie with nothing that original about it at all. You don't really see his deaths, and even those aren't consistent, with large gaps in the storyline/background of the Expendables. Like for one, people keep asking him what death is like, but they only update his memory once a week so he wouldn't ever even REMEMBER the deaths...though for some reason he seems to remember every single one. Then, though each Mickey has the same memories, suddenly Mickey 18 is totally different. He talks differently, stands differently, thinks differently. In fact, the only thing they have in common is they look alike. I'm sorry, but if I died today and they reprinted me next week with today's memories, I would be the exact same person I was today, not suddenly a serial killer. Then, the movie just turned into the cliché "Aliens vs the Indigenous...well, rolly polly bugs that have human level intelligence." I've seen that movie a million times, but never have I seen one with the concept of the Expendables. Also...is he the only expendable? Because I don't see any others...

Then there's the villain...so one dimensional with no character arc. Instead of giving him any story or personality, they just basically did a Saturday Night Live Skit-Level Acting version of Trump. I usually ADORE Mark Ruffalo, but if you're going to pretend to be Trump, at least do it well enough that I believe it. Instead, I saw all the acting because Mark Ruffalo wasn't taking his character seriously. Instead, he was mocking his own character, which goes against everything you learn even as early as Acting 101 (become the character, don't phone it in). I usually love Toni Collette too but, again, I didn't believe her character for half a second and, again, the acting was more on the level of SNL and not something an actual actress, versus a comedian, should ever be doing.

Robert Pattinson's accent was super annoying as well, and, again, which is a theme in this movie, I saw the acting...or attempt at it. It did have good parts, but the ongoing slaughtering of Mark Ruffalo, and the huge plot holes, were so distracting that they kept pulling me back out of the movie. It became totally expected, especially today, instead of what I thought I was going to see: something novel and fresh and new. Also, there was no chemistry between Robert Pattinson and Naomi Ackle. It didn't help that their relationship was just thrown in there without actually really making their on-screen relationship build up. That's everything that was missing, from Mickey 1 to Mickey 17... And the whole part thrown in there with Kai felt totally contrived. Maybe if they had spent half the movie actually building the world and characters (and sticking to the concept that was why everyone went to see it rather than trashing it 10 seconds into the movie), it would have been better. But they would rather spend all their time just mocking Trump. I don't care if you like him or hate him. It's not about that. It's about the fact that basing an entire movie on that is really uncreative and, again, it wasn't even done well. I shouldn't see the attempt to be Trump. It should be done so well that I believe that person IS Trump. That they think Trump is the greatest, most badass person to ever exist. That they agree with everything he does or thinks (since every person thinks of this about themselves). Maybe if they'd paid more attention to something beyond dissing Trump, they would have noticed all the massive plot holes and lack of storytelling. Because if they hadn't done all the things I listed above, this would have been a 10 out of 10 movie. They certainly had the concept for that. Instead they threw it away just to make fun of Trump.

author: irusvirus
title: "Expendable" - A Sci-Fi Adventure with a Creative Twist
text:
Mickey, a young guy drowning in debt, sees only one way out-signing up as an "Expendable" for an intergalactic expedition. The job? Taking on deadly tasks that no one else wants to risk, from exposure to lethal gases to testing how much galactic radiation the human body can withstand. The catch? When an Expendable dies, they can simply be reprinted, making them essentially immortal.
The first half of the movie is a fun, darkly humorous ride that keeps you entertained with its clever premise and witty execution. However, as the film progresses, the pacing starts to drag, and the excitement fades. By the final stretch, it feels like it overstays its welcome, making you wish the editors had trimmed at least 30 to 40 minutes.
Visually, the film is stunning, and the concept is fresh and unique. It's definitely a movie that sticks with you, not necessarily for its gripping storytelling but for its creative world-building and thought-provoking ideas. Overall, it's worth watching, but the pacing issues hold it back from being truly great. Final verdict: 6/10.

author: ddangtruong23
title: There's Zero Stakes Whatsoever
text:
I'm amazed at how this movie manages to throw so many ideas at the wall, yet none of them stick.
First, the main character has no personality beyond being pathetic, and by the end, he hasn't grown in any meaningful way. He has nothing to live for, nothing to fight for, and as a result, it's impossible to care about what happens to him.
Second, the threat facing humanity is never clearly defined. The expedition has no real purpose, making it hard to care whether they succeed or fail.
Third, the villains never feel like real threats. They're shallow caricatures, not even compelling enough to hate. Their plans are so unremarkable that you simply stop caring.
After two hours, you walk out of the theater struggling to remember anything significant, despite the movie's constant attempts to shake things up.
It feels like the first draft of a script. Maybe they should have rewritten it 17 times.

author: introducer
title: When a good idea turns into a movie for the pop-corn audience
text:
As an avid admirer of the film "Parasite", I entered the cinema with high expectations, hopeful that-if not a masterpiece-I would at least witness a meaningful and well-crafted two-hour cinematic experience.
Unfortunately, my disappointment was considerable. The film's opening was highly promising and refreshingly original, yet at a certain point, it completely lost focus on the very narrative and thematic elements that initially captured the viewer's attention. It felt as though two entirely different creative teams had worked on the project: the first appeared committed to delivering something distinctive, thought-provoking, and innovative; the second, however, seemed to abandon that vision entirely, resorting instead to formulaic, banal, and overly simplistic American storytelling-suitable for a fourth-grader who had just spent their last pocket money on a movie ticket and popcorn.

author: nERDbOX_Dave
title: A promising Sci-Fi film that opts for a slow death into Political allegory.
text:
Bong Joon-ho's Mickey 17, initially promising a thrilling sci-fi narrative, quickly reveals itself to be a heavy-handed political allegory. If you walk into this film expecting a pure escape into a distant, frozen world, prepare for a jarring and, for some, deeply frustrating experience.
The initial setup is intriguing: a disposable "Expendable" colonist, Mickey Barnes, on a dangerous mission to terraform a frozen world. The concept of repeated deaths and rebirths, each "Mickey" retaining memories of the previous iterations, creates a compelling sense of existential dread. However, the film's second half abandons this intriguing premise in favor of a thinly veiled commentary on contemporary political issues.
While Mark Ruffalo delivers a brilliant, if unsubtle, rendition of a certain political figure, the film's relentless focus on its political agenda becomes increasingly tiresome. The dialogue, often laden with thinly disguised political rhetoric, feels less like organic storytelling and more like a soapbox sermon. For those seeking cinematic escapism, this shift is a significant detriment.
The initial hook of the film's first half, with its exploration of identity and mortality, is unfortunately squandered. By the time the credits rolled, I found myself checking my watch, a clear sign that the film had lost its grip on my attention.

author: jorgesosadiaz
title: What does it feel like to die?
text:
Are we always the same, or do we change? What defines our identity?

There lies the paradox-if we don't change, we can't evolve, but if we change completely, we cease to be ourselves.

"Knowing you'll be replicated the next day takes away the fear of death, doesn't it, Mickey?"

"I'm always afraid. No matter how many deaths I go through, the fear never goes away."

Every day we die when we close our eyes, only to be replicated the next day as if nothing happened.

Every day we go through grueling and painful trials to make way for a new Mickey the next day. And yet, the fear of death remains...

We never stop being ourselves, but our story shapes us. Every Mickey that wakes up each new day is slightly different from the one before.

If we met a previous Mickey-a younger version of ourselves-we might be surprised. Some wouldn't even recognize themselves at first.

Does it make any sense to be continuously replaceable, at the mercy of the harsh tests reality throws at us?

Maybe the answer lies in that part of us that never changes and always stays with us.

So... what does it feel like to die?

Tell me tomorrow when you wake up.

author: jonathanr-67660
title: Bong Joon Ho does it again
text:
Mickey 17 was my most anticipated movie of 2025, and for good reason. It's directed by the South Korean legend Bong Joon Ho, who also made Parasite and Snowpiercer. It also looked very interesting and had Robert Pattinson as the protagonist, who had already starred in Tenet and The Batman just a few years back so I knew I was in for a treat. Unsurprisingly, this movie did live up to my expectations and could very well be my favorite film of the year.

Mickey 17 is about a man named Mickey Barnes who joins a space program as an expendable after Earth has become so corrupted. This film is set 30 years in the future (at the time of writing this) and features advanced technology that doesn't exist yet, like human printing machines. As an expendable, the organizers conduct different experiments on him to see how they affect the human body and a new Mickey is reprinted after the old one dies. However, when the 17th Mickey is presumed dead after falling into a cave full of mysterious creatures called creepers that are believed to be dangerous. The creepers turn out to be friendly creatures and save Mickey's life, but by the time he gets back to the ship, they have already printed a new Mickey and he has to learn to deal with his clone on the spaceship.

I really liked the idea behind this film and was invested as soon as I saw the trailer for it. I was hoping the movie would focus more on the deaths of the Mickey clones but the story it tells is equally interesting and didn't disappoint me at all. There's so much to like about this film. First off, it explores themes that are present in Bong Joon Ho's other films, such as capitalism, social inequality, and mystery, and combines them all gracefully. There are bits of comedy added in too and the movie is funny exactly when it needs to be. Second, the cast members really put their all into their performances. Robert Pattinson is fantastic here. I love how he manipulates his voice for this role which is something I did not know he was capable of. I liked him as the lead character, or characters, cause there's two of him on screen for much of the film. Naomi Ackie also gave a great performance as Mickey's girlfriend Nasha and Mark Ruffalo was fantastic as the villain as well. Back to story telling, the movie does it so cleverly. We learn that the Creepers are friendly creatures when they save Mickey's life, and later on when the Mickeys are sent out to destroy them, which they don't want to, they learn to communicate with the creepers and find out that they must return their baby in order to prevent the humans from being killed and the way it does that is totally unexpected. I also liked how the movie allows us to connect with both Mickeys, and shows that even clones can have different personalities. And when Mickey 18 sacrifices himself at the end to save everyone on the ship, its a very heartbreaking scene because the audience is really attached to him as much as with 17.

Overall, Mickey 17 is a film I can highly recommend to people. While I don't think its as good as Parasite, its still a fantastic movie from Bong Joon Ho you should check out sometime soon. I'm really glad I got to see this in theaters because it was a wonderful experience from beginning to end.

author: wqnqrzkf
title: Such a bad movie
text: Mickey 17, directed by Bong Joon-ho, is a significant letdown, failing on multiple fronts. The film's narrative is disjointed and lacks coherence, making it difficult for audiences to engage with the story. Despite Robert Pattinson's efforts in portraying the titular character, the screenplay provides him with little substance, resulting in a performance that feels hollow and unconvincing. The supporting cast, including Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette, are given underdeveloped roles that do not allow their talents to shine. Visually, while the film attempts to present a dystopian sci-fi setting, it falls short of creating a compelling or immersive environment. The overemphasis on heavy-handed political satire overshadows the plot, leading to a viewing experience that is more tedious than thought-provoking. Overall, Mickey 17 is a disappointing endeavor that lacks the depth, engagement, and execution expected from a filmmaker of Bong Joon-ho's caliber.

author: boblipton
title: "What Is It About?" Does Not Have A Simple Answer
text:
Robert Pattinson is Mickey. He has to get off Earth fast, so he signs up for a colonizing expedition to a planet called Nifleheim. And because he has no skills, he volunteers to be an expendable: when you need someone to do something that might result in their death, you use him. And, with technology that has been banned on Earth and is in very limited use in colonies, he is, as they say, reprinted, with all his memories. This has happened 16 times, and he's very tired of people asking him what it's like to die. It looks like death #17 for him, as he has been trapped in an ice cavern filled with the giant hairy pillbugs that seem to be the largest native life form. He's abandoned, but the creatures don't eat him. Instead, they roll him out, back to where the colonists have set up, and he makes his way back in. Only to find there's another copy of him. Which is illegal.
There's a lot more going on, and it's good that director Bong Joon Ho has enough respect for his audience that he has borrowed several subplots from Edward Ashton's novel, Mickey 7. There's a love affair with Naomie Ackie which has him constantly puzzled, there's the questions of whether the hairy pillbugs are worthy of our respect, and there's a lot of religious and political cult satire, as Mark Ruffalo goes outside his star persona to play a stupid politician who's in charge of the expedition, and Toni Collette Ruffalo's equally deranged wife.
Several scenes hint at a far greater psychological complexity in the novel that are unexplored, but that's certainly all right. Movies are more about what people do than what they think. However, there will certainly be a tendency to reduce the movie's complexity to one or two points: that it's against, say, imperialism, full stop. Or it's against the cult of personality, full stop. Or it's for a more expansive definition of humanity, full stop. Just because science fiction, like other non-mimetic fiction, can be used to reduce the issues under discussion to their essentials does not mean you can't talk about more than one thing at a time. And this movie does.

author: edgamu
title: Multipass 17
text:
I went to the theater with high expectations of seeing the amazing new sci-fi film from the director of Parasite. In the end, I was left with the classic feeling of "it started well but ended badly."

The film starts like Star Wars, no seriously. It begins with a scene from The Empire Strikes Back, except the friend steals the blaster instead of saving the protagonist getting him into the bowels of a tauntaun. Minutes later, you feel like you're watching a Terry Gilliam film, with that absurd and comical postmodernism of Brazil or 12 Monkeys. Later, you feel like you're watching The 5th Element with the ridiculous chaos created by Mark Ruffalo's pathetic villain (by the way, what a waste to have Toni Collete in the cast for such a ridiculous role), and in the end, we once again feel like we're in the Star Wars saga, but in the bad part, in one of the sequel films by JJ Abrahams and Rian Johnson.

Robert Pattinson is a good actor, but he fails to take advantage of the opportunity of multiple roles.

The best thing about the film in my opinion: Anamaria Vartolomei.

author: nnqdwxdr
title: A slightly flawed instant classic, I guess?
text:
I saw Parasites, which left me curious for more from Bong Joon Ho. I heard - and forgot - that there's a new one, then saw the poster, which to me spelled Ion Tichy, the time-craze story, but I didn't pursue this, or any, thought. When I got up, and out, and into the movie, I was only half aware that I didn't even know what to expect. I go to the movies when any place seems to matter more than the one I feel I'm in. Habit forming, obviously.
So, bar any expectation, I saw a movie, that channeled little big emotions in a way that pulled me along, mostly. An amazing Robert Pattinson brought as much Jim Carrey to the party, as you can have, without having Jim Carrey. In over his head, it felt so good to not be him! Who can' relate. Also, betrayal never fails to move me. The innocent fool, often asked on the one subject, where he should be the only living expert in the room, he can't even aspire to an opinion.
Early on, a truly worthy lady to take his hand and never let go again? The fantasy! Each of us should have experienced this, if only as an illusion - it's formative. And been left wanting, for cinema's sake. This makes it, at least, a guys' movie. What else? Toni Collette brought effortlessly, what my old favorite Mark Ruffalo only desperately wrestled with this time. My secret favorites were the reproduction scientists. I wanted them to suffer until I didn't. Try and find another comment even mentioning them: uncomfortable, I'd venture, but I'm out on a limb. The extraterrestrials-element owes to Starship Troopers, also in a good way. Even Mickey introduced a fleeting, if unlikely notion of Caspar Van Dien at times. My half-realized skepticism died under a thousand little cuts - I almost never really got enough, but never really got too little. A 7.x rating marks a solid, likely watchable movie. For an 8 I want to see something I haven't seen before. And I feel that I have, though I don't really know what it was. My major criticism is, that the movie never made me cry, and you'd have to know me to understand the gravity of this observation. I feel that you may not really like this movie, but I can't imagine anyone regretting the experience (my fault, don't blame me if you do).

author: abbyw-20145
title: Choosing a life that truly belongs to you.
text:
The movie Mickey 17 makes me feel like we finally have a serious science fiction film again. It presents a thought-provoking vision of the future, where humanity faces limited resources and must learn to coexist with alien life.
I found the storyline to be intricate and well-crafted. When Mickey 18 appeared, it became clear that the film was not just about survival but also about identity and self-discovery. It reminded me that, in the face of challenges, we must embrace who we truly are rather than simply conforming to expectations. Mickey 17 offers a deep reflection on existence, making it a compelling and meaningful cinematic experience.

author: Shad0uille
title: Great Potential, Missed Opportunities
text:
Mickey 17 is a film full of potential that intrigues with its original concept and polished direction. Robert Pattinson delivers a convincing performance, and Bong Joon-ho brings his unique touch that's felt in every scene. However, it's hard not to feel that some scenes could have been shot differently to better capture the universe and dramatic intensity. The film sometimes leaves a sense of missed opportunity, as if its full potential wasn't entirely realized.
That being said, it's still a good film that's worth watching, especially for sci-fi enthusiasts and fans of Bong Joon-ho's work...

author: FinbarrReynolds22
title: Disappointed despite Pattinson's Performance
text:
Mickey 17 had all the ingredients for something special. Bong Joon-ho at the helm, a stellar cast, and a fascinating premise ripe for exploring deep sci-fi themes. Coming off the back of Parasite, Bong's direction remains excellent, but the script is shockingly tired and derivative, bogged down by tired heavy-handed US political messaging that derails what could have been a thought-provoking film.
Robert Pattinson delivers a fantastic performance as Mickey, and while the film starts somewhat slowly, it builds intrigue and momentum. Just as it seems to be hitting its stride, however, Mark Ruffalo takes centre stage, delivering an over-the-top and painfully on-the-nose impression of Donald Trump that is so exaggerated it would make a room full of American late-night TV hosts cringe. What begins as an exploration of identity, space colonisation, and the ethics of cloning quickly descends into something about Trump and animal cruelty (Okja 2?).
I had high hopes for Mickey 17, but I honestly can't remember the last time I left a theatre feeling this disappointed.

author: livjehle
title: Well-Made, but Why?
text:
Well-produced, but the story is bizarre. Disturbing scenes and unsettling content throughout.
The first half of the film felt rather slow-paced, and the ending was somewhat predictable. Contemporary themes are addressed and examined through an ethical lens. Still, by the end, it remained unclear what the film's overarching message or goal was meant to be. Political figures are woven into the narrative, adding another layer of interpretation. Many topics are touched upon, and much is said-yet after the credits roll, your thoughts linger on the bizarre scenes, leaving you wondering who could have come up with such a plot. It was entertaining, though.

author: amigothelover
title: Power built on the suffering of others will fall sooner or later, like an echo in the night.
text:
Robert Pattinson is indeed a handsome man, a genetically gifted individual, and on top of that, he is a good actor.
The film's runtime feels stretched; it starts off lively and intriguing, but in its second half, it becomes dull and cliched, with the narrative pace losing momentum. The work is partly a parody, or so it seems to me, a parody of how those in power manage the fates of all living beings based solely on their interests and boundless ambitions, disregarding any sense of morality or ethical standards.
I enjoyed the good and light humor that runs throughout the film. I happily observed Robert Pattinson's acting, as he managed to portray the different personalities of the clones while creating a funny duo from them. Mark Ruffalo, in turn, did an excellent job as the antagonist.
In the end, the film turned out to be decent, especially considering the current state of cinema and its genre. I feel disappointed that there are so few good films in the sci-fi genre, and those that do come out often do not receive the attention they deserve. I can recommend it to sci-fi enthusiasts to watch at least for Edward, even without Bella.
7 out of 10.

author: natalieanneforman
title: Notes from an Infrequent Reviewer
text:
I don't normally write reviews because I think the only real way someone will know if they like something or not is if they experience it themselves! Also, I only see about two or three movies a year so it's a pretty rare occurrence for me. But, I have to share that I absolutely loved this movie. I saw it last weekend and five days later am still thinking about it. Everything about Mickey17 was well done and wonderfully executed. The story was so emotional and engaging. I'm a baby so cried a lot in the latter half. The actors, especially Robert Pattinson and Naomi Ackie, were incredible. RP as Mickey gave him this vulnerability and sadness that made me want to climb through the screen and comfort him, and protect him.
It was just a smart, thought-provoking film and I'm glad it was made and that I got to watch it. I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys sci-fi, or speculative fiction.

Mickey 17, on March 17, my birthday, really surprised me.

Bong Joon Ho, the director of 'Parasite' (2019), adapted Edward Ashton's 2022 science-fiction novel 'Mickey7' by writing the screenplay and directing the film.
