author: imdbfan-9148940254
title: I was let down.
text:
I'll cut straight to the chase and say it - I was a little bit disappointed with this film.

When I first heard that Bong Joon-ho, an Oscar-winning director, was releasing a new film, I was incredibly excited and interested! Some of his best films, Parasite as well as Snowpiercer, are known for their unique storylines, gripping social commentaries, and stunning cinematography. Because of this, I expected Mickey-17 to offer something just as profound and emotionally impactful. And for a while, it felt like it was on track to do exactly that.

Mickey-17 had some strong aspects going for it, particularly in its first half. Adapted from Edward Ashton's novel Mickey7, the film has a unique sci-fi concept. The story follows Mickey Barnes, an "expendable" clone assigned to a dangerous off-world colonization mission. Each time he dies, his memories are transferred into a newly printed body, allowing him to be repeatedly sacrificed for the survival of the crew. His role is essential to humanity's efforts to establish a settlement on this newly discovered alien planet. This was a concept that was intriguing and full of potential. After hearing about it, I was excited and was expecting the film to dive deep into existential questions and themes of spirituality.

Visually, the film was stunning and lived up to its hype. Bong Joon-ho has always had a great eye for cinematography, and that talent is evident in this film as well. The shots of the alien world were breathtaking, and I especially loved how the camera moved along with the aliens, making it feel like you are there with them. The alien creatures themselves were another highlight; they were well-designed and convincingly fit into the film's world. They were also just eerie enough to add a sense of mystery and intrigue to the setting.

Another undeniable standout was Robert Pattinson's acting performance. He brought depth to Mickey-17 and displayed the emotions the character was going through perfectly. Any emotional disconnect I felt at the end of the film wasn't due to Robert Pattinson's acting but rather the writing and overall storytelling. He fully embodied the character, delivering a convincing and nuanced performance despite the film's shortcomings.

For the first half of the film, I was convinced that Mickey 17 had the potential to be Oscar-worthy. It was bold, intriguing, and very unique. I felt like I was really being drawn to Mickey's story and immersed in this new world - it was great! Unfortunately, the second half took a sharp downward turn, and that's where the problems began to outweigh the film's strengths.

One of the biggest issues was that the film tried to cram in too much. Towards the middle, the story became a bit convoluted, to the point where I found myself getting lost in its many concepts. The introduction of Mickey-18, in particular, felt rushed and poorly handled. I felt that there wasn't enough build-up to his character, making his death lack any real emotional weight. What could have been a powerful and devastating moment instead felt like a small plot point that the film hurried through without giving it the necessary impact.

Another major issue was the film's dialogue and translation. Some of the voices sounded strangely artificial and robotic, making them feel less convincing. I could tell that they used AI to translate some of the characters, but it ended up making them sound soulless. Even the script for the English-speaking characters felt unnatural at times. This took away from the film's emotional depth and made it difficult to connect with the characters on a more human level.

Mickey-17 had a strong concept, but it never fully delivered on the deeper themes it hinted at. I feel like the film tried a bit too hard to be funny at times. For example, Marshall's overly large teeth and exaggerated way of speaking often undermined his more intense moments, making it difficult to take him seriously. It also felt like the filmmakers were trying a little too hard to model him after a certain well-known American politician in 2025 (you know exactly who I mean), which made the character feel less original. While some comedic moments landed, others disrupted the tone, making it difficult to stay fully invested in the story. As a result, the film struggled to maintain its impact and ultimately fell short of its potential.

Some plot points also felt a bit clichéd. While Mickey-17 had a unique general idea, certain elements were captured in a way that felt predictable and uninspired. For example, the second half of the film revolves around fighting the Creepers and returning the baby to save the humans; a plotline that completely overtakes the story and disconnects from the more intriguing setup in the first half. It also ended in a cliché way that could be easily predicted from the start - there was really nothing unique about it. Snowpiercer, for example, delivered a sharp social critique within a bold, unconventional setting, whereas Mickey-17 seemed to play it safe by the end, missing the chance to be truly daring.

All of these issues ultimately made the film a frustrating experience. It had all the ingredients for greatness; a talented director, a fascinating concept, an incredible lead actor, and stunning visuals - but it just couldn't hold everything together. The first half of the film gave me hope that it would be one of the best sci-fi movies in recent years, but by the time the credits rolled, I was left feeling underwhelmed and disappointed.

That being said, I wouldn't call Mickey-17 a terrible film. There are still aspects that some audiences may appreciate, especially its lighter tone and impressive visuals. But for those like me who were hoping for something with the same narrative strength as Parasite or the social depth of Snowpiercer, this one falls a bit short. I really wanted to love this movie, but instead, I walked away feeling like it was a missed opportunity.

author: rmadson-67124
title: Is cute the right word?
text:
I Left The theatre blown away by Robert Pattinson's performance as Mickey Barnes. This movie really does have a little bit of everything for everyone. It's not a perfect movie but it's very solid. Solid story, solid soundtrack, solid acting, solid creatures. The social commentary is very spot on and hilarious, and you can really feel that Mark Ruffalo had a fantastic time. His mocking bleeds through the screen, making every scene with him in it that much more enjoyable.
I LOVED the Creepers especially, I want one of my own.
Robert Pattinson's performance was really stand out as Mickey Barnes, and I think every character had their place and that was a good feeling to see. Some plot points felt a little out there but given that it was a sci-fi movie I'm not going to scrutinize it.
The ending felt a little rushed, more of a "Let's sweep this all up so that we can wrap things up with a nice bow on top" type feeling. Though I was rooting for a happy ending, this isn't the ending I really was hoping for.
Overall, a very solid sci-fi movie about environmentalism ripe full with social commentary.

author: mikelavery
title: Seriously what on earth
text:
Just bizarre and one of the worst films I've ever seen. I just watched "Mickey 17" and I'm still trying to process the mess that is this film. Director Bong Joon-ho's latest effort had all the ingredients for a thought-provoking sci-fi epic, but it falls flat due to its overly ambitious scope and poor pacing
The film's themes of colonization, corporate greed, and humanity's relationship with technology are timely and relevant, but they're handled with all the subtlety of a sledgehammer. The satire is heavy-handed, and the film's attempts at social commentary come across as forced and didactic
The supporting cast, including Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette, are wasted in underwritten roles. Ruffalo's character, in particular, is a cartoonish villain with no depth or nuance.
Overall, "Mickey 17" feels like a misfire from a talented director. It's a shame, because with some tighter editing and a more focused narrative, this could have been a truly memorable film. As it stands, it's a messy, overlong disappointment.

author: nickhaertel
title: Multiple Prints
text:
Seems like this movie was pieced together as many times as Mickey was.
Great performances by the cast, but that couldn't save the many different directions this movie forced itself to get pulled into. How many times did I think to myself: "Ok, that's fine. I was looking forward to seeing how this last direction went, but I think this new one could also be good."
Over so many iterations, the equation ended up becoming weirder and weirder and thus failing more and more. At the end, my friends and I were left wondering what in the world happened and why didn't they stick to where the movie was headed to at the beginning.

author: masonfisk
title: A MILD RECOMMEND...!
text: Oscar winner Bong Joon Ho's (Parasite/Mother) latest currently playing in theaters. The titular character, played by Robert Pattinson, is actually the 17th iteration of a clone (we're in the future & clones are used for exploration & experimentation) & he has hit a quandary when his masters think he has bitten the dust on a planet after coming in contact w/some indigenous creatures & a new clone, the 18th, has been spewed. Heading back to base, Pattinson encounters his new self, who has been sleeping w/his girl, Naomi Ackie (from Blink Twice), & is more of a go-getter than he is since he's more outwardly hostile to the powers that be. Into this quandary is a husband/wife team of expatriated politicos, played by Oscar nominees Mark Ruffalo & Toni Collette, hoping to rule the new planet they're colonizing, under the guise the company they're working for of course, while Pattinson's old running buddy, Oscar nominee Steven Yeun, has his own agenda. While definitely being of a piece w/Ho's work (you can't help but think of the swath of different people populating the train in Snowpiercer, the supposed evils of ecology in Okja), the film, based on Edward Ashton's novel, is very scattershot in its targeting of politics, the environment & the us vs. Them caste system where I found myself shifting in my chair whenever a new tone occurred which after a while wore me out but if you can stick w/the not so smooth transitions from one idea to another, then you'll have a good time in the old theater.

author: nekrashevich
title: Don't waste your time, please

It just leaves you staring at the screen, wondering why you bothered sitting through it. No, really, it was the first movie I couldn't keep watching and had to reach for my phone right in the cinema.
The film is a chaotic mess. Scenes change with no direction, yet nothing intrersting happens. There's no tension, no emotional pull, no moments of brilliance-just a disjointed collection of ideas that go absolutely nowhere.
And no, this isn't some misunderstood work of genius that demands multiple rewatches to grasp. It's not deep-it's just bad. This is 220 minutes of ocean deep boredom.
Please, don't waste your time.

author: yManu_
title: My interpretation of Mickey 17 - SPOILERS AHEAD
text:
My interpretation of Mickey 17

(SPOILERS AHEAD)

For me, the film is an analogy for extremist churches. Mickey represents a homeless person, or someone without family, drowning in debt, who joins the church just to have a place to stay.

Being the "expendable," he accepts anything - any job they offer - just to keep his place.

Just like others in the community, people may not like the President of the company (or the Pastor, in this analogy), but they stay not because of faith in him, but because of faith in a better world.

Regarding the characters, the Pastor, during the dinner scene, asks Kai - who represents a devoted follower - if she would serve as a reproducer, almost as if he wanted to become the new God of this planet, using her as an "Eve" without actually caring about her.

The creatures that save Mickey symbolize those outside the church's bubble - people that the church hates, hurts, and spreads lies about to make their own version of the story seem like the only truth.

Mickey 18 is the dark side of Mickey 17, the "sinner," the one who sees things as they really are and refuses to cover up the Pastor's horrible actions.

Nasha, on the other hand, is the soldier of the settlement - someone hired to protect, but not necessarily to agree with everything happening there. That's why she didn't hesitate to help Mickey when the time came.

There are moments when the Pastor/President almost says "church" instead of "company," as if "company" is just a mask for his true intentions. He uses prayers and devotion to distract people from the terrible things he does. The way I saw it, his message was: "Everything in the name of God, as long as I am God."

The movie is really good. Some parts are a bit intense - not exactly scary, but if you pay attention, you start noticing these deeper meanings. It goes beyond just being a weird and crazy film - it carries a heavier, double-layered message.

author: enzomura
title: Best enjoyed without thinking too much
text:
Overall, Mickey 17 is an entertaining film, but as soon as you start looking into the world and how it works, everything falls apart.

The film's messages about feminism, animal rights, disabilities, social classes, religion, colonialism, and ecology are welcome in fiction, but perhaps not all at once in under 2 hours and 20 minutes. References to these themes or current events in press are hammered into our heads with the subtlety of an elephant.

So many scenes lead nowhere, and so many questions remain unanswered:
All the characters are one-dimensional, with no nuance. The villain is always evil in every possible way, and the naive protagonist remains naive and good-hearted throughout.


The subplot about Mickey's friend, the dealer, and his ongoing issues with a creditor from Earth serves no purpose. You could remove this entire arc, and the story would remain unchanged. The same applies to the new world's drug-it has no real basis and creates no meaningful twists or impact on the main story.


Why is Nasha suddenly the new president of Nilfheim at the end? The colonists/pioneers are shown as pro-Marshall throughout the film.


Kai is completely useless for the story's development or the main characters.


Why does Mickey 18 have a different personality compared to the others?


Why do they remember the lives of the previous Mickeys who died, even though no consciousness backups were made?


(- Maybe it's a reference I missed, but why is consciousness literally stored in a brick?)

author: Man0Manit0
title: Mickey 17 (2024) - Sci-Fi with a Unique Identity
text:
Mickey 17 is an intriguing film with a very particular style, directed by Bong Joon-ho and starring Robert Pattinson. The story follows Mickey Barnes, a man who is virtually invisible to human society, as he finds an opportunity to give his life some meaning by taking on a peculiar job: being a Disposable, an immortal guinea pig.

His job is to take on extremely dangerous missions on a hostile planet, as every time he dies, his consciousness and memories are transferred to a new body printed by the Human Printing Machine. However, when Mickey 17 survives an encounter with the mysterious native worms on the planet, while his copy Mickey 18 has already been printed, the film takes an intriguing turn as it explores the relationship between both clones and their existential conflict.

Robert Pattinson delivers an impeccable performance, capturing the vulnerability and sarcasm of his character. Mark Ruffalo, playing the incompetent captain of the mission, brings an interesting presence that slightly resembles Dr. Evil from Austin Powers. The film's tone perfectly blends seriousness with satire, something typical of Bong Joon-ho.

On a technical level, the cinematography is outstanding, with impressive visual direction and well-executed effects. Although the story isn't entirely groundbreaking and draws on references from other sci-fi works, it manages to stand out with its unique approach and engaging narrative.

In conclusion, Mickey 17 is a well-directed sci-fi film with an intriguing story and standout performances. It's not revolutionary, but it is a solid and entertaining proposition.

Rating: 8/10.

author: dngoldman
title: A disturbing but entertaining film
text: This film manages to be both disturbing and entertaining. It transcends its premise, which is well-worn about replicants who are used to doing our dirty work. This is achieved through humor and a visceral portrayal of how quickly we dehumanize replicants when it suits our needs. The fact that the native creatures appear grotesque allows us to believe that they mean us harm. However, the film isn't simplistic. The native bugs are not pacifists because they won't stop once they've had revenge, in addition to restitution. The selfish Mickey 18 is needed, but so is the more gentle Mickey 17. The film asks hard questions about how we understand ourselves and value others. This film is strange and will not be for everyone. And it does feel long. But it has stuck with me.

author: Troyforever
title: A Good Sci-Fi Movie to Pass the Time
text:

Even though the story doesn't initially seem very serious, it quietly exposes humanity's ignorance and how we frequently ignore the consequences in order to further our own goals. The film has more depth than it first seems because of this underlying theme.
With a variety of breathtaking visuals, Mickey 17 is a good sci-fi movie to kill time. Any sci-fi fan will enjoy watching it because it's entertaining without being overly heavy.

author: Blimplarg
title: Tongue in cheek, but thought provoking too.
text:
I think I enjoyed this (I know that sounds odd, but read on). This is a good, thought provoking film, fun and, to an extent, tongue in cheek, I'm still mulling it over which I think, indicates that this is a film that, beneath its surface, challenges a bit.
Whilst this is a science fiction film, there's a lot to it. It's a decent conceit - the story is effective and asked a lot of questions about morals and how society operates. There are also, clearly (and not at all subtle) parallels with some of the political issues (and personalities) facing society today. As well as the political, there are environmental and societal questions posed too.
The cast are excellent. All the lead characters are well played, with Pattinson his usual, excellent and quirky self. The film is well written and directed. The special effects also work well.
I suppose my one criticism is that the film drags slightly and sometimes loses its way. I can also see that it's not everybody's cup of tea. Having said that, definitely worth a view.

author: SuperJabbot
title: A good follow up from Bong Joon Ho
text:

The dual role for Robert Pattinson was executed smoothly, with you being able to tell both characters apart due to great editing and acting performances.
However, being able to tell these characters apart also poses as a downside - as many questions are left unanswered when it comes to how each variation has different personalities.
Multiple jokes landed pretty smoothly - and the cinematography crossed nicely with the lighting and sound to make an overall enjoyable experience.

author: Monomono9
title: A strong sense of spiritual impact.
text: Mickey 17 uses bizarre storytelling to show how technology messes with our humanity-it turns life's fragility and uncertainty into controlled loops. What seems like a tech miracle giving Mickey 'rebirth freedom' actually traps him deeper in identity crises. This battle between tech and human nature exposes the core conflict: chasing immortality just handcuffs our freedom. The movie argues that within tech's rigid systems, true meaning comes from accepting life's impermanence and pushing back-mirroring Buddhism's idea that everything's temporary and interconnected. Like how meaning isn't pre-packaged but randomly formed, real freedom comes from shaping ur present, not chasing fake 'forever' promises. Ultimately, the movie tells us to let go of fixating on identity and feel existence's raw & ever-changing flow.

author: gcsman
title: A gonzo sf outing
text:
Director Bong Joon Ho has risen rapidly to the top rank, particularly because of the award winning 'Parasite' (2019). For 'Mickey 17', which has a very different tone, imagine a gonzo mashup of 'Fifth Element' (1997), 'Avatar' (2009), and 'Starship Troopers' (1997) and you'll get some idea of what it's like. The single central idea is a good sf one, i.e. What are the possible consequences of human cloning. Here it's called 'reprinting' -- upon the human subject's death (here it's Mickey, played by Robert Pattinson), he is not resurrected in a literal sense but his newly reprinted body has his previous memories downloaded intact into it. Whether than means he's actually the same person plunges you into a sticky ethical and moral debate. Is it OK to use Mickey essentially as a lab rat to explore the conditions on an unknown planet (Niflheim) and get killed over and over? By a rather fun accident, the 17th incarnation of Mickey didn't actually get killed by his encounter with the resident aliens (who look like giant pillbugs; the babies are actually rather cute) and when he makes his way back to base he finds version #18 of himself has already been made. Oops. That mix generates the rest of the plot.
It all has a rough, dystopian feel to it, which is common enough these days. I'd welcome a change. On top of the experiences of the main character there is in-your-face social satire centered on entrepeneur Kenneth Marshall (Mark Ruffalo) and his controlling wife (Toni Collette). Marshall acts like a seedy carnival barker with Trump-like mannerisms and dreams of grandeur (not much of a stretch there). His delusions eventually lead where you might expect, but there are numerous twists and turns that keep things unpredictable.
Pattinson is really good as Mickey, and he plays the two versions of himself with drastically different personalities, which is interesting in itself. It's the best acting I've seen him do (and I thought he was good in 'Tenet'). Naomi Ackie has a good supporting role but could have been given a more fully developed character.

author: twocents2
title: Solid Filmmaking
text:
I snuck into this film on the lowest attended weekend of the year, worse than the Super Bowl and Oscar lows. I walked into a vast 250 seat theater containing nine people, all Asian. The lights were on while producer's credit was on the screen. Somebody finally found an employee to address this. It had Korean subtitles, which was annoying.
The film was pretty good. Mickey (Robert Pattinson)'s friend Timo (Steven Yuen) convinces him to invest in macaron manufacturing. Both go broke and owe loan shark Darius. Fortunately, they get selected to leave Earth for outer space, specifically planet Nilfheim. Failed politician Marshall (Mark Ruffalo) is the entrepreneur who created this, a Trump like figure. The departure terminal looks like the Guggenheim Museum, which is very cool. Timo gets to be a pilot with a mere learner's permit credential. Mickey becomes an expendable, a guinea pig who keeps dying and reprinted for another adventure. His memories live on a brick hard drive. He instantly forms a relationship with security agent Nisha (Naomi Ackie). Mickey the 17th falls through ice, breaking his suit. A pack of Creepers (caterpillar/cockroach) descend upon him, but do not harm him. The mother Creeper even drags him back to the surface and releases him. But by the time he gets back to the ship, he's been presumed dead and M18 has been printed. Duplicates are illegal, so they try to kill each other. A baby Creeper is brought on board, a big mistake. Marshall's wife Ilfa (Toni Collette) cuts off its tail to make a sauce. Peace is finally achieved.
Pattinson was very good. His cartoonish accent with shades of Brooklyn grew on me. Ackie was fine. Ruffalo and Collette were crazy over the top magnetic. Yuen is barely even necessary. Film is about 15 minutes too long, but I was rarely bored. I guess the Creepers are analogous to the Dune sandworms. It was all quite a spectacle and the studio will lose money on this. But Oscar winning directors like Bong Joon Ho don't grow on trees and must be indulged for future opportunities. Romanian Artamaria Vartolomei was very sexy as Kai Katz. It was a good experience, but this is not an instant classic by any means.

author: danchilton-71955
title: Its Guys Like You Mickey
text:
The title character of Mickey 17 is the 17th iteration of Mickey Barnes, a failed entrepreneur played by Robert Pattinson who has fled Earth (and a particularly unpleasant loan shark) by signing up to be an "expendable" on a voyage to colonise a new planet. This means he takes on all the most dangerous jobs and simply has his personality and memories uploaded to a newly printed body upon his inevitable death. By the time we meet him, lying at the bottom of a frozen ravine waiting to die, the four year space journey is over and and the ship's inhabitance are trying to get a foothold on the frozen hellscape of planet Niflheim. The first portion of the film sees Mickey recount the events that led to him being in such a situation, fleeing Earth after the collapse of his and dubious best friend Steven Yuen's macaron business, beeing manipulated into becoming an expendable, his relationship with security officer Nasha (Naomi Ackie) and the deaths of many of the proceeding Mickeys. The story then picks up with 17 returning to the ship to discover that, him being presumed dead, another Mickey has been printed. This is a bit of problem since the rules state that in the case of "multiples" both individuals are to be erased.

Mickey 17 has a lot going on. A lot. This is not director Bong Joon-Ho in the intricate sketching mode of Parasite, this is him cashing in his Oscar chips on a bold, big brush strokes sci fi concept movie. He makes the most of the budget with a grimy, industrial future setting and an atmospherically chilly alien world. If you are looking to liken things to the directors previous work, we are in the ballpark of "Snowpiercer" and "Okja", although this has more strings than either. The mixture of brutal space survival, high concepts and mad cap comedy gives notes of cult sci fi show "Red Dwarf" and we even get a long panning shot of the ship exterior.

The clone idea is the heart of the film and it asks interesting questions about accountability and cheapening of life. While some films treat cloning as a form of immortality, it is made clear here that death is death and shared memories don't make up for that. Mickey 18 is a very different person to the number before him. With that in mind, the whole endeavour becomes fairly horrific and the blasé attitude to Mickey's various lives from other crew members is chilling. That director and cast are able to keep the laughs coming in such a bleak scenario is testament to the talent on display.

While the clones provide plenty of thematic material, there are other concepts on show that could be whole films of their own. This is a first contact movie with some not so positive or subtle ideas on colonialism and groovy alien lifeforms. Its a satire of cult politicians, there fanatic followers and shadowy corporate backers, with Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette putting in unhinged performances as religion espousing failed congressman (yes his supporters do wear red) Kenneth Marshall and his controlling, culinary obsessed wife Ylfa. There is also plenty of the biting class commentary you expect from a Bong Joon-Ho movie. The denizens of the ship eat mush and have calorie limits, they aren't even supposed to have sex as it wastes energy, but are assured it will all lead to a life of plenty eventually. Meanwhile the Marshall's fine dine and dream of creating new sauces to prove their civility. Mickey himself is literally printed from the ship's recycled crap.

Pattinson's off kilter performance completely captures the blend of grim futurism and absurd comedy. The only thing more ridiculous than his haircut is his accent (which he tried to convince his non native English speaking director was a regular Pittsburgh drawl), as Mickey 17 stammers his way through one horrendous task after another. Then 18 arrives and is a different kettle of fish all together, aggressive almost to the point of being deranged, he wants to burn the whole thing down. For vocal inspiration Pattinson says he drew on wacky 90s cartoon "Ren and Stimpy" and that is a good indication of the vibe on display. Ackie is also great and her Nasha is more than just Mickey's love interest, she is his possessive protector and the more we learn about their relationship the more real it feels. It's this grounding relationship that allows some of the other cast to go completely off the deep end with their performances and not alienate the audience.

It may be tempting to label Mickey 17 as overstuffed or claim Joon-Ho has bitten off more than he can chew but it is more accurate to say he has bitten off exactly the amount he can chew and is asking the audience to digest it with him. The film is certainly packed to the brim but surely that's to be lauded, not lambasted. It will be a long before we see another sci fi thinker given this kind of big budget shine.

9 genetically pure colonies out of 10.

author: foreverfrantic
title: Robert Pattinson shines, once again
text:
WB did this film a disservice, first with the delays, and then with its horrendous marketing. Despite the trailer for Mickey 17 trying to appeal to the general audience by making it seem like the film was full of slapstick comedy by highlighting Robert Pattinson's physical acting with quirky music as the backdrop, it most certainly isn't that. In fact, Pattinson hands in what may be his best work to date - which is saying something, with fantastic performances in Good Time, The Lighthouse, and his voice work in The Boy and the Heron, already under his belt. Indeed, he continues to prove that he's up to whatever challenge he's presented with as an actor.

Tasked with playing dual roles, Robert does so, seemingly with ease. Mickeys 17 and 18 are vastly different from one another. Just as the 16 iterations before them. Mickey 17 is weak, timid, and down on his luck; 18 is the more assertive (and aggressive) version. Yet, as his love interest Nasha - played by a delightfully spunky Naomi Ackie - says, "They're all my Mickey."

As such, there are many themes that director Bong Joon Ho addresses in this film. Whether it be the psychological implications of survivor's guilt, or the idea of identity and the "shadow self"; to those in the poltical and socioeconomic realm, such as environmentalism, capitalism, and classism; to religious fanaticism, free will, and the moral and ethical complexities of cloning. All of this is seen through a satirical lens.

This is evidenced by the not-so-subtle references to Donald Trump in the guise of Mark Ruffalo, who clearly uses Trump as a reference point to portray his character, the failed politician, Kenneth Marshall. Everything from his mannerisms and movements, to his tone of voice is decidedly Trump. While Toni Collette hands in a zany performance as Marshall's wife, Ylfa, Ruffalo's performance gives credence to the adage, "You are what you hate", which the actor has certainly made abundantly and annoyingly clear any chance he gets. It's no coincidence then, that I'm no fan of the character, nor his inspiration. Even so, let there be no misconceptions. The film is not about Trump, at all.

At its heart, Mickey 17 is a story about acceptance and love; both of yourself and others. Whether that be your fellow man, like Mickey's (in his mind) best friend - the irritating, douchey, self-important Timo, played by Steven Yeun - or your fellow Creeper - the insectoid natives of the planet Niflheim, that Kenneth Marshall seeks to colonize. As Director Bong correctly stated, the Creepers are shaped like croissants of varying sizes. I actually found the baby Creepers to be adorable, as they exhibit behaviors similar to pet dogs.

Overall, for a film that was billed as a "dark comedy", I honestly didn't laugh much at all. As with the book, Mickey 7, from which the film is based, it had a few bits of subtle tongue-in-cheek humor. But as I mentioned above, this was a gross failure of WB's marketing team; because as someone who isn't normally into sci-fi, I did enjoy it.

Mickey 17 is definitely a niche film that won't be for everyone; particularly if you're politically sensitive in these current times. But if you're willing to look deeper - beyond the parodical - it's sure to be a cult classic, in time.

author: Agent10
title: Big Budget Sci-Fi Throwback
text:
Normally, a 100 million dollar movie has to have some really good and focused marketing to illustrate the fact this will not be some Star Wars knock-off. Mickey 17 was presented as a fun and silly satire so to speak, but what we got was a serious 1970s style science fiction story.
The idea that Earth is in decay is not even the main subject of the story. What we get is a pseudo anti-colonialism story, a universal and often times easily relatable plot device. For Americans like myself, it's similar to the falsities we are taught as kids about the Mayflower and such, only to learn we had been in our country for decades exploiting resources. So called religious freedom versus boorish capitalism is better I suppose.
Of course, the story also mimics its era as well. Silent Running was a cautionary tale as environmentalism became huge. Star Trek broached racism and classicism routinely during their show's run. Heck, even movies like a Boy and His Dog and even Soylent Green took on the ecological disasters. Mad Max was all about the oil crisis in the 70s. So what was Mickey 17's haymaker for its time period?
Obviously, political demagogues, media manipulation, so called racial purity, religious capitalism, colonial superiority and classicism. The story even introduced the idea of saving Earth first before colonizing other planets, which is pertinent since many knuckleheads are pushing the idea of Mars and Moon colonies for vacation resorts and what not.
The trouble is, Mickey 17 tried implementing all these ideas and it just didn't work all the time. Maybe they could have toned down the Fascist Trumpism a little because as an American, I know who Mark Ruffalo is lampooning. Or I guess they could have made the film longer, which an extra 20-30 minutes would have been fine with me (make movies three hours again!).
Needless to say, this was a pretty good film. It will develop a cult following for sure and I will definitely be a member. But ultimately it tried a little too hard, and it just did not have the razor like focus Bong Joon-Ho has had in other films. I will say this and I don't care if it ages well, I hope that turd muffin Donald Trump sees this movie. I hope he realizes it's him they're making fun of and the weak, degenerate fool in the film is him. I doubt he will see it but here is to hoping.

author: angelalidder-87601
title: I wish I could delete from my memory!
text:
Mickey 17 is the latest science fiction offering from director Bong Joon-ho, known for the award-winning Parasite. This film arrives with a promising pedigree and a cast that includes Robert Pattinson and Mark Ruffalo, but unfortunately it fails to deliver on its ambitious premise. From direction to screenplay, almost every aspect falls short, resulting in an underwhelming experience. Mickey 17 ultimately struggles to decide whether it wants to be an over-the-top adventure, a sci-fi spectacle, or a dark comedy - and in trying to be all at once, it succeeds at none.

Right from the outset, the direction and visual execution leave much to be desired. The film's tone is inconsistent and muddled. If it aimed to be an over-the-top extravaganza, it doesn't even reach the halfway mark in energy or style. As a science-fiction spectacle, it lacks originality and fails to introduce any fresh, thought-provoking concepts, leaning instead on familiar tropes. Even the comedic elements fall flat - there are scarcely any truly humorous moments, making the supposed dark comedy angle feel half-hearted.

The camera work and cinematography do little to elevate the material. Scenes are shot in a perfunctory manner that fails to inject excitement or personality into the story. In a project of this scale, one expects bold visual storytelling, but here the visuals are as unremarkable as the narrative itself.

The screenplay of Mickey 17 is where many of its problems originate. The narrative presents an intriguing concept on the surface - hinting at themes like the value of human life and the notion of a "superior race" - but these ideas are never meaningfully explored. The mention of a genetically superior race, for instance, is tossed in casually and then abandoned, robbing the story of potential depth. What could have been a sharp dark comedy about existential themes is handled in a disappointingly superficial manner.

Plot coherence is another major issue. Key story mechanics are inconsistent to the point of distraction. For example, the film's cloning premise introduces a memory-transfer mechanism, but it doesn't follow its own rules. The protagonist (played by Pattinson) inexplicably remembers past deaths, even though each clone is only supposed to have memories up until the point of replication. This glaring inconsistency undermines the internal logic of the story.

Similarly, the narrative never offers a logical explanation for why the team fails to ensure a prior clone is truly deceased before initiating the next one - a basic procedural step that would seem obvious. These oversights in world-building and logic make it difficult for the audience to suspend disbelief or stay immersed in the story.

Certain scenes further underscore the screenplay's shortcomings. An ostensibly significant threesome sequence is executed so awkwardly that it carries no emotional weight and fails to elicit any genuine reaction from the characters involved. The moment in which a character named Kai makes sudden romantic advances on the protagonist shortly after a traumatic incident (involving another character, Jennifer) feels entirely misplaced, disrupting the narrative flow. Furthermore, when the latest clone, "Mickey 18," finally encounters his predecessor "Mickey 17," his behavior is oddly nonchalant, lacking the shock or existential conflict one would expect from such a meeting. These moments exemplify how Mickey 17's writing fails to capitalize on dramatic opportunities, delivering scenarios that feel unnatural or unexplained.

Despite a roster of talented actors, the performances in Mickey 17 suffer due to weak material and characterization. Mark Ruffalo, usually a reliable and compelling presence on screen, is saddled with a role that gives him little to work with. His character comes across as a thinly veiled caricature of a public figure (seemingly modeled on Donald Trump) - a creative choice that proves more distracting than effective. Ruffalo does what he can, but the ham-fisted satire undermines both his performance and the film's tone.

Robert Pattinson, in the titular role, unfortunately delivers an underwhelming performance. While he has proven his abilities in past projects, here he struggles to bring depth or charisma to a protagonist that is already underwritten. The lead character needed to anchor the story's emotional core and carry its dark humor, but Pattinson's portrayal feels flat, leaving the audience without a strong figure to invest in.

The film also falters in its treatment of female characters, who exist almost entirely to support or motivate their male counterparts rather than serve as fully realized individuals. Naomi Ackie, for instance, gives a solid performance with the little she is given, but her character is drawn in broad, clichéd strokes. For most of the runtime, she functions simply as "the girlfriend," a role that largely limits her to reacting to the male lead's journey. It's only in the final act that she suddenly appears in a position of power - a twist that is insufficiently foreshadowed and feels unearned. This abrupt shift does a disservice to what could have been a more interesting character arc, making it seem like an afterthought by the writers.

Similarly, Steven Yeun's talents are underutilized in a forgettable role. His character lacks any real development or memorable moments, leaving one of today's most charismatic actors stranded with a one-note part. In a film loaded with potentially rich science-fiction concepts and moral dilemmas, the human element falls flat, as the characters never grow beyond stock archetypes. The cast's commitment is evident, but even strong actors cannot overcome characterizations that are this thinly sketched.

Overall, Mickey 17 is a disappointingly unoriginal and hollow venture that fails to capitalize on its promising premise or its accomplished cast and crew. The film's weak direction and inconsistent tone, combined with a lackluster screenplay and underdeveloped characters, result in a sci-fi experience that lacks both excitement and depth. It's the kind of film that struggles to hold the viewer's attention - one might even find it difficult to finish if watching at home, given how little it rewards one's patience.

It is especially perplexing that Mickey 17 comes from Bong Joon-ho, the same filmmaker who gave us Parasite, a masterclass in sharp social commentary and meticulous execution. Where Parasite was incisive and engaging, Mickey 17 feels aimless and derivative. In the end, this movie stands as a rare misstep for its director, offering only a faint shadow of the creativity and impact that his work is usually known for. Verdict: Mickey 17 reaches for the stars but barely lifts off the ground, making it a missed opportunity that will likely leave audiences underwhelmed.

author: Lewis_Heather787
title: Bonkers fun!
text:
Bong Joon Ho + Sci-Fi + Robert Pattison = Count me in 1000%! I can't think of a more interesting recipe for a film. It just has to work perfectly, right?
Overall yes this film is absolute bonkers fun however I was left wanting more.......more of everything. After all the delays surrounding this film you'd assume that if anything this film would not be lacking in any area. It's not lacking but some of the characters, creatures, story elements feel a little under baked/not fully realised. The film had ample room to marinade a little longer and I would have eaten every second of it.
However maybe this disappointment is my own fault. My expectations were high, as they should have been, thats not the films fault. I was hoping for one of the best Sci-Fi films in recent times but just got a good film in return. Thats nothing bad, not at all. This review may sound very down beat but there is a lot to love in this film. From Robert Pattison's dual performance, only increasing his reputation as one of the best actors working today. Naomi Ackie, Steven Yeun, Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette all bringing their game to the table. Then there is the story which itself both absolutely insane yet scarily plausible for humankind to do one day in the future. It touches on all the right points and issues surrounding our species. Whether thats, political, religious, moral, societal and environmental. The story has something everyone can relate too. My disappointment is I wanted more detail......basically being greedy lol.
70% out of 100! Mickey 17 is a good film with some surprisingly good laughs and great thought provoking commentary on humankind and our actions. I was left wanting a bit more however there are far worse films out there.

author: dzumada
title: A Great Kind of Strange

author: Darthfrodo58
title: So much potential, lost
text:
This movie really did have a lot of potential, both from the comedy and sci-fi aspects, but it never delivers on either. Robert Pattinson plays Mickey 17, an 'expendable' that can be reprinted basically from a 3D printer in the shape of a hyperbaric chamber. Since he's 'expendable' he can be sent on dangerous missions without having a fear of death, hence the name Mickey 17. This movie did ONE thing right, when Mickey 17 is lost and thought dead, they print up Mickey 18 and the two of them (having two of anyone in the future is illegal, in some drawn out makes no sense plot feature) show up in several scenes. Usually when one actor plays two characters it's very easy to tell via lighting and outlines) that it's the same guy. This movie did that effect seamlessly, Robert Pattinson does an excellent job, and I give it credit for that.
Everything else just falls apart. It's not funny although it seems to think it is, it's not inventive from a sci-fi perspective, and none of the characters are really fleshed out. It's just bad.
Mark Ruffalo plays a character who is either channeling Donald Trump for a gag, or a televangelist and he hits neither one as believable AND I LIKE Mark Ruffalo. Toni Collette (whom I absolutely love as an actress) plays his wife, and she doesn't hit the mark either. It's as if the director told them to play it over the top and they tumbled down the other side until they hit bottom. I wouldn't say it's the worst movie I've ever seen, but it's in the bottom two.

But, no. In fact, Mickey .. uh .. gonna need spoilers here.

Yes sure, there were 16 other dead Mickeys before him, but the entire premise on which you build up this unlikable character, that's completely not in the film.

Instead you just get, well, him. This horrible sniveling, snot-covered amoeba, and his evil twin, minus goatee.

I really think this is the biggest fail of the script. I really do not mind at all the surreal, plastic characters such as Mark Ruffalo plays, these same characters did well in films like Fifth Element, Brazil, Idiocracy, the problem is that we're not invested into the situation, so rather than recoiling at the absurdity of a character like Marshall, *in unison with the protagonist*, we see him as something that has no effect on us.

It's such a shame, because the elements of a good film are all here, they are just not stirred properly. A few reshoots and some heavy editing could really have made it into a great little film.

My vote: 6/10 and not recommended.

title: An unexpected ride of a theatrical experience.
text:
Yesterday, or was it the day before yesterday, it was the day that I decided to watch this new movie as I walked past the theatre. Of course, the alluring part was the director and the stars that took part in it. Director Bong Joon-Ho has become an astounding influence in international cinema. From Oscar-winning "Parasite" to many other creations, he has always proven to be made of a refined taste that somewhat has a darker representation of the society around us. With these expectations, I would say that the new movie could be described as a low-quality one compared to the others. In an overview, he delivered a cerebral sci-fi experience that simultaneously amazes and frustrates the audience.

While the film's stunning visuals and profound themes warrant praise, its uneven pacing and occasionally ineffective narrative prevent it from achieving the heights of the director's previous work. It is a story of an "expendable" employee Mickey -a human who can be regenerated with most memories intact after death. The director's meticulous world-building creates a convincing future society where corporate colonization has reduced human life to disposable commodities. The story's main theme took place in a newly discovered land Niflheim, with the introduction of new monster-like creatures.

Even though the film wasn't very satisfactory, the actor of Mickey was able to confirms his status as one of this generation's most versatile actors with his portrayal of Mickey Multiples ( The numbers indicate how many other mickeys were created before ). The portrayal of different mickeys with polar opposite personalities were, in fact, one of the most enjoyable part of the movie. Since the story is built around the Mickey 17 with the later appearance of Mickey 18, we were able to go a long ride with those two. Robert provided a theatrically satisfying moments with the portrayal of each clone that carries subtle differences-a slightly different posture, a varied speech pattern-while maintaining a coherent character core. He navigates the complexity of playing against himself with remarkable precision, creating distinct personalities that still feel connected to a shared origin.

In terms of production and visuals, the design team deserves particular appraisal. The contrast between the sterile, efficient interiors of the colony base and the harsh, uninhabited landscape of Niflheim creates a visual tension that mirrors the story's themes. Cinematographer Darius Khondji crafts images of absolutely breathtaking beauty, particularly in several haunting sequences featuring Mickey wandering throughout the icy wasteland alone. However, the film felt short in the shifts of the story between humour and serious social issues. The pacing also suffers particulary in the film's later part where some other characters were too overloaded with different intentions of the directors but unable to blend it well with the story that was occurring at those moments. Also, the death of Mickey and the regeneration process become repetitive and boring to watch later on. It was unable to stick to a certain serious plot and built every characters around it. On the contrary, the movie uses somewhat funny or boring scenes that would be expected from a new movie filmmaker.

Overall, Pattinson's committed performance, stunning visual craftsmanship, and thought-provoking exploration of identity make "Mickey 17" worth experiencing despite its flaws.

title: It Looks Like A Croissant Covered In S***...
text:
I am this film's intended audience: sci-fi geek, liberal, Democrat, and I couldn't hate Mickey 17 more.
So disappointing, especially for Ho, coming off of Parasite. I usually like to say what I liked first, but there isn't much to like here.
First off, can we say what an awful actor Mark Ruffalo is and what a terrible job he did phoning in his role? That performance deserves razzie of the year. For the politics: this had to have been especially embarrassing for the writers who I'm sure thought a certain presidential candidate was going to win the American presidency, and ultimately didn't. The inclusion of the political overtones and undertones were extremely excruciating. Again, I'm going to remind you dear reader that I am exactly the target audience for this movie.
Had Mickey 17 come out between 2016 and 2021, it might have been able to ride the wave of terrible films that became a commercial darling based on the political moral superiority forced down our throats, but it's 2025, and everyone, including me, is sick of this.
This movie was nothing like the trailer. I felt duped and I am surely going to attempt to get my money back.

If you'd have told me five years ago the top ten billed actors in this film, and asked me who I thought would have delivered the best performance, Robert Patterson would have been at the bottom.
He was fantastic. I am so happy (and dare I say proud?) to see an actor who started off as a cute teenager with poor skills blossom into someone who takes the craft seriously, puts in the work, put in the time and effort, does the homework, does the homework of the homework, and delivers an excellent performance. Unfortunately, he really seems to be the only person who turned in any kind of a decent performance. I know that's harsh of me to say, but there were moments when every other performance had noticeable moments of unbelievability.
Concept was good. The sets were well done. Cinematography was subtle, and I appreciated that. In most space films there's an attempt or expectation to go over the cinemagraphical top, and that was not present here. It gave the film the humanity it needed to work. If only the rest of the film-save for Patterson-put in that kind of effort and attention to detail...
I was hoping this movie would be good. I was expecting it at worst to be not bad. Unfortunately, even my low expectations were dropped to levels I didn't expect.

author: imdbfan-4147142891
title: Loved it! "Mickey 17" and the Repeating Cycles of Oppression
text:
"Mickey 17" is a thought-provoking film that explores deep themes of human rights, freedom, and the exploitation of the powerless by those in positions of authority. The movie is carried by a phenomenal performance from Rupert Grint, who plays the lead role of Mickey 17-and later, his body double, Mickey 18. Grint delivers a remarkable interpretation, bringing depth, vulnerability, and nuance to the character as he navigates an oppressive system that treats him as nothing more than a replaceable asset. His acting is both gripping and emotional, making the viewer fully invested in his journey.

What makes this film even more fascinating to watch is its satirical and ironic narration, a classic Bong Joon-ho signature. Mickey 17's dark humor keeps the audience engaged, making us laugh and reflect at the same time. This clever balance between comedy and tragedy is what elevates the movie beyond just a sci-fi drama, transforming it into an entertaining yet deeply critical look at the absurdity of our own reality.

Through its compelling narrative, the movie delivers a strong critique of social class separation, highlighting how the powerful systematically oppress and devalue those beneath them. This is particularly evident in the way the protagonist is treated-seen as disposable, a mere tool rather than a person with autonomy. The story cleverly exposes the harsh realities of hierarchy, control, and the way society often prioritizes progress over human dignity, raising important questions about identity, oppression, and the cost of blind obedience.

To a more cultured audience, these themes may feel familiar, as cinema has explored the injustices of the powerful and the struggles of the working class many times before. However, history has a way of repeating itself, and stories like this serve as an essential reminder-especially for new generations who might not have been exposed to these issues as often. In a world shaped by capitalism, where workers are frequently overlooked and power remains concentrated in the hands of a few, it's refreshing to see such a compelling and accessible film bringing these discussions back into the spotlight.

Beyond its critique of class oppression, "Mickey 17" also delivers a strong environmental message: if humanity does not learn to coexist with nature, we are doomed to destroy our planet. Throughout the movie, it is clear that Earth is dying-evidenced by recurring sandstorms and a desolate atmosphere-forcing many to flee aboard Marshall's spaceship in search of a new home. But when they finally reach another planet, Marshall is immediately ready to dominate and exterminate the native species, proving that humanity's greatest flaw is its egocentrism. We believe ourselves to be the only species worthy of survival, blindly repeating the same mistakes that led to our downfall in the first place.

Another refreshing aspect of the film is its portrayal of strong female characters, particularly Nasha, Mickey's lover, who stands out as a determined and strong-willed Black woman. It is empowering to see women depicted as multidimensional, intelligent, and capable rather than being sidelined or reduced to secondary roles.

Ultimately, the entire movie serves as a critique of our modern society, where the population is oppressed by the elites who control the economy and force people into a capitalist system that treats workers as mere numbers. In this reality, everyone is replaceable, and we are pushed to exhaust ourselves under the illusion that success is within reach-when, in truth, it is nothing more than a fabricated promise to keep us obedient. The film brilliantly portrays how this system thrives on manipulation, not just through economic control but also through religion, as seen in how Marshall uses faith to justify his decisions and maintain his authority. "Mickey 17" is not just a sci-fi story-it's a mirror reflecting the inequalities of our world, making it a powerful and necessary watch.

Given its bold themes, it's not surprising that "Mickey 17" wasn't heavily promoted by Warner Bros. And that its production was repeatedly delayed. One of the film's most striking elements is the character of Marshall, played masterfully by Mark Ruffalo, who is a clear parody of former U. S. president Donald Trump. From his exaggerated gestures to his speech patterns, the resemblance is undeniable. Moreover, there are several hints throughout the movie that Marshall is a revisionist figure, obsessed with creating a so-called "perfect" white world-a theme that is particularly controversial given the current political climate in the United States. Addressing such a divisive topic in a major Hollywood production is a risky move, which might explain why the film received less marketing push than expected. However, this only reinforces the importance of its message, making it a film worth watching, discussing, and reflecting upon.

And yet, despite all the darkness and criticism embedded in the story, what truly surprised me was its ending. Bong Joon-ho is known for his dramatic, often devastating conclusions that leave audiences unsettled, but "Mickey 17" takes a different approach. This time, he offers us something unexpected-hope. The ending gives us the rare feeling that humanity, despite its flaws, is still capable of change. In a film filled with heavy themes of oppression, destruction, and greed, this glimmer of optimism is not just refreshing but deeply meaningful. It leaves us with a question: maybe, just maybe, we can break the cycle after all.

author: PotassiumMan
title: Bong Joon Ho re-emerges with an unwieldy, cold-blooded futuristic saga
text:
Robert Pattinson gives his most offbeat performance to date as a ne'er do-well in a bleak, dystopian, future. He and his degenerate friend (Steven Yeun) opt to join a pilgrimage to start a human colony on a distant planet. Unlike his friend, he agrees to become an "expendable", someone who can die as many times as possible in service of the colony. This voyage eventually turns into a battle for freedom and civilization. The film has enough ambition and ingenuity, that it cannot justifiably be dismissed as paint-by-the-numbers. The end result is hit-and-miss; it's forceful and dynamic, but also lumbering and tortuous at times.
The toughest part of the film to watch is its depiction of human barbarism in encroaching upon alien territory. Ghastly and infuriating, this plot thread will fill you with righteous anger just in case you were still on the fence, wondering which side to root for. Human depravity is unflinchingly depicted by Bong Joon Ho, doubling down on themes he only touched on in "Snowpiercer" back in the day. The contrasting of human cruelty and megalomania with the compassion of an alien species is portrayed with conviction here. The film's juvenile sense of humor and dialogue provide some comic relief in a world where corruption and authoritarianism run rampant.
Although Pattinson is very effective, he sometimes has to carry the film himself. Naomi Ackie is good but only has a small role as his muse. Mark Ruffalo gives a rare one-dimensional performance as the buffoonish tyrant who runs the colonization expedition. Toni Collette is slightly off-kilter as his ice-cold wife. The film has a sustained running time that it has to overcome, which makes it more taxing than necessary. Through it all, however, it finds a way to end in the best way possible that makes it go from an ordeal to an odyssey. Not everyone will be on board, but this is one of the better sci-fi adventures, one that will make you smile. Recommended to open-minded and patient viewers.

author: Stanlee107
title: Micky are you ok..., are you ok?
text:
*Mickey 17* is a highly anticipated dystopian film, but despite the hype, its premise-cloning a person indefinitely for "scientific purposes"-feels far from original. Robert Pattinson delivers a solid performance as the titular character, a man whose very existence has been signed away.

The story follows the 17th iteration of Mickey, as each death merely results in his replacement with a new version. This particular cycle sees him on a mission to colonize a new planet. Alongside his friend Timo (Steven Yeun), Mickey agrees to embark on this journey as a means of escaping a ruthless loan shark who will quite literally extract his "pound of flesh" if payments are late.

While the film sets up an intriguing premise, the execution falters-particularly in its underwhelming conclusion. Unlike Neil Armstrong, this film fails to stick the landing, which is a shame given its potential. The cast is strong, with notable performances from Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette as exaggerated villainous figures. Ruffalo's character is a thinly veiled caricature of Donald Trump, but the portrayal is so on-the-nose that it teeters between satire and self-parody-leaving the audience unsure whether to laugh or cringe.

There are clear inspirations from *Starship Troopers*, but *Mickey 17* never reaches the same heights as Paul Verhoeven's cult classic. While the film ties up its loose ends, the resolution is far from satisfying, leaving the audience wanting more-or perhaps something different entirely.

author: lord_orsum
title: A mix of very good and very bad
text:
In the future, a worker is cloned (reprinted) every time he dies, until a mistake causes two copies of him to exist at the same time. If this sounds a lot like the premise of Moon, then you would not be wrong.
Robert Pattinson gives an excellent performance as Mickey. As an actor, he continues to impress in a wide range of performances, leaving Twilight a distant (and somewhat embarrassing) memory. Most notable is his portrayal of Mickey 17 vs Mickey 18. At a glance you can tell which one you are looking at, simply from the body language and the face expressions.
On the other side, there are some good SF ideas thrown around, but none are really explored properly. The film starts with a very long exposition sequence, which is darkly funny, but eventually outstays its welcome and leaves you wondering when the film will start.
Mark Ruffalo plays the narcissistic and comically moronic leader of the expedition with cartoonish abandon. He is almost the same character as in Poor Things. There have been a number of reviews about Mickey 17 which complain that Hollywood is once again parodying at Donald Trump.
Narcissistic and comically moronic leaders (especially political ones) have existed as fictional characters forever. It seems to me that anyone that immediately equates such a character to Donald Trump is acknowledging that he is the epitome of that stereotype.
The plot tends to lurch all over the place and at no point did I feel that the stakes were real. Some points ("we're the aliens, you moron!") were hammered home with all the subtlety of a steam train. Characters act in unbelievable ways, even for a farcical comedy.
So, should you see this film? Overall, I fall on the "yes" side of that question. But not by a large margin...

author: frankde-jong
title: Hitting the sign of the times with a mad dictator
text:
As the successor of the highly succesful movie "Parasite" (2019, Bong Joon Ho), "Mickey 17" was one of the most eagerly awaited movies of the year.
"Mickey 17" differs however a lot from "Parasite". It actually resembles much more "Snowpiercer", an earlier Bong Joon Ho film from 2013.
"Mickey 17" is a dystopian film a la "Blade runner" (1982, Ridley Scott). In effect the film goes a little further in the sense that the expendables are no longer robots or replicants but real human beings that can be replaced using some sort of 3D printer, hence the 17.
"Mickey 17" is also a film with benign extraterrestrial life, just like "ET" (1982, Steven Spielberg). Unlike "ET" the extraterrestrial life remains on its own planet and it is the human beings who are the visitors. Therefore the use of the description "aliens" by one of the characters in the movie is rather inappropriate. I interpreted the use of this word to be meant ironcal (by the director, certainly not by the character).
Although Mickey (Robert Pattinson) is the title and main character of the movie, the character of Kenneth Marshall is just as important for the nature of the movie, maybe more.
Kenneth Marshall is a dangerous (and crazy) dictator. "The great dictator" (1940, Charlie Chaplin) comes to mind. Chaplin once said he never could have made this movie had he known how dangerous his dictator really was.
In the case of "Mickey 17" the character of Marshall is frequently compared to Donald Trump. Director Bong Joon Ho maintains that this character was not modeled after a specific dictator but after dictators in general. He has a point in the sense that production for the movie was ended in 2022, long before Donald Trump started his second term.
On the other hand the facial expressions of Mark Ruffalo, the actor playing Kenneth Marshall, reminded me neverheless very much of Donald Trump. Ruffalo gives in my opinion a very good performance. I know Mark Ruffalo from "Poor things" (2023, Yorgos Lanthimos), a film that is just as extravagant as "Mickey 17". By the way Toni Collette, known to me for her role in "Hereditary" (2018, Ari Aster), gives an equally strong performance as the wife of Marshall.
Given the fact that: (a) the character of Marshall is ridiculed in the movie and (b) the character of Marshall is identified by many with Donald Trump and (c) criticising Donald Trump was a sensitive issue in the United States at the time of release, many worried about the performance at the box office. After all Ali Abbasi had also difficulties financing his movie "The Apprentice" (2024), which is about Donald Trump for sure. The visitor numbers in the first weekend didn't confirm these anxieties.

author: yorgokennos
title: Mickey17 Missed the Depth That Made Mickey7 Great
text:
Spoiler: I will be comparing my thoughts on Mickey7 and Mickey17 having read then watched. I won't dive into all the differences as much as I would like to.

While my peers enjoyed the film I was left disappointed. The book had a well developed narrative, and more serious while diving into the philosophy of multiples. Bong Joon-ho took a more satirical and exaggerated approach-one I might have enjoyed more if I hadn't read the book first.

The book's characterization was strong, especially with Mickey himself. His struggles physically and existentially, felt grounded and believable. Mickey8, who initially seems like an antagonist, is clearly shaped by his own unique experiences, making him more than just a "bad" version of Mickey. The book also does a great job portraying the cold pragmatism of leadership through Commander Manikova, who-while ruthless-isn't some cartoonishly evil dictator with a partner who wanted to kill the creepers for food. Rather a realistic survivalist leader concerned about the limited resources the colony has left.

Ultimately I was left dissatisfied, and hoping Bong Joon Ho went for a deeper smart, engaging sci-fi story with real ethical dilemmas, strong world-building, and well-developed characters. This political satire and obvious social commentary seems new for the director and while done well, missed the mark for me.

If you want a thought-provoking, well-crafted sci-fi novel, read Mickey7. If you're looking for a flashy, more superficial adaptation, Mickey17 might be worth a watch-the slight name change makes it clear that it isn't the same story.

author: cdjh-81125
title: Something Only Bong Joon-ho Could Deliver
text:
Some movies manage to hook you from the core premise alone and others have a cast and crew that convince me it's something I have to see, Mickey 17 was lucky enough to have both working in it's favour. Following up a film as monumental as Parasite would always be tricky but Bong Joon-ho brings his sensibilities to a story that feels like something only he could've executed in this way and I can honestly say that I've never seen a film quite like it before.
I think the best thing I can say about Robert Pattinson in this movie is that when he's playing 2 different versions of the same character it's still easy to tell them apart purely based of the performance he's giving. He manages to play a character who's fairly pathetic but never unsympathetic and I truly believe that this movie doesn't succeed to the degree it does without his work. He managed to easily stand out in a supporting cast of characters that I unfortunately found to be a bit weak. It's not a matter of the performances, as they're all uniformly great, but other than Naomi Ackie's character I found basically everyone else to be a bit too one noted.
While I wanted to film to wrestle with its own moral implications a bit more I still think it does a good job at making the most out of its premise. The many deaths of this character is largely played for humour and it mostly works. It's the type of scenario where you just have to laugh at the absurdity of it and because of that the tone overall really worked for me. I also liked how much darker it become as the film went on and there were more than a few moments that disturbed me in exactly the right way.
With it being a Bong Joon-ho movie it's obviously immaculately directly. The way he moves the camera feels unique to him and I think the first half in particular flows so well with his trademark dark comedy on full display. The visual effects fit in so seamlessly with the rest of the film and from a cinematography perspective it's absolutely stunning. Also like many of his other films class structures is the main point of focus and I couldn't help but think things were a little too surface level. The parallels are definitely thought provoking but they aren't that deep overall. These leadership characters played by Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette are far too over the top to the point where I didn't find much of anything to do with them to be that interesting. I also think the film becomes a little too messy in the second half where it feels like the pace of the whole thing grinds down after how quickly everything flowed in the beginning because there's just so many elements at play.
Mickey 17 might not nail everything in its execution but it's unbelievably enjoyable as an experience where I just couldn't wait to see what would happen next. Robert Pattinson is perfectly cast as this character and the whole film does such a good job a putting you in his perspective. It's not as deep in its commentary as I would've liked but it's thought provoking nonetheless and it's just a world I was constantly interested in. It's really satisfying to see a film of this scale where a director is given complete free rein and I appreciate Mickey 17 for that if nothing else.

author: waltermwilliams
title: What Walt's Watching
text:
"Mickey 17" is both written and directed by Bong Joon-Ho.
He's got a long history of being in total control of his projects including Oscar winning Best Picture, "Parasite" (2019).
TBH Ho is big on social themes, dark comedy, genre mixing etc.
"Mickey 17" can at times feel a bit preachy on global warming, colonialism, First Nations creatures ("we are the Aliens!") and so many other current issues, but luckily the black comedy balances it out.
A perfect example is how Mark Ruffalo as Church/Corporate Leader of Marshall industries, "Kenneth Marshall", channels US 45th & 47th President Donald Trump even doing his daggy dad dance on a stage/table.
Ruffalo is OTT as Marshall.
Always by his side and in his ear is Aussie Toni Collette as his wife, "Ylfa", who is obsessed with sauces.
She's not the only talent from Down Under.
Sydney born, Daniel Henshall as "Preston" the preacher has worked with Joon-Ho before on "Okja" (2017).
"Mickey 17" is based on a novel by Edward Ashton ("Mickey7") about the titular character played by Robert Pattinson ("Mickey Barnes", no relation to Jimmy from "Cold Chisel") as you've never seen him before with multiple personalities.
Watch out for: Naomi Ackie as "Nasha"("Blink Twice" 2024) putting in a stellar performance and Brad Pitts name in the end credits as an Executive Producer.
Also car buffs keep a keen eye out for a Toyota MR2.
"Mickey 17" is one of the strangest concepts to hit the big screen in 2025.
"Expendables" are essentially people who sign their life away to become experimental human Guinea Pigs who are as the name suggests, completely expendable.
Once they die in so many horrible ways, on this ice planet in a permanent state of winter, hence the Norse name "Niflheim", that they are trying to colonise, the replicants are "reprinted" in a machine complete with their whole memory which is stored on a literal "brick".
It feels like a technology dig at our earliest mobile phones.
One of the "Mickey's" deaths on the Space Ark is an homage to Monty Pythons famous "Bring Out Your Dead" scenes in "The Holy Grail". 197?
"Mickey 17" is a unique movie that defies genre, based on an intellectual property that deserves a far bigger audience than the generic stuff Marvel is churning out repeatedly.
This film looks amazing and will spark debate and divide audiences.
Once "Mickey" becomes a "multiple" (meaning there's two "Mickeys" in existence at the same time, the movie takes a very different turn.
"Mickey 17" is an art house Sci-Fi film, but made on mega Hollywood budget (over 100 million US dollars).
Budgets that only Academy Award Winning Directors get to play with.
"Mickey 17" Is dying to save mankind from bland formulaic cinema because it's so different.

author: starwarsalex1
title: Mickey
text:
Bong Joon Ho's English language films have always been weaker than his Korean films, and Mickey 17 is sadly no exception. It feels like he's re-treading the same political and social themes of Okja and Snowpiercer. He hits the same notes about class distinctions, rich demagogue politicians, and environmental awareness. All of this with his dark humor and satirical tone that borders on the absurd.

The story starts out promising with some a interesting sci-fi premise. The initial worldbuilding is interesting and paints a bleak but foreseeable future. The dystopian world feels believable in a ridiculous but fun sort of way. And the film intelligently grapples with the age old sci-fi question of what makes us human. The reprinting of humans and the accidental duplicates brings up a lot of fun and interesting thoughts and the film explores these lightly but never seems to get too deep into them.

Instead the script gets bogged down with a bit too much thematic weight. After an hour and a half the film feels out of steam - and it dramatically shifts gears into a totally different plotline about slug aliens. It's certainly nice to be surprised by a movie - but it feels a little like it abandons it's own premise and themes in favor of this new weird storyline.

There's a fun and committed performance from Robert Pattison. But the rest of the characters feel cartoonish. Most especially Toni Colette and Mark Ruffalo - who stands in for an obvious Trump/Musk style villain. I mean f--- both those guys - but it has been 9 years now of Trump criticisms and parodies, and it does get a bit tiresome at this point.

I didn't think anything would be able to follow Parasite - but it is sad to see Bong Joon Ho spin his wheels a little on this one. Hopefully his next film tackles some different subjects and maybe it should be in Korean. I just think his wild tonal shifts, and sometimes melodramatic acting works better in that setting and language.

author: DocFacilier
title: Lovely space opera
text:
Though the film occasionally lost my attention, it was not without its charms. Robert Pattinson delivers a captivating performance, effortlessly carrying the emotional weight of the story, while the supporting cast holds their own in complementing his journey.
The narrative unfolds at a deliberate pace, initially leaving me uncertain about its direction. However, once its thematic core became clear, it resonated beautifully. At its heart, the film is a poignant exploration of grief, guilt, and redemption-a man burdened by the loss of his mother, punishing himself as a means of atonement, only to discover that happiness is still within reach.
While the film's pacing may test the patience of some viewers, its emotional payoff is deeply rewarding. It's a story that lingers, not just for its performances but for the quiet, introspective moments that make its resolution all the more profound.

author: masonsaul
title: Flawed vision
text:
Mickey 17 is a very messy sci-fi satire that is ultimately a heartwarming adventure about someone who keeps being told they are literally expendable realising their own self-worth and that they deserve happiness. It gets more muddled as it goes along bringing in lots of ideas which don't always go somewhere, exacerbated by an indulgent run time, mainly held together by its extremely talented leading man doing double duty.
Robert Pattinson is incredible thanks to his ability to make both of the main Mickeys feel like totally different people since 17 has a sad puppy dog energy contrasted by the confident anger of 18. It's nice to see Mark Ruffalo continuing what he started in Poor Things with another incredibly over the top performance even if it isn't as successful here. Naomi Ackie is just as vital to the heart of the film as Pattinson, supporting him through everything with an unwavering strength and moral core.
Bong Joon Ho's writing and direction struggles to maintain a firm grip on all the ideas and weird creative choices crammed into this, which feels out of character but there's enough individual scenes that are great at what they're doing. The $118 million budget may seem bold for a film destined not to turn a profit however, it's always clearly seen on screen, especially in the highly detailed and tactile production design by Fiona Crombie.
