author: junkmail-30870
title: A mess of a script!
text: I found this movie to be interesting in concept but aggravating to watch. The script is a total mess with too many side stories to keep up with. ! It felt like the writer/director Bong Joon Ho was writing on the fly, throwing things on the wall and seeing if they would stick, or he did a lot of rewriting in the editing room. Steven Yeun's pilot character has a double chainsaw on a spaceship to carry out a torture contract? The Senator has a "war-room" is in the incinerator room while the Expendable Mickey 17 has a living quarters, on a space ship, bigger than most studio apartments? Naomi Ackle's police-officer/fireman character has to prevent a tortured and dangling indigenous creature (Creeper) from falling into the same incinerator by holding the rope in her teeth while her hands are merely handcuffed in front of her? Toni Colette's character sucking down blended Creeper tails for no known reason? A lot of piecemeal ideas without a clear narrative. But I'm giving it three stars for the fine creature ideas, creations, and effects.

author: alessiavannini
title: What does it feel like to die?
text:
Mickey 17 is a bald-faced critique of colonialism and, more broadly, of wars and unwarranted violence in general. Similarly to what other movies have done - I'm thinking, for example, about the Avatar and the Planet of the Apes sagas - yet with his touch of uniqueness, the one and only Bong Joon-ho brings to the screen a finger-pointing story that aims to denounce imperialism.
Through this movie, the director ponders the meaning of life and, by following the vicissitudes of the characters, we spectators embark on a journey that is as unrealistically sci-fi as it is extremely human and grounded. Joon-ho poses as the main focus of his survey some of the biggest existential questions, like what does it take to be human, to have the right to live and to decide who lives and who dies, and what does it feel like to die.
As clear as it is, Robert Pattinson does a majestic work portraying different versions of Mickeys, especially considering how different 17 and 18 are from each other. At times, it is very hard to believe that that's the same actor playing both. Via Mickey, the director conveys the crucial importance of overcoming fears and leaving the phantom of the past behind.
The supporting cast is also amazing and, among them, Naomi Ackie, Toni Colette and Steven Yeun clearly stand out from the crowd.
The antagonist is spine-chilling as well. Mark Ruffalo gives an excellent impersonation of Donald Trump and his obsession over chasing away "aliens" that are actually the natives of that land and, thereby who have possibly more right than him and his fellow colonizers to be where they are. In his mannerisms, Kenneth Marshall is also reminiscent of Benito Mussolini, with his powerpose and his silly and spellbinding speeches professed to an audience who worships him without actually fully understanding his intentions and his contradictions. In this list of totalitarian bosses, the quintessential one cannot be left out. Marshall is, indeed, moved by the same desire of "cleansing the human race" that the Fürher Adolf Hitler was so obsessed with. The toxic gas aimed to exterminate a whole species that means no harm, the experimentation on humans, the burial of "errors", of "expendable", isn't too far from Hitler's or even Stalin's idealized view.
While Mickey 17 might seem a joyful and entertaining ride - which it certainly is, outwardly - under its surface it hides (and not even that much) a brutal commentary on our contemporary situation. Bong Joon-ho speaks out against human stupidity and violent, totalitarian regimes, shouting to the world about his mistrust of the system and of our current political leaders - those of United States, Russia, Israel, Italy, France, his motherland South Korea and so on and so forth.
The writer-director-producer provides the masses a film dressed up as a blockbuster - pretty far from his arthouse, Oscar-worthy masterpiece Parasite - that will reveal itself (at least to the brightest minds) as a sharp satire about today's political situation, just like his previous and masterful movies were. Without ever feeling predictable or trite, Bong's new movie is ultimately a breath of fresh air, in an industry that often prioritizes and prefers sequels, prequels and remakes to genuinely original ideas.

author: Junebug23057
title: He weakest film. Still not awful
text:
As a long-time fan of Korean cinema-ever since I took a university course focused on Asian films back in 2007-I felt a mix of excitement and trepidation going into *Mickey 17*. Korean films have a certain depth and craft that often seems missing from Hollywood, though there are understandable exceptions. With acclaimed director Bong Joon Ho at the helm, I was hopeful this sci-fi venture would capture some of that unique flair, even if it's a western production.
The premise of *Mickey 17* is intriguing. Mickey Barnes, an Earthling turned space colonist, repeatedly faces death in a hostile, icy universe. Every time he dies, his memory is uploaded, and a new clone is created. However, chaos ensues when a second copy of Mickey is made, leading to legal and existential dilemmas. While I won't spoil anything further, the story is anchored in the classic dynamic of the downtrodden against the elite, familiar territory for Bong Joon Ho fans, echoing his previous work *Snowpiercer*.
What I appreciated about *Mickey 17* is that it doesn't simply tread the well-worn paths of remakes, sequels, or adaptations of existing media. It's based on a book, but it feels fresh and original-something I sorely miss in contemporary cinema. Much like *The Creator*, it stands as a testament to the power of storytelling outside the repetitive cycles of Hollywood.
Yet, as much as I wanted to love it, I found myself struggling with Mickey as a character. Rather than embodying the endearing charm I expected, he often felt more annoying than relatable. His naïveté-though perhaps meant to add humor-came off as cartoonish at times, which made it difficult for me to root for him as the protagonist.
The love interest in the film also left me scratching my head. Her character seemed to fluctuate dramatically throughout the narrative-at times, she displayed confidence and strength, only to inexplicably revert to a more passive demeanor. This inconsistency made her character feel less credible and more like a plot device rather than a fully realized individual. At one moment, it seemed we were headed for a rich, meaningful relationship, but her sudden changes in personality diluted that potential. Additionally, another intriguing character who seemed poised to develop into a significant romantic angle vanished without much resolution, leaving me perplexed and somewhat dissatisfied.
Also worthy of mention is the supporting cast. While their performances were solid, many of the characters felt a bit one-dimensional-often feeling more like plot devices than fleshed-out individuals. One character, who seemed to have an intriguing arc, vanished without much resolution, making me wonder if something was cut from the final edit.
On a positive note, the film introduces fascinating alien creatures reminiscent of giant, furry caterpillars, and I found myself unexpectedly rooting for them. They added an emotional layer to the narrative that I didn't anticipate, showcasing Bong Joon Ho's signature ability to create empathy for even the most unconventional beings.
Visually, the movie is a feast for the eyes. The sweeping shots of enormous snow-covered terrains, especially the scenes featuring massive jeeps, were beautifully executed. The music, set design, effects, and costumes were all top-notch, immersing audiences in this distant world.
Despite its many strengths, I can't help but feel that *Mickey 17* is perhaps the weakest link in Bong Joon Ho's impressive filmography. It's not a bad movie by any means and certainly deserves praise for its creativity and visual flair, but it misses the poignant emotional connection that his previous works often achieve. I'd give *Mickey 17* a solid 7/10-worth a watch for fans of science fiction and the director, but perhaps not a must-see for those craving the emotional depth typical of his best films.

author: gavinp9
title: Slightly different, semi-bleak space comedy
text:
'Mickey 17' is a different type of interstellar sci-fi, as you'd expect from Joon-ho - we're at some unspecified point in the future where humankind has the ability to travel to distance planets, as well as having the ability to back-up memories and 3D-print humans after the die. This is where Mickey (Pattinson) comes in, as he signs on to the colonisation attempt of the planet Niflheim as an "expendable". The back-story in the first 30min of how he got to be on this distant planet is both funny and a little sad, but establishes Mickey (#17) as a naive but nice guy, in love with Nasha (Ackie).

The film's score is always slightly mournful, ensuring that we know the humour is a little dark or bleak. Especially when we see who is leading the expedition - Marshall (Ruffalo) and Ylfa (Collette), who both appear so fake, they come across exactly as delusional evangelical cultists. Ruffalo particularly relishes the role, and perhaps has some fake teeth in? Good to see him having fun. Timo (Yuen) is Mickey's friend from earth, with a bit of a twist - but no where near as many twists as 'Parasite'.

Whilst not overly original, the film doesn't waste any effort in explain the unrealistic sci-fi components - it's takes them as read, assuming we've seen these tropes in plenty of other films before. The inhabitants of Niflheim are an interesting flea/elephant/bison hybrid that seem semi-realistic, but would've been interesting to see them as animatronic puppets & not CGI. What's most interesting is how you sometimes forget the different versions of Mickey are the same actor - credit to Pattinson. Ending is a slight letdown.

author: pedroquintaoo
title: Mickey 17
text:
I went into Mickey 17 with high expectations. Bong Joon-ho gave us Parasite, a masterpiece that had me glued to the screen, so I was hoping for something of the same caliber. And while I did enjoy the film, I left the cinema feeling like something was missing, as if the story didn't go as far as it could have.
The social commentary is there, and it's one of the film's strongest aspects. The idea that we are disposable, replaceable, just cogs in a system that exploits us to exhaustion without any regard for individuality, is unsettling-because we already live in a society that operates this way. Then there's the theme of neocolonization, which the film explores in a sharp way: if we ever discover a new, inhabited planet, we'll probably behave just as cruelly and disgracefully as we did centuries ago during the Age of Exploration, because, let's be honest, it's in the DNA of too many of us to be unscrupulous bastards.
However, Mickey 17 struggles with an inconsistent tone. It feels torn between being an existential sci-fi film and a comedy, but it never quite finds the right balance. Some of the humor works, but other times it completely undermines the impact of the film's deeper ideas.
And then there are the villains. Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette are fantastic actors, but their characters here are so cartoonish that they lose any sense of menace. Instead of being intimidating or manipulative figures of power, they just come across as ridiculous. This weakens the narrative, turning the central conflict into a joke and stripping away the potential for a much stronger ideological clash.
That being said, there are things to appreciate. Robert Pattinson continues to make bold choices, and his performance effectively conveys the character's existential crisis. Visually, the film is also captivating, with production design that creates an authentic sense of a dystopian reality within a spaceship setting.
In the end, Mickey 17 isn't a bad film, but it falls short of what it could have been. The ideas are there, the social critique is relevant, but the execution falters in key moments. Is it worth watching? Yes, especially for the thought-provoking themes. But anyone expecting something on the level of Parasite might walk away feeling a little disappointed.

author: mesaxi
text:
As far as adaptations go this was pretty bad. I won't get into the specific gripes about how it wasn't exactly like the book, I knew it couldn't be because the story of the book is pretty short, padded with a lot of internal monologue and talk about food rations and Mickey working our his situation. The real issue was that the many themes of the book regarding trust, betrayal, friendship, personal accountability, interstellar colonization, how alien intelligence may differ from ours, all of that was completely thrown away in favor of some half-assed political message.

This turned out being a PRIME example of how hijacking a movie with left-wing propaganda has become a tired, and even embarrassing. Like they weren't satisfied that Nasha was already black in the book, that she was already tough, so they had to make her become the ruler of the colony at the end? Even though her qualifications were being a security guard known for committing assault and using drugs and was recently arrested for attempted murder with a chainsaw, it makes absolutely no sense at all but "representation" lol. Then of course Ruffalo doing some sort of despotic RFK mixed with Trump, which I'll say he did a great job at, it was just an obnoxious change to the character. It also made me laugh that they seemed to anticipate Trump losing and committed hard to the character having lost two elections in a row. Whoops. And I think Toni Colette's whole character was just because Bong Joon-ho is into animal rights or something? I thought she would have been perfect for a character that wasn't even in the film, instead we got a demented Paula Deen or something.

The biggest attraction of the movie is the indulgently cute animation of the Creepers, I would never have pictured them as roly-poly elephant pig things but it worked well. That and the performances of Pattinson and Ruffalo would be all I can really say in favor of this movie. Production wise it looked pretty good. Maybe reading the book first was a bad idea, but the politics were such a turn off that I don't think it would have mattered very much. There were also some tonal issues, maybe just poor editing. Like that strange dream sequence out of nowhere at the end and the weird sad credit music.

Major disappointment overall. A book chock-full of great material wasted in favor of a pseudo-political ass blast.

author: larkintheclouds
title: A Lab Rat on a Block of Ice
text:
A beautiful film. It's incredibly funny, but has surprising depth and understanding. Robert Pattinson plays his part incredibly well and comes off incredibly memorably in all aspects. Every actor did a great job, but Mark Ruffalo managed to play the part of the 'Charisma Black-Hole' that was demanded of him expertly; in part, openly mocking cults of personality forming around the dumbest people on the planet. Additionally the film has a surprising critique of religious zealotry and capitalist colonial drive and fascistic dehumanization of a population. Although not saying anything groundbreaking, or with enough depth to watch it on those merits alone, it still manages those critiques well and their inclusion in the narrative fits well and drives the plot forward in a believable (if comedically exaggerated) way.
Conclusion: Really fun and enjoyable, worth a watch. More depth than expected, but not shifting mountains.
Some other notes:
It was directed very well; it worked well visually. The aliens were very cute. Although Mickey 17 and 18 were contrasted very well throughout the film, variations between the previous iterations were only mentioned passingly and we didn't actually see those expressed directly.

author: ThereelscoopwithKK
title: A Difficult Act That Succeeds
text:
Based on seeing the trailer shown before other films I wasn't particularly drawn to it and thought I may pass. I really enjoy space thrillers when they hit, but when they don't I find them to be huge busts. Alas, I hadn't seen one in a while so I thought I'd give it a go. Admittedly the timing of the show also fit my schedule well...
To summarize things, this was a great decision. It is incredibly difficult for films to mesh comedy with an actual story. So much can go wrong, the comedy can distract the viewer from the story, or the story can lose its momentum by unwarranted clips of comedy. Even further it requires an exceptional cast to put it all together.
Hats off to director Bong Joon- Ho as he took this risk as not many directors these days do and we get a lot of the same cookie cutter stories.
Robert Pattinson is simply incredible playing all of the Mickey's. I never knew he was capable of the range he displayed. I admittedly caught myself for a second not realizing it was the same actor at certain parts. That shows some real talent on his part. It was clear he was enjoying this role a lot. Mark Ruffalo, who I don't particularly enjoy as an actor and often find bland, did a really good job as the villain. The facial expressions and remarks were hilarious and fit the role of tyrannical, incompetent politician perfectly. There are some articles about how the cast especially enjoyed making the film and it shows in the work.
I will say the comedy is not for all though. It's aggressive with a decent amount of swearing. I wouldn't exactly say it's a made for the whole family kind of film.
Beyond all its silly moments, you do feel like you at least get to know the motivations of some of the characters. The method of having Mickey narrate the story is also highly effective.
The movie deserves a much better showing at the box office than it currently has received. I hope it gets better results because if a movie like this fails then moviegoers will get more of the same bland cookie cutter stories and likely remakes that studios can rely on to at least deliver break even results.

author: qkgsrhdx
title: Unsubtle, Unwelcome, and Unoriginal: A Political Lecture in Disguise
text:
So let me see if I understand the not-so-subtle implications of this film-
The idiot cis white male protagonist is a bumbling pushover who can't handle life's challenges. He's too passive to succeed. Meanwhile, the black female lead is the smartest person in the film-the savior (of course). The more aggressive and dominant version of him is also the one she's attracted to. Mark Ruffalo plays a ridiculous authority figure clearly meant to be a stand-in for Trump, warning us about the dangers of his leadership. Earth's future is bleak, corporations are destroying the planet, and humanity is forced to flee into space to survive. The "aliens" we encounter are harmless, but we treat them as a threat, stealing their land while pretending they're dangerous. And most importantly, the expendable working-class clones bear the brunt of society's suffering so that the privileged can thrive.
Did I get all that right?
This film is beyond horrible. The characters are so exaggerated that they barely function as actual people, instead serving as thinly veiled political mouthpieces. The messaging is as subtle as a brick to the face-about as much of a "farce" as Borat, except it pretends to be deep and thought-provoking instead of just saying the quiet part out loud. It's the worst kind of midwit storytelling-simultaneously acting like it's making some clever, subtle commentary while actually being as blunt and obvious as possible. It's like the film wants you to believe it's being cryptic and intellectual when it's really just screaming the most surface-level takes imaginable.
And of course, this kind of left-leaning, hyper-contrived narrative gets praised, even though it presents a completely one-sided perspective, ignoring any middle ground.
The most frustrating part is the bait-and-switch. The trailer sells this as a fun sci-fi adventure, but the actual film is just another over-the-top political lecture disguised as entertainment. Nobody goes to the movies to be force-fed a message they already get nonstop from the news. If you're going to be this overt, at least have the balls to be upfront about it.
And then there's Mark Ruffalo-easily the worst part of the whole thing. He plays the same delusional, self-righteous clown that he is in real life, blindly clinging to every cause he doesn't understand. His entire presence in this film is unbearable.
I think this film is exactly why Hollywood gets derided and why the theater industry is dying. Why do we need to be tricked into this kind of nonsense? This is the reason superhero shlock dominates the box office-because adults don't want to be ambushed with a lecture and are losing faith in movies thanks to the constant barrage of left-leaning pandering. So instead, kids end up deciding what gets made, and real films get sidelined.

author: Jeremy_Urquhart
title: What is this, Bong Joon Ho?
text:
A 25-year-long directing hot streak comes to a sad end with Mickey 17. I almost can't believe this was directed by Bong Joon Ho. I'm devastated by how much I didn't like this. I imagined it would kind of be Okja-level at worst but it made me wish I was rewatching Okja. At least that one was funnier and made me feel things here and there. Mickey 17 feels like that film, Snowpiercer, Don't Look Up, a so-so Black Mirror episode, and Starship Troopers were left out in the sun for too long, and then thrown in a blender, and then you were made to drink the subsequent smoothie over the course of 137 minutes. It's a hodgepodge of all these movies and maybe some others, but it's inferior to just about anything you could compare it to.
None of the cast members are on the same page. Robert Pattinson and Steven Yeun probably come the closest to giving good performances, but it's hard to look past the awfulness of Mark Ruffalo's performance.
Speaking of, I understand what the movie is satirising. But satire needs to evolve, I think. This is milquetoast and ineffectual nonsense. I don't want to pat myself on the back and recognise who this movie's making fun of. That person is still at large and worse than before, and if The Apprentice didn't put a chip in his armour, then there's no way Mickey 17 will. His supporters won't watch the movie and will laugh at how limp its box office returns are. He'll keep on winning. He deserves all the criticism in the world, but I just don't like laughing at satire this broad. It's not funny anymore. It's unfunny in the way SNL political skits from the 2010s are (extra) unfunny now. It feels insincere. I want to take the state of the world seriously or, preferably, watch satire evolve. The Substance, which was like a hyper-satire (and about admittedly different things), is probably a step in the right direction.
If I saw Mickey 17 on Netflix by chance, I might think it was a watchable but forgettable approximation of a Bong Joon Ho sci-fi movie. Coming from the man himself, though, I'm just so disappointed. It's an unconfident, largely unfunny, and visually drab film that will hopefully be the biggest swing and a miss of the year. No one in front of or behind the camera felt on the same wavelength here, the opening act and the final couple of scenes had some atrocious editing decisions, and then a lot of what happens in between is mildly amusing at best and utterly tedious at worst (that climax felt like it took about two hours to get through).
Even giving this a 4/10 feels generous. I guess I have minimal appreciation for some of its general weirdness, and a couple of the actors are doing their best with a messy screenplay and what feels like confused direction. I'm just so sad I didn't enjoy this very much at all.

author: imdbfan-7180118470
title: Just not it
text:
Robert Pattinson delivers a solid performance, but the script doesn't give him enough to work with. Supporting characters, including those played by Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette, feel underdeveloped, and their motivations remain unclear. While Bong Joon-ho's signature visual style is present, it can't compensate for the weak storytelling and uneven pacing.
The satirical elements, which could have provided sharp commentary on colonialism and corporate greed, end up feeling underwhelming. The humor doesn't always land, and the emotional beats lack depth, making it hard to connect with the characters or the stakes.
While Mickey 17 isn't a complete disaster, it never fully capitalizes on its intriguing premise. With a tighter script and more focused storytelling, this could have been a memorable sci-fi film. Instead, it's a visually stylish but ultimately forgettable experience.

author: CinemaSerf
title: Mickey 17
text: "Mickey" (Robert Pattinson) is desperate to avoid a grisly fate at the hands of a loan shark, so decides his best bet is to get off-planet. Thing is, there are an whole load of like-minded folk so his only hope is to be an expendable. That means he gets used for all the dangerous and experimental tasks and if he gets killed or seriously maimed, they just lob him in the incinerator and reprint him - complete with all his old and quite a few new memories. Travelling through space, he meets "Nasha" (Naomie Ackie) and they have a good thing going, even if the imperious couple in charge - Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette - have forbidden the wasting of the 100 calories it takes to have sex! Things start to go a bit wrong, though, when he unexpectedly survives one chilly mission only to find upon his return they have already duplicated his successor. "Nasha" thinks the ménage-à-trois thing could work quite well but "Mickey" less so, and when rumours of their duplicate existence starts to abound, well things get distinctly dodgy. Meantime, the indigenous population of the planet they have landed on are getting a bit cross with the murderous attitudes of their human interlopers, and so perhaps it's gonna be for "Mickey" x 2 and "Nasha" to sort things out before the pitch changes altogether. It's quite good fun this, but I kept thinking of "Galaxy Quest" and couldn't decide if Ruffalo was having a go at Donald Trump or Val Kilmer with his rather hammy performance. Also, despite being easy enough on the eye, Pattinson is a remarkably charm-free actor and here, even when there are some daft scenarios and the CGI works flat out to create a perfect series of images, he just underwhelmed the whole time and when the film is about more than one of him, that mattered. Collette and Steven Yeun are relatively under-used and it's simply far too long to sustain the thinness of a plot that does raise some interesting issues around human cloning, exploration and that especially American cinematic trait of shooting extra-terrestrials first and then asking question later, but I was disappointed with this, sorry.

title: A Fun, Dark, Albeit Messy Ride
text:

As with many grim futuristic satire films, Micky 17 expertly uses it's setting and characters to show you the extremes of human pride in a way that's intense, yet oddly familiar.
That being said, It was a bit messy in it's presentation, and I think had just a little bit too much going on to follow properly. It felt as though there was some unease in believing the audience would keep up with the surreal nature of things (most likely from the studio given the delays). author: SpaaceMonkee
title: Hugely Underwhelming
text:
After Okja and Parasite, I was excited to see the next work of art from the same director. Sadly, I couldn't wait for Mickey 17 to end, and I left the theater feeling so disappointed.
The movie follows Mickey, a kindhearted but unremarkable person who joins a colony ship while fleeing a loan shark and signs up as an "expendable" to get a spot on board. Expendables are humans whose personality and memories are downloaded onto a (literal) brick, and then the physical person can be "printed" over and over again after they die. This technology is hugely controversial, banned on earth, and allowed only on a colony ship run by Kenneth Marshall, a politician who keeps losing elections. Marshall is a character clearly playing on Trump, and he has been given command of this particular colony ship by a company/church (not kidding). He's planning to create a beautiful new planet colonized by his first-rate supporters.
This isn't "reading into" the movie in any way. Bong Joon Ho's movies can be masterful, but they're not masterpieces of subtlety. That his films (generally) manage to be as good as they are is a testament to his skills as a director. He can be darkly funny, hit you with on-the-nose social commentary, and make it work, except not in Mickey 17.
The first third or so of the movie is intriguing. There are dozens of ideas coming at you, ranging from capitalist critiques to social commentary on human cruelty, mortality, technological ethics, and so on, with the Marshall/Trump character and political commentary largely operating as background forces.
In the second half of the film - and particularly in the final fifth - it's all Marshall/Trump, all in the foreground, and the other interesting ideas either fade away or else are annihilated in the overbearing shadow of the grating, farcical buffoonery of the Marshall/Trump family's leadership and its sycophantic enablers. The jokes start falling flat, and the dark comedy just becomes a dark, unpleasant plot line.
I predict that in twenty years, younger people will watch this film and find it beyond implausible. They may say things like, "why would anyone follow a man so cruel and self-aggrandizing as Marshall, who seems, in the end, to offer so little to his supporters and to care only about himself? Why did these other seemingly smart people enable him?" Perhaps that's all part of the concept: an art film masquerading as a high-budget space opera designed as a time capsule with built-in planned obsolescence to be discovered a generation later as an artifact representing the misguided politics of our current era. If so, it's quite the elaborate work of art. In theaters, though, it just feels forced, overly long, and unfunny. And that is a shame, because you risk missing the human element of the story, that of Mickey 17 trying to find love and happiness.

author: imdbfan-5944183497
title: a masterfully acted, self-contradictory mixed bag of a sci-fi movie
text:
Let's start with what's good. The acting. Robert Pattinson is an absolute savant and I'm glad he got the boost he needed from The Batman to becoming a true A-list actor, he properly portrays a man who's sick of being walked over but can't really do anything about it. Mark Ruffalo is also excellent, he portrays a fanatical, insecure, hammy, not-so-subtle clone of Trump/Elon/takeyourpickbillionaire who has no idea how to run a colony and tries making up for his incompetence with hate. Naomi Ackie is also poignant, I didn't like her character as much because of how flawless she was but she's seething with rage when she's needed to tell a moral and she's likable when she's needed to be a perfect romantic interest.

Now to my main criticism of the movie: the fuddled allegory. The whole movie is set up as being a dark, biting satire of corporate greed and colonialism and how they cause us to value human life less, but the movie goes and turns its back on these scathing portrayals at the very end to serve its huggy-kissy ending.

To give an example, there's Marshall's (the main villain) supporters. They are very blatant copies of Trump supporters, with reddish hats and everything, but the movie doesn't finish the jab. It then turns around and has these people (with very little set up in the way of showing that they've changed from being fanatical Marshall supporters) elect the perfect Nasha as their leader at the end. It makes the moral of the movie confusing, because what is this trying to tell me, yes corporatism, state religion, and colonialism is bad- unless it's Nasha wearing those robes, then it'll all work out. Then all the colonists will live in harmony with the native oversized tardigrades and they'll be a happy society.

It's particularly confusing because this same character, Nasha, gives an absolutely ripping speech about how colonists are the real aliens in this alien world, which is so on-the-point that it might as well be talking to the audience. But she doesn't spearhead a takedown of the corporation that's responsible for these damages, and she doesn't make the colonists go home. She just- takes over, and that part is really strange to me.

There are some other parts of the movie where the satire doesn't quite hit as hard as it could. Marshall explicitly says that he wants the future of this colony to be white, but he never is shown in any other scene being a racis, in fact, there are plenty of black and Asian characters sprinkled in that you would think Marshall would have a problem with but it's simply never shown. The main evil corporation of the movie is shown to be vaguely religious- while at the same time being a stand-in for the freemasons? That doesn't really compute. What exactly this movie's true beliefs on religion are mystifies me because even though the bad guys are obviously parodies of Christian conservatives it's also told that they're at odds with religious groups on Earth who think cloning is blasphemous. Plus as I said, Nasha is shown donning the robes of the company and making everything right. That reminds me, how did Nasha even get on board with the colony in the first place? She's not a Marshall follower, (in spite of this, she does police work for him) and unlike Mickey, she's never given a backstory of anything to escape on Earth. Her lack of character flaws are at odds with the satirical angles of the movie and make the movie conflict a battle between the angel Nasha and caricatures of real-world figures.

With all that criticism out of the way, I must say that in spite of the risky and self-contradictory plot that Joon-ho was given he definitely elevated it to the point where the movie itself is perfectly watchable (and even at times very entertaining). The dialogue is funny when it wants to be, and there's also a great deal of visual comedy that's great, too. Mickey's characters, with 17 and 18 working as the angel and devil on his combined consciousness's shoulder, were very well-acted and entertaining to watch. Robert Pattinson portrays a pushover well, though the fact that Mickey relegates most of the heavy lifting to his girlfriend means that the message I get from the movie is that everything will work out as long as a perfect person is in charge, which isn't particularly uplifting. But like I said, even though the roles that the characters have are strange, the acting and well-written dialogue makes up for it most of the time.

And to finalize it, the directing, sets, costume design, and all that stuff was also fantastic. Maybe the budget was a little overblown, but there weren't really any scenes that felt like they were lingering on the grandeur of the set, instead, to my delight, the characters were the main focus. The focus on how miserable a person at the bottom feeding of a corporation is, the focus on how much of an evil Marshall and his wife are.

All in all, it's a movie that's at odds with itself. It wants to be goofy, harshly satirical, dark, and noble all at the same time, and while Bong's a good director who knows how to make a movie entertaining, the story has flaws that can't be overcome no matter how good of dialogue and cinematography it has, so I don't fault him for the fact that this movie's a mixed bag. My attention was firmly grasped the entire way through the movie, but after I left the theater and started to think about what the movie was trying to say I was left with more questions than answers. On a more objective note, I don't think this movie will do too well at the box office, it's too biting to appeal to people who just want a fun movie but it aborts its own moral in favor of a sickeningly sweet blockbuster movie resolution, meaning that people like me who expect hard-hitting social commentary to think about are left unsatisfied.

author: ngkubisiak
title: Let me explain.
text:
I was expecting a silly adventure of a guy who dies a bunch. I was not expecting a subversive Si-Fi mixed with in-your-face political commentary. It's bonkers, but it works. Let me explain.

My interpretation, Mickey is a universal character, representing the changes we go through in life and the many different versions of ourselves. After this version, what will you do next? How will you use your change? How can you contribute to the world as the most evolved version of yourself? That's what I got from "Mickey 17" by the end of the film. Speaking of Mickey, oh my god, Robert Pattinson can ACT. This is the best acting I've seen from him, he's just perfect in this movie. I'm actually not sure if this movie would work without him, as he's the most standout thing about it.

The direction is, I'll say it again, bonkers. It's bonkers, but in the best ways possible. The cinematography is gorgeous. Unexpected twists and turns kept me intrigued throughout. I need to see more. I actually haven't seen "Parasite", which might explain my praise for this movie. Still, as a first impression, this guy's an amazing director. I never knew what to expect until the end (the ending is one of my only problems, and we'll get to that).

Now, the political themes may seem out of left field, but they're really an essential part of the movie. It adds not only the most humorous characters in the film, but an essential commentary. A warning. Especially considering our current political atmosphere in America. The movie didn't have to include this aspect, but it did anyway, and I admire it for that.

I think the criticism comes from a strong misunderstanding. It has similar "problems" as another one of my favorite movies, "Barbie". It's extremely in-your-face in some areas yet totally subversive in others. It shouldn't work, it seems like too much of a contrast. Yet, that IS what makes it work. It's not for everyone, I get it. It's not a safe movie, therefore not everyone will like it. To me, though, that's why it's good.

All that said, there are some problems I just can't deny. The main problem, considering the amount of twists and turns the movie goes for, the ending is too safe. Satisfying ending, but that's the problem. It goes all out, and in the end, decides to play it safe. Oh well. One other thing, it at times feels unintentionally Oscar-grabby. I think it's great, and I honestly think it should be nominated, especially for best actor. But, c'mon, it's like they're asking for it. Everyone working on the movie should've just trusted the crazy ideas. They didn't need to double down. It's almost perfect, but these aspects unfortunately dial it down a notch. Then again, those are the only real problems, and if it is Oscar-worthy, maybe it's okay to flaunt it. For the most part, it's thought-provoking and engaging enough for these problems to fade into the background. Ultimately, the message and heart of the film completely make up for these problems. No matter how many versions of you there are, live all your lives authentically and with purpose. Or, at least try, even when the world tries to stop you.

Maybe this movie just resonated with me personally, but I genuinely believe it's a misunderstood masterpiece.

author: kluseba
title: It Feels Like We Have Been Here Before
text:
Mickey 17 is a science-fiction satire loosely based upon the novel Mickey7 by American author Edward Ashton that only saw the light of day three years ago. This movie takes place thirty years in the future and follows an indebted man who runs away from home by signing up as an expandable worker for a spaceship crew aiming to colonize a planet known as Niflheim. Mickey Barnes has to accomplish dangerous missions for manipulative religious leader and failed politician Kenneth Marshall. Whenever he dies, a clone of him is printed and programmed with the protagonist's original identity. Problems start to occur when one version of the protagonist is believed to be murdered by mysterious aliens who actually save his life and a new clone is already being printed in the spaceship.
This science-fiction satire has a few strong elements that deserve to be praised. The camera work is calm and precise. The visual special effects are on the pulse of time but never exaggerated. The aliens are intellectually appealing. This film criticizes numerous elements such as cloning, colonialism, militarism as well as religious and political agendas that can still be found frequently in our real world. This film's story and style often remind of Bong Joon-ho's Snowpiercer released twelve years earlier that is based upon a four-volume French climate fiction graphic novel.
However, this new movie also has multiple flaws that need to be mentioned. The film's plot is predictable from start to finish and fails to come around with any noteworthy twists and turns. The movie's pace is dragging as its length overstays its welcome by at least half an hour. The acting performances and character depth are often repetitive and superficial as viewers will have a hard time emphasizing with anyone in this film.
At the end of the day, we have an average science-fiction film that fails to explore new ground. Fans of the contemporary Dune movies might want to give this film a try. Occasional science-fiction aficionados can however skip Mickey 17 without any regrets. Fans of director Bong Joon-ho might feel slightly disappointed by this film and should rather explore his greatest films from the past such as atmospheric psychological thriller Memories of Murder.

author: DanLawson146
title: A good mix of fun and thought-provoking
text:
POSITIVES:

1) The performances are excellent. Pattinson thrives in the lead role(s), while the supporting cast are all brilliant too, especially Mark Ruffalo who plays Donald Trump (in all but name) very well.

2) The first two acts of this film are basically flawless for me. The film is really funny whilst also being really thought-provoking and unnerving. I particularly loved all the moral and ethical questions it poses around the ideas of reprinting and expendables.

3) The film feels like it was made with such love and attention to detail in areas like costume design, production design, sound, etc. It's been six years since Parasite came out and you can really tell that Bong Joon Ho has spent that time pouring everything into this film.

NEGATIVES:

1) Steven Yeun's character was just too annoying for me to handle. He wasn't funnily annoying in the way Collette and Ruffalo's characters were, and it really frustrated me that he never gets any kind of punishment for any of his actions. He basically wins at the end which I didn't think was good writing.

2) The final act of this film is just far too silly for me. I think the film is baggy and overlong anyway, which meant I was already struggling a bit by the third act, but then the third act that the film serves up just had me rolling my eyes several times and honestly just waiting for the film to end. I think the direction the film takes is far too focused on the Creepers. This means it essentially skips over the premise that would've been really cool of seeing how the two Mickeys learn to co-exist with each other; because instead the two Mickeys are almost instantly caught out as being multiples, which I didn't think was a good writing decision to make.

author: bowmanblue
title: Good fun, despite its flaws
text:
I didn't know that much about 'Mickey 17' and only really saw it because the other half has a thing for Robert Pattinson. I've mainly only seen him in the 'Twilight' franchise, but, every other time he's popped up in something I've watched, I have to admit that he's shed his 'twinkly' former self and is actually quite a good actor.
Anyway, here we find him in a bit of a dystopian future where mankind have the option to board giant spaceships bound for far away planets where they can colonise. And, because poor ol' Mickey doesn't have much in the way of 'skills' required for such a mission, he signs up to be an 'expendable.' This means he's the one sent on all the most deadly missions and if (or should I say when?) he dies, they simply reprint a copy of him the next day - they can do that, by the way.
Personally, I really enjoyed 'Mickey 17' as it's actually a lot funnier than I thought it would be (at first I thought it might be a horror, or at least a 'Starship Troopers-esque' action sci-fi film. Robert Pattinson is easily the main draw and elevates the film to be more than it otherwise might as well have been. His on screen presence carries the 'slower' portions of the story. Which brings me on to pacing. 'Mickey 17' - like so many modern films - could probably lose about twenty minutes of their overall runtime and be all the better for it. The movie does drag in a few places, but the major flaw is the film's villains. Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette are both good actors, but they're so over-the-top and comic they feel like they belong in a kids' movie. Plus, I'm not really into politics and would rather my entertainment also didn't remind me of all the worst things in the real world, but even I picked up on the - not particularly subtle - similarities to a certain famous/infamous politician.
But, luckily, I found the film was quirky and fun enough to ignore the flaws and I could occasionally tune out when it dragged a bit. Overall, a nice little film - probably not a classic, but definitely worth a watch (especially when it comes to streaming if you're unsure as to whether you want to pay full price at the cinema).

text: Mickey 17 is a solid sci fi film from Bong Joon Ho. The premise is pretty cool and I like the way they explore it. Robert Pattinson is fantastic. author: Zzacarias
title: Absolutely nails the humor
text:
Mickey 17 by Bong John is a dark comedy set in a dystopian future where cloning is a reality, but more intriguingly, where humanity is the invading force rather than the invaded. This inversion of the typical alien invasion narrative is a compelling perspective, though I have to admit, I was a bit surprised by the film's commercial approach. I went in expecting something more obscure, maybe something deeper in tone. That said, it's still a highly enjoyable film.
Bong Joon-ho's signature themes are unmistakable throughout. The film delves into personal sacrifice, critiques of authoritarianism, and the rigidity of cult-like ideologies. War is explored not through large-scale battles but through the decisions of a select few who shape the fate of many-often with reckless disregard for the consequences. Communication, or the lack thereof, plays a crucial role as well, mirroring our own world where language barriers fuel misunderstandings, sometimes with dire consequences.
One of the film's most striking ideas is its depiction of annihilation-not just in the physical sense, but in the erasure of an entire species' identity. It paints humanity as reckless, destructive, and dangerous. This is a theme we grapple with in real life, where it's easy to accept certain narratives without questioning them. The film cleverly presents this concept through a comedic lens, where we laugh at characters who seem foolishly impressionable. But beneath that humor lies a sharp critique of how easily people can be manipulated into adopting a single perspective without engaging in actual dialogue.
I was particularly reminded of The Host (2006), though this film leans more into comedy. On that front, it absolutely nails the humor. Mark Ruffalo delivers a fantastic performance with superb comedic timing-his mannerisms, the way he grabs the microphone, and his exaggerated grin make him totally unlikable in the best way possible.
However, where Mickey 17 falls short for me is in its more conventional elements. The romantic subplot, the dramatic sacrifice-it all felt a little too packaged, almost like a fabricated, studio-friendly addition. Not that these ideas are inherently bad, but given Bong Joon-ho's track record, I was expecting something less formulaic.
Another interesting aspect is how it handles cloning. The film raises the idea that if someone is infinitely replaceable, their value diminishes in the eyes of others. The clones share the same memories, yet their individual choices shape them differently. This challenges the assumption that people are solely shaped by their experiences, suggesting instead that personal choice plays a significant role in defining who we become. The contrast between Mickey 17 and Mickey 18 illustrates this well: one is gentle and kind, the other aggressive and defiant. Neither is portrayed as superior, reinforcing the idea that even with identical circumstances, we're still free to choose our own path.
Overall, Mickey 17 is a highly entertaining film with sharp humor and engaging themes. While it doesn't always go as deep as I initially hoped, it still offers plenty to think about, especially regarding identity, communication, and how easily we accept the narratives presented to us. It's a fun, thought-provoking ride-one that might not redefine the genre, but certainly leaves its mark.

author: ryanpersaud-59415
title: About as many good things as bad. A film that sorta feels like it needed some editing.
text:
Mickey 17 is acclaimed South Korean director Bong Joon-Ho's 2019 masterpiece, Parasite. Understandably, expectations were very high, but to be honest, I think Bong's English language offerings are always a bit of a step down from his Korean ones (Snowpiercer might be the exception).
Like many of his films, Mickey 17 uses science fiction as a vehicle to critique capitalism, class stratification, exploitation, and (as many Americans will quickly notice) political demagoguery. On the positive side, the world building here is really great; Bong has a distinct and kooky style that's impossible not to at least be amused by. This is a dystopia that appears far more realistic; mostly, people getting in a world everyone understands is deeply unfair and messed up, but are striving for change.
Mickey 17's world is brimming with features and idiosyncrasies that are a joy to explore. Everything from the "human printing" tech to the obsession with caloric output to the quasi-religious governmental structure, it's all great.
Unfortunately, there's a sense that Bong has too many strings dangling and not enough hands to pull them. I was a bit disappointed in the direction of the story (without spoiling, if you've seen Okja, this movie is honestly quite similar in tone and messaging). It felt like the most obvious and least interesting aspect of the world to me. Why not explore human printing more (as it's...what the movie is about). We get very little about what this technology means for humanity, either at the psychological, societal, economic, or political level. It seems quite strange that tech like this wouldn't fundamentally change EVERYTHING about human civilization.
The film also introduces many quirky, interesting characters, whom are mostly surface level. We have a pantheon of great actors, but little substance to any of them. It almost feels like certain characters, like Steven Yuen's Timo and Anamaria Vartolomei's Kai, are there until they aren't. And it's a shame, because these two characters - especially Yuen's - really needed more screen time.
Naomi Ackie's Nasha is genuinely one of the most confusing and poorly presented characters I've EVER seen. She's portrayed as a bit sex obsessed and self-serving, only to become this valiant hero out of basically nowhere. It's made worse by us learning about her SOLELY from Mickey's narration.
Speaking of which, Robert Pattinson, who plays all 18 Mickeys (mostly as 17 and 18), is definitely making a choice here, and I don't know if I loved it as much as I deeply respected it. It's truly incredible the career he's had post-Twilight; starting off as a heart throb to honestly being one of the best and most admirable actors of the era. His performance elevates this film every single scene he's in, but he can be grating and almost cartoonishly dense at time. Despite the film being ABOUT him, I felt he lacked interiority and depth.
This movie needed to be a character study, but shifts into a big sci-fi blockbuster, largely to its detriment. It's too plot heavy and not introspective enough and I don't understand why. We really didn't need a subplot about weird aliens; we needed to learn more about Mickey.
I'd recommend Mickey 17 to people; it's still fun, fresh, and interesting...but I can't help but feel so much was left on the table.

author: elicopperman
title: He's Dying to Save Mankind
text:
As of this month, South Korean filmmaker Bong Joon-ho has returned with his latest creative endeavor, Mickey 17. Based on the sci-fi novel Mickey7 by Edward Ashton, the film has garnered fairly decent responses from critics and audiences and I can safely call it a delightful sci-fi black comedy with quite a lot going on. Much of the film is carried by Bong's direction and the lead actor Robert Pattinson.
The film's main premise follows a man named Mickey Barnes who joins a space colony as an a disposable worker who gets cloned every time he dies for research purposes. As wacky as that concept sounds on paper, the film mostly takes its premise with the right amount of silliness and cynicism as the titular character initially loses much purpose having been cloned and regenerated time and time again after death. However, as soon as another Mickey clone comes into play, the stakes get more intense and we get to see a lot of range from Pattinson exhibiting contrasting personalities from each Mickey clone. Not only does the digital compositing look quite convincing, but it becomes easy to empathize with both Mickeys despite their separate personalities. It also adds some needed conflict between the Mickeys and his love interest Nasha, although the antics between others discovering the different Mickey clones are funnier on their own.
While the film doesn't delve into the concepts behind the cloning device used to regenerate Mickey too much, it does instead detail the suffering of some interesting caterpillar-like lifeforms referred to as "creepers". Given how much visual effects work was done on display, these creatures are as impressive to marvel at as they are initially intimidating. Perhaps what could be a throw off for some viewers is how the film delves into somewhat of an environmental message that also comments on the pettiness of greedy tyrants disguised as commanders. I personally think that the filmmakers handled this storyline pretty well since the fate of humanity partially lies in Mickey's hands already, although the expedition leader Kenneth Marshall comes off more one dimensional than anything else. That said, the inclusion of Mickey's childhood friend Timo is a nice addition to the set up and payoff of both characters ending up in space, and it's always nice to see Steven Yeun again.
As much as I enjoyed Mickey 17, I think it's best to check it out for yourself if you're truly curious. While it might not reach the same stature as Bong's other efforts, it's still a fun thrill ride all on its own. With the right blend of acting talent and chaotic storytelling, talented filmmakers like Bong can adapt someone else's work into something purely fun for the late winter / early spring season just fine.

author: iamianiman
title: Robert Pattinson's Best Performance Yet? Mickey 17 Might Just Be It
text:
Mickey 17 is a beautifully bizarre experience and we mean that in the best possible way. In a cinematic landscape flooded with sequels, reboots, and remakes, this film stands out as a beacon of originality. It's weird, it's unpredictable, and it keeps you on your toes from start to finish. The choices it makes are often ridiculous, but that's part of its charm. It's not a thriller designed to make your palms sweat or your heart race, but it never lets you feel fully relaxed either. Instead, it is meant to be a strange, delightful journey into the unknown.
And at the heart of this madness is Robert Pattinson. We're gonna say this... this is his best role yet. For anyone still seeing him as the brooding vampire from Twilight, Mickey 17 will be a revelation. Pattinson dives deep, delivering an offbeat, multifaceted performance that shows his full range. He plays multiple personalities with ease. He channels a sort of James McAvoy-in-Split energy, and even his voice feels transformed. There's a tension, a grit, a squeezed intensity to the way he speaks and it's mesmerizing. This role proves that Pattinson, with the right limelight, can actually be nominated and even won an Oscar.
The supporting cast also brings their A-game. Naomi Ackie is wonderful as Pattinson's romantic partner, while Steven Yeun nails his role as the guy you love to hate. Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette? Absolute scene-stealers, playing a power-hungry couple who mock the idiocy of real-world political leaders with biting, hilarious precision. And keep an eye on Anamaria Vartolomei, she's a rising star with undeniable charm.
But beneath the madness and humor lies something deeper. Mickey 17 tackles heavy themes like cloning ethics, animal cruelty, and the value of life. Through Mickey's journey, the film explores how society treats clones as expendable, as less than human and it forces you to confront some uncomfortable questions. Just because something can be replaced, does that mean it's okay to treat it as disposable? The film's message hits hard, even when wrapped in absurdity.
That said, Mickey 17 won't be for everyone. It's marketed for a wide audience, but its weirdness might alienate some. The third act takes some radical turns, and the film's creative freedom might feel like a bit too much for more conventional viewers. It's a film that demands you embrace its silliness and let go of your expectations.
Verdict: Mickey 17 is an eccentric, thought-provoking, and wildly original film powered by a career-defining performance from Robert Pattinson. It's weird, it's messy, and it's brilliant. It's a chaotic reflection of our world's political and ethical failures wrapped in sci-fi madness. Whether you love it or hate it, one thing's for sure: you won't forget it.

Mickey is a volunteered disposable human clone on a space expedition to colonize a new planet called Niflheim. Mickey's deaths are used for experimental reasons exposing him to all kinds of substances and viruses. One day, Mickey 17 makes it back to ship after a near-death incident, only to discover another Mickey has already been created. Chaos ensues.
I've been waiting to watch this movie for over a year and it was well worth the wait. Mickey 17 is a hilarious, absurd, creative and entertaining sci-fi comedy that has a lot of heart. It feels so grand, much more than I expected.
On the surface, Bong Joon-ho has crafted an entertaining as hell story. Mickey's experience with the worst job I think I have ever seen a character have is fun to watch in of itself, but the story really picks up when Mickey 18 is introduced. Interesting plot points are started involving a love triangle (or diamond), the idea of multiples being too dangerous, the Mickeys having completely different personalities and more. Bong does a great job using these fun ideas to build up drama and stakes for the story even though Mickey could easily come back. The plot line with the Creepers clashes with the absurd tone a little bit, but it makes the film more grand and gives it a bigger picture on why the villains are scum of the earth.
The movie also has a lot of political commentary here. A lot of the story deals with corruption and lack of empathy from higher ups. Mickey is treated as a chew toy by all of the scientists as they make him die in bizarre and often painful ways. It's clear they couldn't care less about how he feels about his job and how he feels when he dies. There is an even bigger picture though with invasion. The creatures on the planet are not as dangerous as they seem, but they are treated as threats to the human race even though humans are the invaders here. Mickey 17 is not subtle at all with its messages against colonization, but I like that. I feel more movies should worry less about being subtle at this point with powerful messages like this.
Even in the more dramatic moments, Mickey 17 never takes itself too seriously. It has all kinds of gags from physical, to editing jokes, to clever dialogue, and subtle moments like the insanely long line Mickey stands in to get his job. I found this movie to be a riot. This movie has a lot of funny moments that flow well with the story, but the comedy never takes away from the drama.
Robert Pattinson is so good as Mickey. His voice alone is unrecognizable at times and his comedic timing is immaculate. He does a great job narrating the story and his shy attitude as 17 is so endearing to watch. His duel role as Mickey 18 is just as fun to watch as he is so much meaner and blunt than 17. Robert Pattinson makes this movie so entertaining with his dual performance as 17 and 18 here.
Naomi Ackie is awesome as Nasha here too. She is such a strong presence who gives Mickey a reason to keep going showing a great combination of strength and sweetness. Ackie's performance is filled with personality from excitement, fun, caring and angry making Nasha a memorable character. It helps that Ackie shares great chemistry with Pattinson and it is fun watching them in every scene.
Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette both make for highly entertaining villains. Ruffalo goes all in here with his hammy performance of the most evil politician imaginable and reveling in the fake politeness towards everyone. It helps that although Marshall is very silly, it does not make him and his wife any less despicable and I like how their motives never make them the slightest bit sympathetic. They are truly irredeemable and I love that. I also like seeing Toni Collette play as a bad guy because she almost always heroic in her roles so it's interesting to see her as an irredeemable villain.
Visually, the movie looks outstanding. The sets capture the look of a space colony that looks like a prison to the workers beautifully. The caves look very interesting to explore as well. I love the way the Creepers look. They are the most adorable "ugly" creatures I have seen in a movie in a long time and the effects on them look very solid. The cinematography by Darius Khondji is very slick with its composition and visual storytelling. I personally really like the shot where the line for Mickey's interview for the job is multiple floors long. The cinematography plays into the comedy of the movie in subtle moments such as that. The editing is great too with a funny death montage and two different arguments building up at the same time raising the drama. The editing keeps this movie going at a steady pace.
I love the score by Jung Jae-il. It has a classical music feel to the score and it fits the tone of the movie perfectly. I really like the score of that plays during the credits and I want to listen to it on my own time.
In general, Mickey 17 is a great movie that juggles its different elements pretty well, but there a couple times where I felt that some scenes could have been paced a bit better and I think it is a bit overstuffed with how much it tries to do. I do not think it is as uneven as I heard it was though because the movie never loses its sense of humor.
Aside from a couple minor issues, I really dug Mickey 17. It is a humorous sci-fi epic that does not pull any punches with its commentary and features some amazing comedic performances. I just love that we got a beautiful, crazy and unique sci-fi blockbuster film that is not action driven. I cannot wait to see what Bong Joon-ho does after this film because between this and Parasite, he is an insanely talented filmmaker.

author: pgrancharov
title: Mediocre
text:
While Bong Joon Ho is celebrated for his visionary storytelling, Mickey 17 seems to fall short of expectations. The film's plot, centered around a man who is repeatedly cloned after dying on a distant ice planet, feels aimless and overly absurd. The narrative lacks coherence, with heavy-handed themes and scattered storytelling detracting from the overall experience.

Robert Pattinson's performance as multiple versions of Mickey is commendable, but his exaggerated accent and the repetitive nature of his character's plight can become grating. The supporting cast, though talented, is underutilized, and many characters come across as selfish and unlikable. The film's pacing is another issue, with its two-hour-plus runtime feeling unnecessarily stretched.

Visually, while the icy landscapes of the planet Niflheim are striking, the film's reliance on quirky humor and rushed subplots undermines its more serious themes. The political and philosophical discourse, though ambitious, often feels superficial and fails to resonate as deeply as Bong's previous works like Parasite.

Overall, Mickey 17 struggles to balance its dark comedy, social critique, and sci-fi elements, leaving audiences with a film that is more frustrating than thought-provoking.

author: Papaya_Horror
title: " Mickey 17's" Bong Joon-ho, is a Bold, Bizarre, and Brilliantly Bleak Sci-Fi Satire!!!
text:
It's hard to describe "Mickey 17" without sounding completely unhinged. Bong Joon-ho, the mastermind behind Parasite (2019), has crafted a film so odd, so unrelenting in its dystopian goofy satire, that it feels like a fever dream of the world we're currently drowning in.

Based on Edward Ashton's Mickey7, this is a sci-fi odyssey about cloning, capitalism, colonialism, and the never-ending cycle of human stupidity. It's not just about survival - it's about what we're willing to sacrifice (or, more accurately, who we're willing to sacrifice) in the name of progress.

Robert Pattinson plays Mickey Barnes, an "Expendable" with one job: die. Over and over. His consciousness is uploaded, his body is reprinted, and he's sent out again to suffer for the sake of humanity's colonization of the ice planet Niflheim.

He's cannon fodder for science experiments, the guy who breathes the toxic air first. The one who checks if a vaccine is lethal. And because he's been "reprinted" so many times, he's developed a sense of detachment - his own existence feels more like a bureaucratic inconvenience than anything sacred.

But then something goes wrong. Two Mickeys exist at the same time: the pragmatic, pacifist Mickey 17 and the more ruthless, violent Mickey 18. And suddenly, the fight isn't just for survival - it's for identity, agency, and what it really means to be human.

Let's be honest..."Mickey 17" is weird...Not in a cutesy, quirky way, but in an unsettling, disorienting way that makes you question if you actually understand the movie while watching it.

Bong doesn't hold your hand - this is an ambitious, sprawling narrative packed with sharp political commentary on the post-Trump era, South Korea's government, and ongoing social issues. Its sweeping visuals create a world that's, both eerily alien and disturbingly familiar.

The pacing is uneven, the runtime overstretched, and the sheer amount of ideas crammed into it can be overwhelming. But here's the thing: IT WORKS. The disorientation is intentional. The absurdity mirrors the absurdity of our own reality.

Pattinson delivers a career-best performance (yes, even better than The Lighthouse). His ability to oscillate between existential exhaustion, dark humour, and sheer terror makes Mickey, both relatable and deeply tragic. Naomi Ackie, Steven Yeun, Mark Ruffalo, and Toni Collette round out an insanely stellar cast, each bringing their A-game to characters who, in lesser hands, might have felt one-note.

Special mention goes to Collette, whose portrayal of Ylfa - Kenneth's Machiavellian wife - feels like a twisted blend of Lady Macbeth and a Michelin-star chef obsessed with perfecting sauces.

And then there's the planet itself. The native creatures - massive, woolly centipede-like beings - are first framed as terrifying, only to be revealed as intelligent, peaceful beings just trying to defend their home. The colonial allegory is impossible to ignore.

The film is a brutal critique of how power manufactures fear, and how propaganda turns indigenous populations into "monsters" to justify exploitation.

Kenneth (Ruffalo) plays the ultimate dictator, stoking division and selling the illusion of progress while reducing women to mere baby-makers, treating them as expendable. But Bong, as always, finds complexity even in the villains.

The two Mickeys - one advocating for peace, the other for rebellion - are where the film gets really interesting. It's a battle between submission and resistance, between working within the system and tearing it down. It's a question we face every day. Can we create change peacefully, or is a more forceful approach necessary?

The film doesn't offer easy answers, but it does suggest that both sides of that struggle exist within all of us.

For all its bleakness, "Mickey 17" closes on a note of cautious hope. Justice, in some form, prevails. But as the credits rolled, I felt a familiar emptiness creep in. Because of all the film's satire, it never stops reflecting on our own broken world.

The difference is, that Bong seems to believe there's still a way out. And maybe that's the kind of delusion we need right now.

author: SAFEOWN
title: Mickey 17 Delivers Thrills, Depth, and Stunning Visuals
text:
Bong Joon-ho has done it again! Mickey 17 is not just another sci-fi film; it's an intellectual and emotional rollercoaster that redefines the genre. With a gripping storyline, top-tier performances, and stunning visuals, this film is easily the best sci-fi movie of the year.
The story follows Mickey Barnes, an "Expendable"-a disposable human used for dangerous space colonization missions. Every time he dies, his consciousness is transferred into a new clone, allowing the mission to continue without interruption. But things take a wild turn when Mickey 17, presumed dead, miraculously survives and returns-only to discover that he has already been replaced by Mickey 18. With two versions of himself existing at the same time, they must navigate this impossible situation without being discovered, as having more than one clone at a time is strictly forbidden.
The film masterfully explores deep existential and political themes, from identity and self-worth to class inequality and exploitation. Mickey, as an Expendable, represents the dehumanization of labor-a person reduced to nothing more than a tool for corporate interests. The way Bong Joon-ho weaves in these thought-provoking elements while maintaining a gripping narrative is simply brilliant.
Robert Pattinson Delivers an Oscar-Worthy Performance
Pattinson's performance is next-level phenomenal. He flawlessly portrays two versions of the same character, making each Mickey feel distinct. His body language, tone of voice, and subtle facial expressions immediately tell us who is Mickey 17 and who is Mickey 18, even before a single word is spoken. It's a level of dedication that truly makes the film immersive.
An Exceptional Supporting Cast
The supporting cast is just as impressive. Naomi Ackie, as the female lead, plays a crucial role in the story, adding depth and emotional weight. Steven Yeun, Toni Collette, and Mark Ruffalo also shine in their respective roles, with Ruffalo delivering a villain so infuriating that you'll want to punch him through the screen. His political ideology, which justifies using clones as expendable workers in space colonization, is disturbing yet eerily realistic.
Visual Effects That Push the Boundaries of Sci-Fi
Visually, Mickey 17 is a feast for the eyes. The work of DNEG, Framestore, Rising Sun Pictures, and Turncoat Pictures is nothing short of breathtaking. The CGI is so seamlessly integrated that you forget it's even there. The space environments, the cloning technology, and the alien designs all feel incredibly realistic, elevating the film's immersive experience.
A Sci-Fi Film with Political and Philosophical Depth
At its core, Mickey 17 is more than just an action-packed sci-fi thriller-it's a political and philosophical statement. The way it handles the theme of human prejudice against the unknown is particularly striking. The film challenges our instinctive fear of aliens, making us question why we always assume extraterrestrial beings must be hostile. It holds up a mirror to humanity's own history of colonization and oppression, forcing us to confront uncomfortable truths.
Final Verdict: 10/10 - A Sci-Fi Classic in the Making
Bong Joon-ho's direction is impeccable, blending stunning cinematography, masterful storytelling, and a thought-provoking narrative into a cinematic masterpiece. Mickey 17 is not just the best sci-fi film of the year-it's one of the best of the decade. If you love intelligent, socially relevant science fiction, this film is an absolute must-watch.
