title: Already flawed film ruined by 2 awful razzie performances
text:
Bong Joon Ho's big budget Hollywood film falls victim to the culture within Hollywood that has for the past few years been leading to its slow demise. Mickey 17 had a lot of interesting ideas that could have been fleshed out into something special, something that Bong Joon Ho's cleverly did in his Oscar winning 'Parasite'. He's an incredibly talented director whose other films such as 'The Host', 'Mother' and 'Snowpiercer' I have greatly enjoyed.
Robert Pattison is great in this film as the expendable Mickey, who has elected himself for various dangerous tasks on a space mission to colonize a planet. Every time Mickey dies, he is re-printed once again with his memories of the previous Mickey left largely intact, until a regeneration mishap leads to 2 of them being alive at the same time. The protocol in place for expendables is that, only one can exist.
The themes of existential dread, death and rebirth could have made for a very interesting film, but they are sadly cast aside in favour of some strange choices where this film suffers from multiple identities not knowing what kind of film it wants to be.
Mickey 17 suffers from many flaws because of this (especially the long drawn out third act) and isn't perfect. This is severely impacted by Mark Ruffalo who seems to think this film is the perfect vehicle to have a therapy session at the audiences expense, by parodying someone who he has made very clear he hates with every fibre of his being.
Toni Collete's performance is also terrible, but at least she's not going full TDS.
Mickey 17 is just an average film that aimed for greatness, and like Icarus its wings have been severely burnt by it's ambitions.

author: arungeorge13
title: Maybe not a future classic, but it's still worth your time. [+72%]
text:
Part of me thinks the film would've made for extremely biting dark-comedy-satire purely as an identity crisis drama featuring the Mickeys (that ain't a spoiler, duh), but Mickey 17 is still a finely crafted film as is. It does remind you occasionally of Bong Joon Ho's previous works Okja (for its commentary on meat consumption), Snowpiercer (for its icy, dystopian setting and hot takes on classism), Mother (that might lead to a spoiler, so NO!), and more. In essence, Bong's works all carry that undertone of contemporary outburst. In Mickey 17, it's just all too obvious but given a large studio's involvement (WB Pictures), I was only wondering how much of Bong's narrative signature would be present. It's safe to say that Mickey 17 is STILL VERY MUCH Bong Joon Ho's, and also a film where he tries mashing one too many genres.
Not all of that genre-mashing ends up a ravishing success, though from the perspectives of cinematography (Darius Khondji), production design (Fiona Crombie), music (Jung Jae-il), and edits (Yang Jin-mo), it's a winner. The performances are superb-Pattinson internalizes and presents two contrasting Mickeys, both worthy of a larger discussion; Naomi Ackie (as Nasha) offers a melting pot of different emotions including a solid lose-it-all scene in the final act; Steven Yeun as the conniving buddy is a blast; and of course, the main baddie duo, a very Trump-Musk-esque Mark Ruffalo (as failed politician Kenneth Marshall) and Toni Collette (as Marshall's wife Ylfa). Special shoutouts must go to Anamaria Vartolomei (as Kai), Cameron Britton (as Arkady), and Patsy Ferran (as Dorothy).
Now, let me bring up some of the things that didn't work all that much for me. Firstly, the descriptive voiceovers -- why? Most of it was conveyed visually, so a lot of it comes off as spoonfeeding (almost saying, hey this is a very simple movie if you didn't crack that already). Also, like I said initially, the film doesn't explore themes like colonization and cloning as much as it should've.. which is also why Mickey 17 isn't as UNFORGETTABLE as Parasite or Okja. Still, still, still.. there's plenty of FUN to be had (that dinner scene, especially, was an absolute riot!).

author: sweetzero_ita
title: Bong Joon-ho disappointed me for the first time
text:
First of all, I should state that I have been a huge supporter of the director's films since Memories of Murder and, of course, Parasite.
When I first heard about this movie, I thought I would watch another very high-quality movie, so I bought my ticket on the first day it was released and went to the cinema for the first time in a long time. But I can say that I was definitely a little disappointed.
If we come to the reasons for this; first of all, the movie is not a bad movie. But it is a movie that does not suit the director. The genre of the movie is definitely not science fiction. It is more comedy-science fiction. In fact, the comedy part is much more dominant, and sometimes the science fiction part is left far behind. From this perspective, I likened it to the movie Poor Things. From my perspective, I divide the movie into two. The first 45 minutes and the last hour and a half.
For the first 45 minutes, I thought I was going to watch a really good science fiction movie. Especially Mickey's loneliness and character are very well integrated into the movie. Also, in this part, the movie manages the science fiction part very well. However, in the continuation, the movie turns into a complete comedy movie, and this is the part I did not like as much as the first part.
The acting in the movie is quite successful. Robert Pattinson has portrayed Mickey 17 and the other Mickeys (I won't give details here to avoid spoilers) very successfully. He is very good at switching between different emotions. He may not give a performance that would carry the movie on its own, but he doesn't need to do that anyway.
First of all, Naomi Ackie and Steven Yeun also gave very successful acting. Steven is very cute, Naomi has a very predatory image. Naomi's performance in particular adds value to the movie. I'm sure we will watch her in many more projects in the future. Now, let's come to the performances that really need to be talked about. Of course, I'm talking about Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette's performance. Although these two are very good actors, the characters they play seem like very cliché characters to me. Even though they act very well, I think they damaged the tone of the movie. Especially Mark Ruffalo (who I really like) turns the movie into a comedy with the character he plays. Unfortunately, Toni Colette also supports him in doing this.
As for the technical aspects of the film, I can say that I liked it. You can get the feeling that it was all shot in a studio while watching the film. But this doesn't bother you that much. Both the interiors and the snowy atmosphere outside are well incorporated into the film. In fact, a famous Iranian cinematographer was employed and he did a very successful job. The production quality was also quite sufficient.
To write the last sentences, I would have been much happier if someone else had made this movie. Unfortunately, it was not a movie I wanted to watch from Bong Joon-ho. He made the ending very fait accompli. The ending of the movie resembles a comedy movie more than a science fiction movie. I wish it had been a more enviable movie. I don't think I will ever go to Bong Joon-ho's movies again from the first day :)
p. Anamaria Vartolomei looks very beautiful in the movie.

author: tm-sheehan
title: Great Sci Fi comedy satire
text:
My Review- Mickey 17
My Rating. 9/10
In Cinemas now
I wondered if I would enjoy South Korean Director Bong Joon Ho's first feature movie after his brilliant Oscar winning movie of 2019 Parasite ,especially being his first movie in the English language so I was pleasantly surprised with the originality and clever satire of Mickey 17.
The impressive cast that includes Robert Pattinson, Toni Collette and Mark Ruffalo was sufficient enough reason to capture my interest however as I've often said in my reviews big star names are not enough to make an impressive movie .
Mickey 17 however has a skilled writer and Oscar winning director Bong Joon Ho at the helm plus great cinematography and special effects .
I would describe this movie as a satirical Science fiction black comedy that sends up charismatic politicians, the consequences of planetary neglect ,untested modern technology and the expense and folly of plundering other worlds when we are destroying the one we inhabit.
I've been a fan of Robert Pattinson's acting and range of varied roles for years in movies like The Lighthouse and The King 2019 as well as The Twilight franchise and Little Ashes 2008 and this role of Mickey 17 is a career highlight in my opinion.
In Mickey 17 he plays two lead characters which are referred to as expendables which are the disposable crew members on a space mission, selected for dangerous tasks because they can be renewed when their body dies
with their memories largely intact.
With one regeneration however things go very wrong when Mickey 18 appears on the scene as he has a very different tougher personality to Mickey 17 who is a more benign sweet guy who's life was spared in a savage cave encounter with alien creatures called the creepers .
The creepers who resemble huge crablike creatures allow Mickey 17 to return to the ship where he meets girlfriend Nasha played by Naomi Ackie who is rather pleased to have two different versions of her lover Mickey .
I want as many people to see Mickey 17 as possible as I think this could possibly become a cult classic like Dr. Strangelove 1964 or Don't Look Up 2021 so to divulge to much of the plot would be unfair and spoil the surprise.
My only criticism of this original ,funny and spectacular sci fi movie is that I think 2hours and 17 minutes is about 30 minutes to long however it held my interest right up to the exciting conclusion.
Bong Joon Ho adapted his screenplay from the novel Mickey7 by Edward Ashton and was quoted as saying that none of the characters portrayed were meant to be mirroring active politicians .
However I couldn't help but compare the charismatic evangelical but unhinged media personality of Mark Ruffalo's character Kenneth Marshall with a certain prominent politician constantly in the media today ,there's even a reference to a severed ear in the script.
Both Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette as his exotic wife Ylfa who has more ambition driven influence than charm must have had a ball playing their roles .
Production of this movie commenced in August 2022 and finished in 2023 when Bong Joon Ho worked on the final cut which premiered at the 75th Berlin International Film Festival in February this year.
Mickey 17 was a total surprise for me it's funny ,thought provoking ,entertaining and very satirical adventure I thoroughly enjoyed it .

author: petraktheman
title: A Bizarre, but Very Imaginative Sci-Fi Dark Comedy
text: A fascinating and immensely entertaining dark comedy filled to the brim with bizarre setups, morbid curiosity, and a great balance between sharp political satire and expressive physical comedy. Great sci-fi concepts about transferring human consciousness into clones and potentially living on years after your expiration date, but opening an ethical can of worms with all the possibilities for exploitation. Robbert Pattinson kills it (literally) playing against himself in the dual lead roles with such an expressive range of acting. Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette's characters are entertaining. They start off as sharp satires of current shady politics and corporate short-sighted greed, but devolve into cartoonish buffoons by the last third of the movie. It's hilarious, but admittedly bit too on the nose. The cute roly-poly "creeper" aliens are cute and serve a nice subversion for what we typically perceive as animalistic alien life. The movie definitely isn't for everyone, but personally, it had me on the edge of my seat the entire time and I strongly recommend it for those with an open mind for sci-fi and dark comedies. Mickey might be expendable, but Bong Joon-Ho's imagination certainly isn't!

title: Really dull and wasteful movie
text:
The first act of the film was really interesting. This is mostly what you see in trailers.
But when the second act begins, the enjoyment ends.
It's as if the writers had a great log-line but didn't know how to plot it out intelligibly, and just made it up as they went along, paying homage to Terry Gilliam but lacking the wit.
It's really a shame, because Bong Joon Ho has made some really good movies, my favorites being The Host, Snowpiercer and Parasite.
Sadly, Mickey 17 is a huge toe-stub for him.
Honestly it got to the point where about half way through the movie I just started daydreaming, because there was nothing else to do.
The script had lost its way so badly that it was just throwing useless dialog at badly designed characters who had no continuity of behavior.
The main character, Mickey Barnes (Robert Pattinson), at least had an excuse to be a little different as the movie progressed. But while he tried his best to bring his character(s) to life in different ways (no pun intended), Pattinson should have turned down this awful script, because it did not help his career.
Mickey was not very likable from the start of his story arc, and there wasn't much of an arc; it was more of a straight line that began with a dumb decision and bounced him chaotically through a series of misadventures designed by a set-chewing charismatic nincompoop named Kenneth Marshall (Mark Ruffalo in a role that was WAY beneath him).
Sorry Ruffalo, don't play dumb characters ever again. Stick to the intelligent ones.
Marshall was by far the worst figure in the movie, with a cardboard personality who acted like a wind-up clown with dialog that was so pointless that I literally suffered trying to listen to him.
So much of the movie was wasted opportunity. It was a long, long plot that had no idea where it was going, taking caricatures on a joy ride that sent them all over the place without accomplishing any goals I could track, and leaving me without any chance of suspense and nobody to relate to.
The movie was supposed to be a comedy but aside from a chuckle here and there, I found it more frustrating than anything else.
Don't waste your money on this one folks.

author: shaht-16429
title: It has everything you would want in a Bong Joon Ho movie, but less
text:
Mickey 17 tells the story of Mickey Barnes (Pattinson) who signs up to become an 'expendable' after his life on earth falters. His job is to die over and over again so the scientists aboard the ship he's on can study how to adapt to the world they hope to colonize, dubbing the new world "Nilfheim'. After 16 deaths, Mickey #17 is left for dead, but miraculously survives after a group of indigenous creatures dubbed 'creepers' brings him back to the base, and in that time he comes into contact with Mickey #18, a more hardened and fearless clone, compared to the meek and obedient Mickey #17.
It has been five years since Bong Joon-ho Oscar winning masterpiece Parasite, and it was always going to be a tough act to follow. 'Mickey 17' explores its very fun premise of space colonization with cloning and adds an element of social commentary, with the idea of expendable clones, colour coordinated roles, the dastardly commander Kenneth Marshall (Ruffalo) and his over bearing wife Ylfa (Collette) exploring the idea of human disposability and social hierarchies. Mickey being treated as a lower life form bodes well for the narrative as he even acts as if he is less than his coworkers. Pattinson delivers a career best performance making the most of his roles, giving both version of Mickey very well defined body language and vocal ticks. Its a difficult task to make two well defined versions of the same character, but the dedication of the role is felt even in his facial muscles. The movie also excels in its humour, it has a very dark humour and makes a lot of jokes with its premise of cloning and colonization, but it doesn't quite go all the way.
The world of Mickey 17 is quite an interesting one. Mankind is fleeing to space to colonize nearby planets because life on earth is bad, economically, environmentally, sociologically, and this is where the movie kind of falters. Kenneth Marshall is very Trump-coded, but Ruffalo's performance feels like he's doing a less flamboyant Austin Powers impression, especially the way he moves his teeth and hands. It's not a terrible performance but it's pretty distracting. It sometimes feels like the movie is sacrificing its interesting concepts and fun dark humour to take some cheap political shots. I'm all for a movie being political, taking a stand and jabbing Trump but not at the expense of telling a fun story. There are a couple of characters who do not realize their full potential, for example Kai (Vartolomei), an upper tier soldier who stands up to some of the abuse of Mickey #17, she appears for a few minutes and then the plot drops her two thirds of the way in the movie safe for a couple of scenes. Another character, Timo (Yuen) is a pilot who is Mickey's close friend and business partner, who has a drug subplot that felt like it was ripped out of Avatar, as well as an earth subplot, and his storylines are not really woven into the narrative in a satisfying way; they just exist and are resolved independently as a footnote in the movie. However, the main plotline, involving the creepers, the space colonies, power hierarchies and cloning are actually explored well and in a satisfying way.
I don't know how the movie made tarantula-millepedes-pill-bug hybrids both scary and adorable, but like Okja, it managed to make us fall in love with otherworldly beasts. Toni Colette managed to be scarier, as intended. I went into this movie not expecting it to be better than Parasite, and I exited the theatre pleased. It's funny when it needs to be, the pacing is good, the score is majestic and the visuals and set pieces look realistic enough for the high concept movie. If you are expecting a Bong Joon-ho movie with eccentric characters, social and environmental commentary, absurd sci-fi concepts, with some extremely tense and funny moments, then you won't be disappointed.

author: MovieWarfare
title: Robert Pattinson doing another funny accent is always worth the price of admission
text:
Five years after winning Best Picture for Parasite, Bong Joon-ho returns with Mickey 17. The big question is: does this live up to his previous work, or is it a disappointing step down?
What initially drew me to this movie was its intriguing concept. The idea of a person whose sole job is to die repeatedly for the sake of humanity-thanks to cloning technology-is both fascinating and disturbing. For the most part, the film explores the political, religious, and ethical dilemmas that would arise if such technology existed. Bong Joon-ho uses this premise to craft a sharp satire on American politics while exploring deeper themes about identity and what makes us truly human. The writing is strong, filled with clever comedic moments, subtle jabs, and a genuine message. At its core, Mickey 17 also functions as a quiet coming-of-age story for its protagonist, leading to a satisfying and well-earned conclusion.
Visually, the film is stunning. The production design-from the sets to the costumes and even the CGI-is impressive. The ship's muted colors and claustrophobic layout reinforce Mickey's status as a disposable worker, making his existence feel suffocating. This contrasts beautifully with the planet Niflheim, which is bright and open, creating a striking visual juxtaposition. The alien designs are both grotesque and strangely adorable, a testament to Bong's ability to balance the bizarre with the endearing.
Robert Pattinson delivers a phenomenal performance as both Mickey 17 and Mickey 18, giving each iteration a distinct personality. His chemistry with himself is oddly compelling, and he also shares strong on-screen moments with Naomi Ackie, who plays his love interest. Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette are a delight as the film's over-the-top, egomaniacal antagonists, fully embracing the darkly comedic tone.
That said, their performances might be divisive. Ruffalo and Collette lean into cartoonish villainy, which contrasts with the relatively restrained performances of the rest of the cast. Given the film's dark comedic edge, I think it works, but some viewers may find it jarring. Additionally, supporting characters played by Steven Yeun and Anamaria Vartolomei are saddled with underdeveloped subplots that feel tacked on rather than essential. Vartolomei's character, in particular, seems to be heading toward a revenge arc that never fully materializes, and both their storylines are wrapped up in an unsatisfying manner.
If I had any nitpicks, I wish we had seen more of Mickey's past deaths, considering he's died 16 times before the film's events. The movie establishes that each clone has a slightly different personality, but rather than showing this, it's mostly told to us. There's also an expository scene explaining why having multiple clones is forbidden, featuring a backstory so compelling that I almost wished that were the film instead.
Overall, Mickey 17 is a fun and thought-provoking addition to the sci-fi genre. While it doesn't fully capitalize on its ambitious concept, the story it tells remains engaging and entertaining. It works as both a popcorn flick and a film with meaningful themes. Plus, Robert Pattinson doing another funny accent is always worth the price of admission.

author: DanTheMan2150AD
title: Unfortunately, I didn't see Mickey 2 to 16. Can anyone fill me in on what I missed?
text: Veering from slapstick to absurdism to horror and back again, often within a single shot, Mickey 17 has all the makings of a thought-provoking sci-fi epic but loses momentum somewhere between its intriguing premise and its bloated runtime. Balancing absurdity with poignant commentary, it creates a compelling narrative despite the oddities in its story and the washed-out photography. Thankfully, it more than makes up for these shortcomings due to a thrilling central performance from Robert Pattinson and some engrossing direction from Bong Joon-ho, crafting a darkly humorous yet surprisingly optimistic satirical sci-fi romp about life, love, mortality and identity amid the stars, even in the bleakest of circumstances. One can't complain too much about a loving genre craftsman making another wacky sci-fi action caper with enough ideas to fill another 3 films, but that makes it somewhat incoherently uneven at points. Cramming a career's worth of fixations and passions into one overstuffed narrative, Mickey 17 will unfortunately suffer from comparisons to Bong Joon-ho's earlier works, yet it possesses plenty of creativity to spare.

author: gwendilinb
title: Uneven but still enjoyable
text: Pattinson and Yuen deliver phenomenal performances, as expected, in this sci-fi slapstick comedy. The film cleverly employs a lighthearted approach to explore weighty and familiar ethical issues, making for an engaging and thought-provoking experience. The first half shines, offering genuine laughs at the expense of our hapless protagonist, showcasing clever writing and impeccable comedic timing. However, the second half unfortunately falters. The plot begins to drag, feeling overly bloated as the initial premise wears thin. The film relies too heavily and for too long on the same comic mechanisms that initially felt fresh and inventive, leading to diminishing returns. While entertaining and certainly watchable, the film doesn't offer anything truly groundbreaking or conceptually new. It treads familiar ground in the sci-fi genre with a comedic twist. Despite its shortcomings, it's a worthwhile watch for any devoted Pattinson fan and serves as a solid introduction for those yet to be acquainted with his range. Yuen's performance is equally compelling and adds another layer of enjoyment to the film. Ultimately, the film is a fun, albeit somewhat uneven, ride.

author: divineflame06
title: Bong Joon Ho and Robert Pattinson Deliver a Darkly Funny, Thought-Provoking Sci-Fi Ride
text:
Yet another winner from Bong Joon Ho's hat! Mickey 17 is wildly funny and thought-provoking, blending Bong's signature social critique with sudden, thrilling tone shifts. Robert Pattinson is a darling in this one-ironically, the more of him there is, the less there seems to be! He delivers a brilliant performance, effortlessly switching between different versions of Mickey with charm, vulnerability, and just the right amount of madness.
The film follows Mickey (Robert), an 'expendable' in a space colonization mission whose sole job is to die and be cloned back, over and over again. What starts as a darkly comic premise soon unravels into a layered exploration of identity, morality, and the cost of survival. Bong's direction is as sharp as ever, seamlessly balancing absurd humor with deep existential dread. The visuals are stunning, with slick, immersive world-building that enhances the film's eerie yet oddly intimate tone. The narration keeps you hooked, revealing just enough to keep you questioning everything. Mickey 17 is another masterful ride-unexpected, clever, visually striking, and deeply human.

author: adamgresch
title: There are only two reasons this movie hasn't gotten a higher IMDB rating
text:
Let's start with the first and most obvious reason: this is political commentary that is tailor-made to upset anyone that truly espouses today's brand of free market capitalist and socially conservative ideals. I get it. If a movie lampoons the guy you voted for and everything he stands for, you'll be too busy seeing red (get it?) to enjoy the film.
The second reason this film might not be receiving the flowers we might all have expected is nearly as obvious as the first. Bong Joon-ho had the unenviable task of following up on the masterpiece that was Parasite. It should be no surprise that Mickey 17 was always doomed to be judged the lesser film when measured against such an unattainable benchmark.
All of that being said, Mickey 17 is still an incredible movie. Bear in mind, I've yet to read the book, so I cannot speak to its treatment of the source material. But, taken on its own, this is a fantastic movie. The acting performances were absolutely first rate. Mark Ruffalo is quickly becoming one of my new favorite actors after I'd previously written him off for playing a mostly wooden Hulk in the MCU. Robert Pattinson and Toni Colette were both stellar, as always. One negative I would have on this front was that Steven Yuen did feel underutilized, as some others have mentioned. Though, you could just as easily say that he left us all wanting more screen time from him than we were given.
The story felt well-paced, the satire never felt ham fisted, and the cinematography was really well done. Overall, this is another top-tier film from Bong Joon-ho. Fair or not, it only gets a 9/10 from me on the sheer fact that it's not Parasite.

author: rendanellifilms

author: rgkarim
title: Mickey 17: So Many Tales, So Little Time
text:
LIKES:
Shot Well
Great Society Reflections
Believable Science-Fiction
Good Acting
Very Good Visuals/Settings
Dark Humor Decently Toned Down
A Decent Story
Great Climax
DISLIKES:
A Little Too Sexual
Some Pointless Story Elements
Not As Exciting
Very Slow Opening
I Don't Like Animal Torture
A Little Eccentric/Assertive Acting At Times
The VERDICT
Mickey 17 is a movie with the style of Ho coming to life with Ashton's imagination. The movie is stylish, a fantastic cinematic experience that brings amazing visuals to life to illustrate "humanity's future" in a way that only Ho can envision. Strong use of CIG and a fantastic costume department give our cast a realistic sheen to the Sci-Fi piece. It provides the desperation of the situation an extra edge without tripping into too much fictional territory that this genre sometimes strays into. Mickey's cinematic splendor holds a lot of nuances alongside the visual prowess, an extra easter egg that will add some more enjoyment to the curious mind.
In regards to the story itself, the movie is very intelligent in the presentation of such a sensitive and controversial subject as societal roles. Mickey 17 has a lot of elements to it as the genres of Adventure, Sci-Fi, Drama, and Comedy come together in a decently balanced way. The adventure element is nicely placed in the excavation and pacing, working hard to establish a motif for all the antics and expand on the world that Mickey volunteers into. The Sci-Fi is the setting and tone, with a few elements embedded into the adventure to help give it more than Ho's last grounded piece. Where the movie thrives is the drama and comedy elements, a large character developing tale that puts an oddball among a lot of factions and trying to help decipher the goods and bads of this expedition. Ho and Ashton's writing come together brilliantly to examine a lot of modern-day themes, where an Expendable like Mickey doesn't have any super powers to face the growing pressures set by the elite. The twist worked for me, and the multi-level pokes helped flesh out the characters to be believable and entertaining to watch. Comedic stabs were present, and a lot of darkness worked into the lines that crossed the lines at most avenues just right that had me and the audience laughing. I found most of it kept intact, and the relevance/matching of the situation to modern life is remarkably startling to carry more merit than I had expected. Such a believable tale holds surprisingly good climactic finishes that don't get lost in special effects and maintain the direction they started with the crazy tale.
All of this is brought to life by a great cast, each member doing their part to make this voyaging group feel very personable and relatable, and a dynamic congregation that does representation just right while maintaining the story. Pattinson, in particular, impressed me with his range, each Mickey holding just enough quirks to make him change his approach while sounding so different from the usual roles I've seen him play. The others did just fine in their roles, but for time purposes, I'll move on to the dislikes.
All the likes I have for the movie come with some surprises that I didn't expect for someone of Ho's caliber. For one thing, Mickey's dark humor goes toward more sexual tones that don't do much for me when slung about so haphazardly. It's not the most indulgent, but it seems like it will be a bigger plot point and then becomes just a vulgar side-story that didn't feel necessary to the extent we got. Sadly, this movie has several other factors and plot points that were alluded to being big impacts, yet sort of fall to the side for large swaths of time before they reemerge in some factor that often felt unimpressive and hastily remembered. This isn't Ho's normal style, and I feel that Mickey 17's tale had a lot of things he wanted to address and a time limit that did not allow it, resulting in elements that felt jumbled, inconsistent, and ill-timed in parts. Even more surprising was the fact the movie's trailers suggested a bit more action and excitement to the film, given the dangers that Expendables are assigned, but alas, the movie lacks very little action or suspense and at times feels dull. This was especially true for me at the start, where the world-building was a tad too extensive as all these characters and stories tried to make their mark. Though many elements were intriguing, the length and final result didn't collect the best for me, leaving me fighting sleep while things settled. Instead, the "hyper" elements were also things I didn't particularly like. One is animal torture, something this movie does a bit too much of for my liking, despite having a purpose and the creature being fake. It's got a lot of effects that drive a spike into my enjoyment, so I warn sensitive viewers of this. The second is not like "antagonistic" villains; their design is a tad too annoying with their agendas and hyperbolic qualities that are one part very funny, but not the antagonistic escape I wanted.
When everything is assessed, I enjoyed my time with Mickey 17. This realistic science fiction movie holds a lot of merit and intelligence in the way it handles the content with relatable characters, good messages, and a surprisingly restrained comedy. Beautifully shot, this film doesn't reinvent the wheel, but rather makes this nice twist that had me surprised at how much they got away with in this tale. Alongside great acting and a balance of the genres, Micke 17 is another great piece of Ho's storytelling prowess about societal challenges in an ever-changing world. Yet, the movie struggles mainly with time, and it feels as if a lot of elements are waiting for a director's cut to tell the complete story. Without it, the editing seems a tad jumbled, various arcs are not fully included, and it bloats a movie that feels very slow at times with world-building that then doesn't come to fruition. I did not like some of the darker elements, but those pale next to just how much this movie feels like a couple of chapters with plans for more, something I think is a hindrance rather than a boon. Is it worth a thrip to the theater? If you like the artistic flair, good visuals, and a relevant story/comedy, yes, but I think many will not like the storytelling limitations and darkness like I did at times to say most should go. My scores for the film are:
Adventure/Comedy/Drama/Science Fiction: 8.0
Movie Overall: 7.0-7.5.

title: A wasted opportunity for commentary on human life.
text:
If the ongoing, worldwide disregard for human life you are witnessing shocks you, remember that it's nothing new: the human race has a legacy of greed, abuse, brutality and destruction going as far back as history can record it. "Mickey 17" is a savage reminder of how little we value each other and ourselves, even to the extremes of objectification and indifference. In terms of production quality: the cast's performances are excessive and over the top; a very poor choice by the director and an obvious directorial decision, given the pedigree of the actors. Mickey 17 lacks a continuous musical score, and that absence is notable. The film's graphics, props, set and wardrobe, are all exceptional, despite the cinematography being only mediocre.
At first, Mickey 17 appears to deliver comedic political commentary, but it quickly devolves into the chaos of a current day partisan production. The indisputable evidence? All the female characters are portrayed as exceptional, all the males as inferior, and the entire human race is painted as reproachable. A film made in this vein would be fine if it weren't part of the larger bias of today's film industry. Practically all current day media follows this schedule of indoctrination, rendering the movie more of an advertisement of a creed rather than a work of entertainment.
In conclusion, whether Mickey 17's political criticism is fitting or not doesn't matter: the hatred and disgust with which its meaning is delivered overshadows the production. The film's lack of goodwill prevents any true morale from developing. Mickey 17 grossly dismisses the opportunity to comment on the value of human life, replacing an incredibly relevant issue for jabs at a political party. The shortsightedness of its message confines Mickey 17 to a mediocre, contemporary production, in lieu of the legacy commentary on the richness of existence that it should've been.

author: alexandergotzp
title: Why Doesn't Mickey Get a 10?
text:
Let's start with the most important thing: you need to watch this movie. Stop reading and go see it. If you're still not convinced, let me give you a few reasons why Mickey 17 is one of the most intriguing films of the year.
First, let's talk about the screenplay-this is the kind of adaptation that wins awards. The script is polished, every scene moves the action forward, and Bong Joon-ho makes brilliant use of first-person narration through Robert Pattinson's character. This not only adds depth but fully immerses you in the world and Mickey's existential crisis.
This film has everything-you'll laugh, you'll question existence, and if you have a soft spot for human dilemmas, you might even feel deeply for the characters. By the end, Mickey 17 connects you to something-whether it's the fear of death, the pain of rejection, the struggle for survival, or the unsettling truth that in a society obsessed with power, your worth is dictated by others' perceptions.
Now, let's address why this movie isn't a 10. The film ambitiously tackles too many themes-death, identity, existence, interplanetary colonization, oppression, religion, oligarchy, friendship, and even the paranoia of whether your partner is cheating... on you, with yourself. While these themes are fascinating, not all of them are explored to their full potential, leaving some feeling underdeveloped.
The performances are phenomenal. Robert Pattinson delivers one of his most compelling roles, while Mark Ruffalo, Steven Yeun, and Toni Collette bring weight to the film. However, the secondary characters feel hollow-despite their importance, they lack depth, making some of the film's emotional beats fall short.
At the end of the day, Mickey 17 is bold, fresh, and nearly flawless. With a tighter focus and stronger secondary character development, it could have been an undeniable masterpiece. Even so, it remains one of the most thought-provoking sci-fi films in recent years, and that alone makes it a must-watch.

author: brentsbulletinboard
title: The First Great Film of 2025
text: Some movies have a way of hitting things right on the head, either intentionally or by happy accident. And such is the case in both regards in the latest offering from Oscar-winning writer-director Bong Joon Ho, a hilariously insightful sociopolitical sci-fi satire that knocks it out of the park in more ways than one can count. In an age of casual throw-away culture, "Mickey 17" takes this idea to an entirely new level by following the dubious exploits of the title character (Robert Pattinson), who works as an "expendable," a human charged with determining just how lethal various new technologies and environmental conditions are in an off-world colony of the future. The ironic, questionable term for this profession is derived from the fact that its practitioners are considered wholly disposable in every sense of the word but are fully capable of being regenerated in full thanks to a form of digital human printing, allowing subsequent iterations of these beings to be created as often as needed. However, life isn't quite so "simple and straightforward" for the Mickey expendable when he gets caught up in a series of complicated developments involving an illegal double, the whims of the maniacal cultist colony leader (Mark Ruffalo) and his self-absorbed wife (Toni Collette), the scheming of an unreliable, self-serving childhood friend (Steven Yeun), a relentless loan shark (Ian Hanmore) from his days back on Earth, and an aspiring romantic interest (Anamaria Vartolomei) who tries to get between Mickey and his girlfriend (Naomi Ackie), a passionate but badass security officer. The narrative's various story threads blend well together (even if a few of them are a little stretched out or aren't developed as fully as they might have been), but they collectively tell a well-integrated tale that generally keeps viewers riveted throughout. This captivating yarn is superbly supported by the picture's inventive visuals, expert editing. And stellar performances, most notably Ruffalo, Collette, Ackie and the first-ever portrayal by Pattinson that I've actually liked. What makes this offering especially and somewhat inadvertently effective, however, is the timing of its release, which was originally scheduled for a year ago but was delayed due to the SAG-AFTRA strike, a truly fortuitous blessing in disguise. Given current conditions in today's turbulent sociopolitical climate, particularly the unpredictable leadership of one particular politician, "Mickey 17" couldn't have debuted at a more pertinently appropriate time. (While I'll spare the specifics here, let me just say that MAGA fans and evangelical conservatives probably won't find this picture much to their liking.) In addition, the film deftly addresses a number of pressing social and cultural themes, such as how the average, everyday working class individual is looked upon and treated these days, the expendability question coming front and center. Some might see these attributes as somewhat heavy-handed or preachy, but then such "excesses" are the essence of good satire, and the filmmaker holds nothing back here. I'm also amazed that all of this was foreseen so far in advance of the emergence of current conditions, decidedly prescient and poignantly relevant in its insights. Indeed, this is genuinely is a cinematic fable for our times - a rather scathing one, to be sure, but a damning fable nevertheless. Moreover, if this release is any indication of what 2025's crop of new pictures will be like, I warmly welcome it given the awful movie year that has just passed. And, where "Mickey 17" is concerned, let's hope that this all comes to pass - both on the big screen and otherwise.

author: heyflp
title: A Sci-Fi Spectacle That Can't Find Its Focus
text:
"Mickey 17" is an ambitious mess that, despite flashes of Bong Joon Ho's genius, never quite finds a balance between its social satire and sci-fi spectacle. Adapting Edward Ashton's novel Mickey7, Bong builds an intriguing universe filled with provocative concepts and stunning visuals, but the execution feels scattered, tripping over its own grand ambitions. If in "Parasite" he masterfully wove layers of social critique into a gripping thriller, here he gets lost in a bloated narrative structure that can't decide if it wants to be a character study, a space opera, or a sharp commentary on exploitation and identity. The result is a visually impressive film with a fascinating performance from Robert Pattinson, but one that gets tangled in its own messaging and never quite lands the emotional or satirical impact it's aiming for.
The premise is compelling: in a future where humanity colonizes distant planets, Mickey (Pattinson) is an "Expendable," a disposable worker whose job is to repeatedly die on dangerous missions, only to be recreated in a new body with all his memories intact. The concept alone holds incredible potential for exploring deep philosophical questions about identity, consciousness, and the value of life, but Bong takes a more chaotic approach. The story starts to unravel when Mickey 17, presumed dead, returns to base only to find that a Mickey 18 has already been printed. This dilemma could have made for a powerful psychological thriller, but the film gets distracted by disconnected subplots, cartoonish characters, and humor that swings between sharp and just plain goofy.
Robert Pattinson fully commits to the duality between Mickey 17 and Mickey 18, giving each version of the character distinct nuances. One is more timid and uncertain, while the other is aggressive and cocky, and their dynamic works well within the film's heightened, exaggerated tone. Pattinson's performance is magnetic, carrying the film even when the script loses its way. His chemistry with Naomi Ackie, who plays his girlfriend Nasha, adds some of the film's more vibrant moments, though the romance itself never feels fully developed. Meanwhile, Steven Yeun-always a fantastic actor-ends up underutilized in a role that never gets the dramatic weight it deserves.
Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette play the film's villains with an over-the-top energy that's sometimes entertaining but often just grating. Ruffalo, in particular, portrays Kenneth Marshall as a grotesque, smug tyrant, clearly inspired by real-world authoritarian figures, but without the subtlety needed to make the satire truly work. The film's critique of imperialism and capitalist exploitation is present, but it's so on-the-nose and heavy-handed that it loses its impact. Bong has already proven he can turn political allegories into sharp, compelling narratives, but here he leans too far into preachiness, spoon-feeding the audience his ideas in a way that dulls their effect.
If there's one area where "Mickey 17" truly shines, it's in its visual world-building. Darius Khondji's cinematography creates a fascinating dystopian setting, where cold, industrial interiors contrast with the planet's harsh, unforgiving landscape. The production design adds layers to the futuristic world, and the visual effects are top-notch, especially in the interactions between the two Mickeys. However, despite all this visual richness, the film never quite achieves a true sense of immersion. Instead of pulling the audience into its world, it constantly reminds us of its own artificiality, with scenes that seem to exist more for aesthetic impact than for meaningful storytelling.
The third act is where the film completely falls apart. The already messy plot descends into full-blown chaos, throwing together conspiracies, uprisings, and alien creatures in a way that feels more disorienting than exciting. The so-called "creepers"-a bizarre mix of armadillos and octopuses-seem to be introduced to add emotional stakes, but they end up functioning as just another noisy element in a film already overloaded with half-baked ideas. The ending tries to tie up loose ends, but by that point, any emotional investment is gone-the audience is more exhausted than engaged.
"Mickey 17" is a textbook example of a talented filmmaker with too many ideas and no clear direction to tie them together. There are moments of brilliance, particularly in Pattinson's performance and the film's striking visuals, but it never finds a consistent tone. Its social critique is too obvious to be truly thought-provoking, its narrative is too convoluted to be immersive, and its humor is too uneven to be effective. In the end, it's stuck between wanting to be a sci-fi blockbuster and a sharp satire, without fully succeeding at either. Bong Joon Ho has already shown he can balance social commentary with compelling storytelling, but this time, it feels like he lost himself along the way.

author: elly_kalman
title: "Mickey 17" is a sharp, sarcastic sci-fi comedy about a world where human life has long lost its value and become just another resource.
text:
The elite rules under the guise of pseudo-religious doctrines, while cloning technology has turned people into disposable tools for colonizing new planets.

The protagonist, Mickey Barnes (Robert Pattinson), is escaping debt on Earth and agrees to become an "expendable" on a distant colony. His job? To die. Dangerous missions, lethal conditions-it doesn't matter because every time he dies, he gets reprinted on a 3D bioprinter. The catch? He remembers every single painful death.

The film is wildly relevant, razor-sharp, and gloriously unhinged. Mark Ruffalo, playing a charismatic yet terrifying corporate leader, delivers a cartoonishly evil dictator-he might as well have studied real-life politicians for the role.

Of course, this isn't Parasite, but Bong Joon-ho's signature satire is alive and well. Instead of a classic rebellion against the system, the film paints a bleak picture of a society that has already sold itself out, turning even death into cheap entertainment. The result is chaotic, sometimes absurd, yet disturbingly accurate-a reflection of a world where human life is worth little more than a disposable cup.

But despite all its darkness, "Mickey 17" is still a comedy. The laughter here is nervous, almost hysterical-like that of someone who just realized there's no way out. The film is a grim reminder that progress isn't always for the better, and ironically, the most human character in the story is the one designed to die over and over again.

This movie won't be for everyone, but if you enjoy dark humor, biting satire, and Pattinson on the verge of madness, "Mickey 17" is absolutely worth your time 😍

author: imdbfan-1053168755
title: Mickey 17 - A Disappointing Letdown
text:
I went into Mickey 17 with high expectations for 2 major reasons. First, it's directed by Bong Joon-ho, the mastermind behind Parasite, which was nothing short of a cinematic masterpiece. Second, the early reviews were overwhelmingly positive, making me believe I was in for something truly remarkable. Sat for the IMAX, ready to embark.
Needless to say, I couldn't ignore the fact that Robert Pattinson was the lead. I've been a huge fan of his since Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire and, of course, the Twilight franchise. Beyond his undeniable good looks, height, and sharp jawline, his acting has always been solid-even in roles he personally dislikes (ahem, Edward Cullen 😹).
But I must say, I was very much disappointed with Mickey 17. The film suffered from a lack of depth in character development and a weak, shallow storyline. Instead of focusing on meaningful themes, it felt like the movie was filled with irrelevant details that served only to inject humour-often at the most random moments and at the cost of the greater message. Any potential for emotional or philosophical depth was overshadowed by forced, lighthearted comedy scenes, making it difficult to take the movie seriously.
And then there were the dialogues-oh boy. Horrifically amateurish, to say the least. At times, it felt like the script was trying too hard to be witty, only to end up sounding unnatural and cringeworthy. You'll know what I mean, especially towards the end of the movie. Sigh...
Plot-wise, the film gave off Hunger Games/Divergent vibes, with themes of political foul play and power abuse. However, where those stories managed to create tension and build a compelling world, Mickey 17 felt hollow-as if it was trying to be something grander but never quite made it.
Overall, while Robert Pattinson's performance was, as expected, solid, it couldn't save Mickey 17 from its lackluster execution. Bong Joon-ho has proven he can craft thought-provoking and genre-defying films, but unfortunately, this one missed the mark.
Final Verdict: 4/10 - A wasted opportunity.

author: Sees All
title: Ho-hum Sci-fi
text: "Mickey" is an "expendable." That means that it is his job to get killed repeatedly for science. He gets killed in various ways and then his remains are autopsied and analyzed, with the results used for scientific research with the goal of colonizing planets deep in outer space. He is then "reprinted" and reanimated. But this time, there's a glitch and he is accidentally reprinted without having died. So now there's not only a Mickey 17, but a Mickey 18 as well. It is a crime to create multiples and both of them must die. But Mickey's survival instinct isn't about to let that happen. After seeing the trailer, I was expecting something delightfully fresh and original. I was disappointed on both counts. Has the sci-fi genre been completely exhausted? I wonder. MICKEY 17, as far as I can tell, has not one drop of originality. The plot appears to have been cobbled together out of old STAR TREK episodes and SUPERMAN comic books of the 1960s. The technology and special effects are all old-hat by now. With CGI virtually anything can be done. Special effects can't dazzle us anymore. Projectile vomiting and splattering blood-and-guts doesn't gross us out anymore. We've seen it a lot by now. On top of this there is an overlay of heavy-handed political satire that is also extremely predictable to anyone who's seen an episode of SATURDAY NIGHT LIVE in recent years. The jokes fall flat. At most, there's a mild chuckle now and then. The movie is all rather routine. The cast of fine actors who have all done good work in other films is wasted, especially Toni Colette. (When is she going to get another role worthy of her talents?) This movie is two-and-a quarter hours long, but seems much longer. I kept checking the time after half an hour. I can only recommend this movie to people who just want to kill some time.

author: bastille-852-731547
title: An underwhelming "Parasite" follow-up lacking in genuine cleverness and insight
text:
First things first: I'd like to start my review by stating that "Parasite" is not just one of the best films in recent memory, but it's truly one of my favorite films of all time. Bong Joon-Ho's genre-bending 2019 masterpiece utterly blew me away when I saw it for the first time. I was enthralled and riveted by its brilliant craftsmanship, timely and clever social satire, memorable characters, and--most importantly--its impeccable commitment to original and creative storytelling. So needless to say, I was incredibly excited to see Bong's next film. The trailers looked a bit bizarre and eccentric, but I always trusted Bong to make a great movie. Unfortunately, I was pretty disappointed in "Mickey 17." I found it a largely pointless exercise lacking in insight or creativity compared to "Parasite." And given how much I loved "Parasite" and was hoping to love this film, it really pains me to say that.
The film centers around Mickey, an astronaut who is an "expendable," meaning that he is sent on deadly missions and a newly regenerated (cloned) body is printed out again when he "dies." Unfortunately, the story isn't as clever or hard-hitting as it thinks it is. The narrative often feels fairly pointless, filled to the brim with so many scenes of Mickey getting killed off in different ways with little other purpose, which gets tiring after a while. I frequently questioned what the point of a lot of it was, which is unfortunate. The film's messages about cloning and contemporary politics come off as fairly on-the-nose rather than interesting or profound. But above all, the film just isn't as interesting (tonally, aesthetically, or in terms of character development) as you would hope a Bong Joon-Ho film would be. Robert Pattinson does pretty well with the material he is given (including playing multiple Mickeys with multiple accents,) and I liked Naomi Ackie's supporting performance. But I was less than enthusiastic about Mark Ruffalo's supporting role as a Trump-esque, buffoonish villain and Toni Collette as his wife. They weren't very engaging characters, despite Bong's attempt at creating political satire. The cinematography, editing, and score are good, but nothing mind-blowing or memorable like the filmmaking techniques that were on display in "Parasite."
So, "Mickey 17" unfortunately just didn't click with me. That's too bad, but in no way does that ever change or minimize the fact that "Parasite" is an extraordinary modern classic that deserved every single one of the many accolades it received. 5/10.
Note: I saw the film in Dolby Cinema. The picture and sound quality were good, but it was not one of the best Dolby presentations I have seen.

author: Apireon
title: 7.5/10 - A Brilliant Idea That Falls Short
text:
I'm torn on Mickey 17. It introduces such an exciting premise-an expendable worker who dies and is constantly recreated-but instead of fully exploring the ethical and existential dilemmas that come with it, the story plays it too safe. It's as if the film is afraid to go all-in on the deeper questions it teases.
Robert Pattinson is excellent as Mickey, carrying the film with his performance. The best part of the movie is the concept itself-being reprinted over and over again, losing and reclaiming your sense of identity. Unfortunately, the social commentary feels forced and surface-level rather than naturally integrated.
One of the biggest issues is pacing. Even with a strong setup, the film drags in places and feels longer than necessary. Mark Ruffalo, who is usually great, overacts here to the point where it becomes distracting. In contrast, the voice acting of Pattison is very well done.
Visually, the film delivers. The icy, desolate setting is immersive, and the cinematography works well for the story being told. Still, with such a great foundation, the movie had the potential to be something much more profound. Instead, it settles for being a solid but somewhat underwhelming sci-fi film. But I liked it.

author: fundaquayman
title: Bong Joon-Ho's 2026 contender for Best Picture
text:
I'll skip the plotline summary as you can get that just from seeing the trailer. As a fan of this film, it's interesting to see so many film critics comparing this film to PARASITE when the two films' stories and genre have nothing to do with each other except they're both directed by Bong Joon-Ho. I'm thinking maybe these critics have not seen Bong's earlier great films like MEMORIES OF MURDER, or HOST, and they have only watched PARASITE, SNOWPIERCER and OKJA on NETFLIX when they wrote their reviews after screening MICKEY 17 - fact is, Bong Joon-Ho has shown he is well-versed across multiple genres, and PARASITE's success isn't necessarily his endgame (personal opinion perhaps, MEMORIES OF MURDER (2003) remains his finest work in his 3 decades working as screewriter and director). It would be more relevant for PARASITE to be compared to AMERICAN BEAUTY, while MICKEY 17 as a Sci-Fi satire stands on its own as one of the best films released so far in 2025, and it would be a travesty if this film and Robert Pattinson's performance don't become favorites in next year's Golden Globes and Academy Awards. Given the current state of the world we live in, it is sad to see that the ridiculousness of fictional characters and events within the film are not that far off from what we have been seeing on the news in the first 10 weeks of 2025. Bong Joon-Ho again knocks it out of the park with MICKEY 17 and he makes this film easy to understand for even audiences who only watch Marvel-Disney commercial films. As much as this movie is a Sci-Fi action comedy, the only plot element that probably isn't believable in 2025 is that when corrupt politicians are caught red/orange-handed in the movie, they actually get punished by the law...
While MICKEY 17 can be compared more relevantly with earlier Sci-Fi films like MOON, BLADERUNNER, SILENT RUNNING, or maybe even SOLARIS, and TOTAL RECALL, those equally iconic films touch more heavily on what it means to live and question whether the world now and in the future can allow humanity to exist within us. MICKEY 17 makes a note on the existential questions, but focus more on the dangerous state our world is in right now in Q1 2025...

author: museoff
title: "Mickey 17: A Sci-Fi Reflection on Humanity and Beyond"
text:
I just watched this movie.
Throughout the film, I couldn't help but think of past and present U. S. presidents, as well as some foolish leaders from South Korea.
Of course, everyone writing reviews here has their own political perspectives, along with freedom of thought and religion. I expect this movie to spark a lot of debate, but I want to focus solely on the cinematic aspects, leaving politics aside.
Let's start by talking about director Bong Joon-ho.
He first caught my attention in 2000 with Barking Dogs Never Bite, a film that convinced me he was an outstanding filmmaker of that era.
Then came Memories of Murder, a film based on real-life serial killings that sent shockwaves through the Korean film industry. This movie cemented his status as a commercially successful director in South Korea.
Following that, he directed The Host, Mother, Snowpiercer, Netflix's Okja, and the Academy Award-winning Parasite, solidifying his global recognition as a filmmaker.
Now, let's evaluate Mickey 17-without spoilers.
This film intertwines modern political landscapes, human greed, desire, the ethical dilemmas brought on by scientific advancements, the philosophical implications of encountering extraterrestrial life, and even religious inquiries.
It is a film that constantly challenges the viewer with profound questions, making you search for the essence of it all throughout its runtime.
Honestly, watching a movie multiple times isn't always easy, but this is one that makes you want to revisit it and reflect on its themes again.
Cautiously, I'd say this film has the potential to compete for an award at major film festivals.
In particular, Robert Pattinson, the lead actor, may very well receive some form of recognition for his performance.
It was an enjoyable film, and I highly recommend you watch it when it gets released.
From a movie lover in Korea.

author: JacksDe6d
title: Bong Joon Ho swings for the fences with his first fully-English feature, while Pattison's performance puts the "Twilight" accusations to rest for the long haul...
text:
MICKEY-17 (2025) takes you on a marvelous journey of meaningful mayhem with dark, self-deprecating humor as its fuel. Bong Joon Ho's thorough investigation of identity, duality, and the relationship between ego and power stick with you far after the film's credits roll. We all have fragmented personalities; various versions of ourselves. Some of these "characters" are consistently active and in rotation while others lay dormant, hidden deep beneath. Unless you're a complete sociopath, you have an empathic, emotional piece of your personality fostered in feelings of both love and fear. However, it's constantly at war with the carelessness, confidence, and bravery we all paradoxically have the potential for.
Classically personified by symbolic imagery of an angel on one shoulder and a devious demon on the other, the moral and spiritual duality of man is a tale old as time... Yet, Joon Ho and Robert Pattison's lovable, highly animated Mickey Barnes breathe new life into the classic concept. The film's as unrealistic and ridiculous as it is refreshing and surprisingly relatable. Pattison's seemingly endless range and raw acting ability are on full display, perhaps more than ever. Not to mention, his natural charm in the role makes for a hell of a good time for audience members willing to give theirselves up to the cynicism and obvious outrageousness of it all.
Joon Ho swings for the fences with his first fully-English feature, while Pattison's performance puts to rest any allegations left he can only play characters in the vein of Twilight's eerie Edward. On the other end, Mark Ruffalo's characterization of the relentlessly greedy and hilariously obnoxious Kenneth Marshall feels as fragmented and frantically scattered (in both its execution and inspiration) as Mickey's rich spirit and diverse personality traits throughout the course of the insanely inhumane scientific investigation he so desperately (and naively) agrees to take part in during the film's effective exposition. Despite this singular flaw, the picture is perfect from top to bottom, nothing new for the work of the Oscar-winning director. We all have our own Mickey-17s and -18s within. Now, much like moral Mickey, I'll find myself asking... "What would eighteen do?"

author: emceeanz
title: Mickey 17 - A Thoughtful, Underrated Work of Sci-Fi Art
text:
I'd give Mickey 17 a solid 8 out of 10. It's not perfect, but it's one of the most quietly bold and intriguing sci-fi films to come out in years. Rather than flattening its themes for mainstream digestion, it leans into ambiguity-offering atmosphere, complexity, and subtext over exposition, which is exactly why it's been misunderstood by so many.
A lot of people walked into it expecting Parasite 2.0, but this isn't that. In fact, I'd argue Parasite, despite its praise, was one of Bong Joon-ho's most conventional films. It was smart, sure-but also very didactic. Its metaphors were handed to you on a platter, every symbol underlined twice in red. Mickey 17, by contrast, dares to be quiet. To not explain. To suggest. It respects the audience in a way most films don't anymore.
It shares more creative DNA with something like Poor Things-not in content, but in spirit. Both films are imaginative, layered, and uninterested in obeying the usual rules of narrative clarity. They build strange worlds and trust you to navigate them without a map. If you enjoyed Poor Things for its willingness to challenge form and spoon-fed meaning, you'll likely appreciate what Mickey 17 is doing too.
Yes, the film spreads itself thin thematically at times. And yes, its commentary on systemic oppression could've used more development. But those aren't fatal flaws-they're the byproduct of a film trying to do more than just entertain. It wants to make you think, even if that means not everything lands cleanly.
And honestly, that's a risk worth praising.

author: chand-suhas
title: It's okay for you to be happy, Mickey Barnes.
text:
It's 2050, where Mickey Barnes and Timo are on the run from a loan shark. They join the space crew on an expedition to planet Niflheim. While Timo becomes a shuttle pilot, Mickey signs up to be an expendable without reading the contract. Being printed for the 17th time, Mickey realizes how badly he is treated by his peers while also having fallen in love with Nasha, the only one to treat him as a real human. He survives falling into cravesse and an encounters the alien inhabitants while his death is assumed and an 18th version of him is printed. Mickey 18 is the complete opposite of Mickey 17 and this breaks the rule of never having a Multiples. With their existence at threat, the duo have to not just work on their own survival but their fellow humans as well when an apparent clash with the resident aliens becomes inevitable. How does they do it while fighting back their oppressing leader, forms rest of the story.
Bong Joon Ho coming up with Mickey 17 was exciting solely for his narrative style and he does present the usual social commentary with the big corporate here. Mickey is used to showcase the social disparity and how he is treated based on the working class. While this aspect connects, the entire segment involving the aliens comes out as underdeveloped narrative. I felt like they had too much on the plate once Mickey 18 arrives. He is more aggressive and an alpha unlike Mickey 17. As these personalities clash to ensure their own survival, the aliens sub plot gets sidelined. When they take the center stage in the final act, it lost the intended impact. The constant narration from Mickey 17 keeps the tone lighter so one thing the director did get right is the tone of the film. This was definitely not a bad film, where it did fail to meet the expectations, the fact remains that the core concept itself was pretty much weird. So a tighter screenplay that balanced the drama and the alien subplot would have yielded better results.
