author: jameswhalls
title: If you like the book - you'll HATE this
text:
As a standalone film Micky 17 is fine. Not great, not even good. Just fine.

The source material is a great read, funny, satirical, fast-paced and sustains your interest. Whereas the film can barely be regarded as an adaptation at all.

The backstory varies, the plot changes but most importantly and disappointingly of all the characters in the main beat little or no resemblance to their entertaining literary counterparts. Mickey 17 (7 in the book) is relatively similar but to have a clone, with uploaded personality to differ so much in character is a huge diversion. And it doesn't end there, Timo (Berto) is somehow a drug dealer and also indebted to the same creditors as Mickey? Nasha has a different job, the creepers have equally altered roles, but worst of all, the character of Marshall becomes a moron rather than an unpleasant boss and he somehow cones with a wife all of a sudden?!

I'm disappointed. I live the director and Parasite was exceptional. I love R Pats and this film has standalone aspects that make it watchable, albeit not worth a cinema trip. The issue I have is the artistic license just takes its freedoms too far from what made this story so compelling.

author: Batsy1501
title: Good but not enough
text:
Mickey 17 by Bong Joon-ho is certainly not a masterpiece. Bong has set the bar so high that even he struggles to surpass it. Mickey 17 is a good movie-with striking visuals, an intriguing concept, and strong performances-but it doesn't quite reach the level of Parasite.
Bong Joon-ho remains a master at making audiences uncomfortable-not with jumpscares, but through heavy silences and situations where morality is so distorted that you can't sit still.
Robert Pattinson continues to prove he has completely shed his past image, delivering an impressive performance that distinguishes between his two characters through body language and tone. Mark Ruffalo also shines, with expressions reminiscent of his role in Poor Things, at times even carrying a hint of political satire.
Visually, Mickey 17 is undeniably grand. Bong crafts a meticulously detailed sci-fi world that looks stunning. However, some scenes drag on longer than necessary, and while the film poses interesting questions about human arrogance, the message isn't exactly new. Sci-fi has explored this theme many times before, and Mickey 17 doesn't sharpen it enough to make a lasting impact.
In the end, it's still a film worth watching-certainly not bad, but not a masterpiece either. Mickey 17 is a smart sci-fi film, but compared to the standards Bong Joon-ho has set for himself, it falls just short of a true breakthrough.

author: ozbandit-43368
title: Mickey 17 (2025) Review: A Dark, Thought-Provoking Dive into Chaos
text:
Mickey 17 is an electrifying, mind-bending sci-fi experience that grips you from the first frame and never lets go. Bong Joon-ho masterfully blends cerebral sci-fi with unsettling existential dread, crafting a narrative that is as chaotic as it is captivating.
From the outset, the film throws you into a dystopian world where cloning and consciousness raise deep ethical dilemmas. Robert Pattinson delivers an exceptional performance, embodying the repeated deaths and rebirths of Mickey with a raw intensity that makes every version of him feel distinct yet hauntingly familiar. The storytelling is layered with dark humor and unsettling philosophical questions-how much of "you" remains when your body is discarded and replaced?
Visually, Mickey 17 is a feast. Bong's signature style-blending the ordinary with the surreal-makes the world feel grounded yet deeply disturbing. Every shot, every detail, feels purposeful, adding to the eerie tension that builds throughout the film. The pacing is relentless, keeping you engaged as Mickey grapples with identity, survival, and the absurdity of his own expendability.
The movie is chaotic, but in the best way possible. It keeps you on edge, questioning not just the characters' choices but also the nature of human existence itself. Unlike some high-concept sci-fi that can lose itself in over-explanation, Mickey 17 embraces ambiguity, letting the audience sit with its unanswered questions.
It's rare to find a film that is as thought-provoking as it is thrilling, but Mickey 17 strikes that balance perfectly. Dark, deeply unsettling, and impossible to look away from-this is one of the most gripping sci-fi films in recent memory. If you love narratives that challenge your perception of self and reality, this one is a must-watch.

author: turnmaxw
title: A classic Bong Joon Ho film...
text:
I went into this movie with close to no expectations other than the fact that it was a Bong Joon Ho film. I refused to watch the trailer, I did next to no research, and actively avoided any mention of it. I did this because I respected Bong Joon Ho as a director and trusted the film to be good. I mention this not to preach my love of his films or to make myself out to be something special, but because this film was exactly what I expected, an extremely solid film, just in line with Bong Joon Ho's style.
The most similar film I can think of is another film by Bong Joon Ho, Snowpiercer. It features a similar theme of a class struggle in a dystopian future, but where Snowpiercer remains serious, leaning into the action elements, Mickey 17 turns to moments of levity. Mark Ruffalo's character is not only an effective villain, but a humorous one. This works because the film doesn't take itself too seriously. It's a little abstract and not entirely realistic (even accounting for it being set in the future), but it doesn't need to be to be a compelling and relevant film.
This of course does not make it perfect. I felt certain characters were never fully developed, even Mickey himself. The film is also struggling between two critical plots, the complications of human cloning, and the broader plot of trying to colonize a planet (I would give more details but I'm trying to avoid spoilers). Both of these plots are compelling, but some moments feel like the film gives up one in order to explore the other. I'm not sure what the solution to this is exactly, I think it was just a classic struggle of trying to condense too much into one film. I wouldn't be surprised if the original book it is based on can handle both these plots and expand on more characters in the exact way I craved. Nonetheless, I appreciate it not being split into 2 parts, too many films do that today.
As a final note, Robert Pattinson absolutely nailed his role in this film. He's one of those actors who seems to often get bogged down by the impression people have of him from his most prominent role, but this film, and the range that he shows, demonstrates how good of an actor he is. I'm convinced that he could play almost any character you give him.

author: BA_Harrison
title: Mickey 6/10
text:
Desperate to escape Earth, Mickey Barnes (Robert Pattinson) joins a mission to colonise the planet Niflheim, his role being that of an 'expendable', the young man performing potentially fatal tasks, his body reprinted and his memories restored each time he dies. After falling into a deep fissure on Niflheim, Mickey is left for dead, but is saved by the planet's indigenous lifeforms; when he returns back to base, he discovers that he has already been reprinted, meaning that there are now multiples, something that the expedition's leader, politician Kenneth Marshall (Mark Ruffalo), has declared to be a serious infringement of the rules.
Directed by Bong Joon-ho (Parasite), Mickey 17 addresses the morality of science, the power of politics, the ethics of colonisation, the cult of personality, the importance of social status and the influence of religion, but with so much going on, it only succeeds in tackling these topics in a superficial manner. I feel that the film would have been much more meaningful had it chosen just one or two themes and delved deeper into them. Furthermore, in setting up the film, Mickey being killed and reprinted several times, it all becomes rather repetitive, as though it is treading water until the threat to the aliens (known as 'creepers') becomes the focus of the plot. At this point, the action becomes a tad messy, Marshall and his wife (played by Toni Collette) turning into ridiculous caricatures (Ruffalo channelling Trump for his performance), the power dynamics switching a touch too quickly, and the abrupt happy ending wrapping things up a little too neatly.
Other issues I have with the film:
I have my doubts that the human race will be colonising planets by the year 2054. The film should have been set further into the future.
Developing a translator in such a short space of time seems unlikely (and a little too convenient for the plot).
Marshall's vehicle at the end doesn't appear to crush any of the 'creepers', despite there being so many of them.
Likewise, a huge explosion conveniently fails to kill any of the creepers that are close by.
The film is too long - half an hour shorter would have resulted in a better pace.
On a more positive note: the central performances are good, Pattinson putting in a strong turn(s) and Naomi Ackie very likeable as Mickey's (Mickeys'?) love interest Nasha; the dark humour is enjoyable; and the production design and special effects are impressive.
Overall, not unwatchable, but could have been so much better. 6/10.

author: stevezh49
title: Not his best but still a good movie

Mickey can be replaced over and over again, but does that mean we can disregard his feelings simply because he is replaceable? Everyone on the ship carries on as if nothing happened, while a bloody hand drifts through space-much like the bourgeoisie, who continue enjoying their lives while choosing to ignore or not paying attention to the suffering of many others. Good satire.

author: Scream_Play
title: The first sci-fi satire to really grasp me since Starship troopers
text:
Bong Joon-ho strikes cinematic gold once again with his latest sci-fi satire, Mickey 17. As always, Bong's deft touch is evident in his exploration of a dystopian world, where he delivers a chillingly relevant critique of a fascist government. The timing of this film's release is especially poignant, resonating not only with the political climate of the United States but with the global instability that looms over us all.
Mark Ruffalo's performance is a standout, delivering a portrayal that is both chilling and captivating. It's clear that he drew heavy inspiration from a certain real-life figure, infusing his character with an intensity that leaves little to the imagination about his motivations and the dark, twisted psyche that drives him.
Robert Pattinson, meanwhile, delivers a stunning dual performance as the titular Mickey, skillfully breathing unique life into two distinct iterations of the same character. His nuanced portrayal showcases his ability to differentiate the two versions, making each one feel fresh and dynamic, a feat that adds layers to the film's complex narrative.
Like many of Bong Joon-ho's films, Mickey 17 is a work that rewards multiple viewings. Its rich, thought-provoking story and underlying themes will unfold more with each watch, revealing new layers and deeper meanings. This is a film that stays with you, demanding both reflection and interpretation long after the credits roll.

author: Ky-D
title: Interesting premise can't overcome bad writing.
text:
'Mickey 17' was extremely disappointing. Too long, too slow, and not nearly clever enough to justify any of it. It's text-book proof that a story is only as smart as its writers. If Starship Troopers did sci-fi satire well, then Mickey 17 is on the planet that is farthest from.
It's full of pointless side plots that don't go anywhere and rarely (if ever) connect back to the central the premise. The main story only advances by either contrivance or deus ex machina and the plot requires that basically every character has to be a full-blown moron until the script suddenly needs them to be competent for one single scene. It also doesn't help that even though cloning is central to the story, the film has almost nothing meaningful to say about it. So little so that they never even bother to adequately explain why they have to kill the Mickey clones and erase all memory data. Seriously, 'Parts: The Clonus Horror' had more to say about the ethics of cloning than 'Mickey 17'.
On the plus side, the performances are (mostly) good, with Pattinson delivering another solid turn. The film generally looks good too, though the camera work may feel a bit art house for more mainstream viewers.
Lastly, impossible to talk about the film without mentioning its politics; the film is aggressively, distractingly, childishly anti-Trump. Now that might be a plus to some, but honesty it's so lazily implemented that it's nothing more than "look at me! I'm Trump and I'm dumb!". Now I like good satire, but this isn't satire, it's broad parody about on par with Alec Baldwin doing a Trump impersonation on SNL. If you are in the market for 2 1/2 hours of Mark Ruffalo doing bargain basement Trump jokes, then you will love this movie.
Not good satire, not good Sci-Fi, just not a good movie.

author: movieroguereviewer
title: The Rogue Reviewer - Mickey 17
text:
I was thoroughly impressed by this dark comedy sci-fi movie. Mickey 17 is easily my favorite film of 2025. The plot is original, the humor is fantastic, and Robert Pattinson has to be a strong contender for Best Actor at the Oscars next year. Mickey 17 should be considered a modern benchmark for how new sci-fi films should look.
I didn't really know what to expect from Mickey 17, as the trailers didn't reveal much. However, the story turned out to be a brilliant concept. Mickey Barnes is such a unique and engaging focal character that you truly feel like you're with him on his painful journey. The film's strange, quirky dialogue and dark comedy work perfectly within the sterile, unsettling spaceship environment.
The acting is mostly excellent. I think this is Robert Pattinson's career-defining role-he's brilliant at playing two completely different versions of the same character. He even creates distinct vocal styles for both Mickeys, helping to separate their personalities. Mickey 17 is pathetic and awkward, while Mickey 18 is aggressive, confident, and slightly psychotic. Naomi Ackie, as Nasha, also delivers a strong performance. I really enjoyed the depth she brought to her character, and her chemistry with Pattinson was fantastic.
My least favorite character-and the one who pulled me out of the movie in every scene-was Mark Ruffalo's Kenneth Marshall. It's clear he based his performance and physical presence on Donald Trump. While it was funny at first, the joke wore thin by the end and became more of a distraction from an otherwise brilliant movie. On the other hand, Toni Collette was fantastic as Ylfa, the sadistic wife. She felt menacing in every scene.
Overall, director Bong Joon-ho-whom audiences may know from the Oscar-winning Parasite-did an incredible job with this film. He creates a uniquely claustrophobic and dangerous environment, immersing the audience in Mickey's journey. The cinematography is stunning, the dark comedy is both hilarious and savage, and the indigenous creatures, the "Creepers," play an excellent role in this quirky sci-fi story.
My only negatives, aside from Mark Ruffalo's performance, are that the ending feels a bit abrupt and like it's missing something. However, this didn't take away from the sheer enjoyment I got from Mickey 17. I give it an 9 out of 10.

author: nebula0024
title: A Parody in All the Worst Ways
text:
This film had the perfect chance to explore what should have been an incredibly fascinating deep dive into what it means to be human, the soul, personality, and the ethical ramifications of cloning. It also had a chance to explore the pitfalls of corporate greed, poor values, elitism, cultural decay, and how technology can be misused.
Unfortunately, the writers instead decided to make some kind of political parody with misapplied "humor" that completely falls flat, and characters that display baffling behavior. The dialogue often had me confused as people flip-flop between different personalities and wildly varying levels of intelligence. Regarding different personalities, that of Mickey was the only one that actually made sense and would have been an intriguing avenue to explore further, which they didn't.
How this film's script was greenlit and such a huge budget attached is completely beyond me. If the film had taken itself seriously, with well developed characters and the odd humorous scene, it could have been a massive success. Instead, all the amazing material they had to work with was completely squandered.

title: Seventeen going under.

To escape a fearsome loan shark, Mickey Barnes (Robert Pattinson) signs up as an 'expendable' on a colonisation trip led by failed politician and cult leader Kenneth Marshall (Mark Ruffalo). An expendable volunteers for dangerous work, and medical testing, on the understanding that he's "reprinted" on his death, with his memories transferred to the new clone. The seventeenth Mickey actually survives a perilous fall, making it back to the ship, only to discover that the assumption was that he'd died, and Mickey 18 (Robert Pattiinson) has already been created.
So, I liked Pattison's performances in this. Though Mickey is restored with the same memories each time, his relationship to those memories sometime alters slightly, leaving him with different personality variations. I liked the look of the film, the spaceship and the ice planet, and their natural inhabitants look good.
I didn't enjoy the story though. I disliked Ruffalo and Toni Collette's characters, but not in the sense I was supposed to. In the sense I was disappointed whenever they returned to the story, "go away heat" if you'll forgive me the wrestling terminology. It's not Bong Joon-ho's fault that his thinly veiled Trump parody has come at a point when thinly veiled Trump parodies are so ubiquitous and I don't know where I wanted the plot to go, but it wasn't where this went.
It becomes increasingly long, slow and unwieldy as the film runs on and I couldn't help but think that something a bit smaller, and more focused, would have been the way to go.

To begin, the performances are all great, with Robert Pattinson being utterly fantastic as the titular expended protagonist. The honourable mentions in the supporting cast go to Naomi Ackie, Steven Yeun and Patsy Ferran, all able to ground themselves as varying insights into the ship's societal stereotypes. The writing is darkly funny and somewhat ambitious although hardly thought-provoking, as it doesn't give much time for the audience to rest to unpack any of the larger concepts with its steadily consistent pacing. Moreover, the content explored is admittedly all very interesting, from the ethics of cloning to the study of animals and then the treatment of people based on class; it's all explored in uniquely fascinating directions.
However, there is a copious amount of subject matter being discussed, with it all being reasonably organised and introduced at first, but then the middle act oftentimes struggles with balancing a bit too much at once, even if it all reaches a decent conclusion by the end. It detracts from the overall experience, and sidelines the film's greatest asset, which is Pattinson himself. Furthermore, Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette play great antagonists, but their performances, especially Ruffalo's, come across as too on the nose and very much blatantly inspired by reckless politicians; they're able to fit into the movie as their own tone, but it's also definitely an acquired taste.
Regardless, Mickey 17 is a damn fine and wholey original piece of satire, even if it means it is unable to have as much fun as it wants in the endgame.

author: stevencsmovies
title: So much fun, but maybe too niche
text: Director Bong Joon-Ho directs with a certain stylistic confidence that I admire. Usually, it's a little strange like SNOWPIERCER, or it's wonderfully wild and amazing like PARASITE. His latest is a fun combination of the two, a sci-fi dark satire called MICKEY 17 (Don't worry, it's not the 17th installment). Based on the book Mickey7 by Edward Ashton, it tells a story of Mickey (Robert Pattinson), a quiet pushover who ends up in debt to a very bad guy with his extremely lucky friend Timo (Steven Yeun), so he signs up for a colonizing mission on another planet. Not reading the fine print, he signs up to be an expendable, somebody who scientists use as a guinea pig to move science forward. Every time Mickey dies, he gets physically reprinted using a giant 3D printer, then gets his downloaded memories back. The ship is run by an egomaniacal failed politician Kenneth (Mark Ruffalo) and his equally horrible sauce-obsessed wife Ylfa (Toni Collete). They both have some wild scenes and make some acting choices that not everybody will love. I did though. Joon-Ho's work has always had strong social commentary imbedded within, this one being no different. It came across as heavy handed in some ways, but I was having too much fun to care. Pattinson is so good you forget he's playing opposite himself. He has rather great chemistry, with himself. He has grown into a terrific actor. Overall, this feels like seeing a genre-bending uncompromised vision of a great director, but its quirkiness might not be appealing enough for casual audiences. Following up a Best Picture winner like PARASITE must have been tough, but MICKEY 17 is as fun and offbeat as only a Bong Joon-Ho film can be.

author: pierrebrown-07469
title: A Very Good Movie 30 mins Too Long
text:
Clocking in at 137 minutes, Mickey 17 drags in spots, especially in the first half where better film editing would have prevented it from losing momentum.
Once it gets going though, it's a brilliant satire of a post-capitalist society, where humans are simply an economic tool as a means to whatever end those in power desire. Robert Pattinson is great in the title role, and in a related supporting role, showcasing how far his acting has advanced since Harry Potter, and Twilight.
Mark Ruffalo provides most of the comic relief in the film, as an unmistakable Trump-esque ruthless politician (replete with facial expressions and clipped speech), that is even more amusing since he strongly disagrees with Trump in real life.
Based on the 2022 book Mickey7, by Edward Ashton, Mickey 17 gets the job done, but it would have done better if it had been edited down to less than 2 hours.

author: mjanelle-24974
title: This movie dies over and over and over again
text:

author: matepolcz
title: Amazing Directing, Incredible Visuals, Beautiful Score, but a Little Too Long
text:
Mickey 17 is extremely fun movie with incredible visuals and score.
The characters are very interesting. Mickey is certainly the most complex one, since there are many of him. I didn't exactly understand how the reprinting worked, because he 18 is very different from 17, while they have the same genetics and memories. Timo is fairly predictable, while Nasha surprised me several times. Ylfa is just too annoying as the mind behind Kenneth. Speaking of him, he is probably the most interesting supporting character and that's probably because of the different aspects of writing and acting. I think the original idea for him was to be a Hitler mixed with Scientology vibes, while Mark Ruffalo definitely went for Trump. The themes of religion, dictatorship and basically slavery are quite thought-provoking.
The directing is amazing, the dark, but also comedic tone of the movie is probably extremely hard to achieve, while everything takes place in space and on an other planet. The cinematography, while restrained, still gorgeous. The use of light is what I probably liked the most. My only bigger issue with the movie is that it's a little too slow sometimes and it's just too long. The visual effects are spectacular even though there's not much practicality. The score is very classical and I loved it, I rarely watch movies that feel old-school because of the music, so I loved it. The cast is great and I have yet to see Toni Collette in a likeable role. Steven Yeun is incredible as the shady, untrustworthy character. Mark Ruffalo's performance is incredible, maybe a little too much, but I enjoyed it. Robert Pattinson is incredible as every Mickey, he showcased that he is one of the most talented actors of his generation.
Mickey 17 is an incredible movie with great visuals and beautiful score.

author: ashusahu-79793
title: Not so sci fi I hoped it would be
text:
The trailer was incredibly promising, compelling all of us to watch the movie at least once. I was expecting a "Lost in Space"-type adventure, where Mickey repeatedly dies for a meaningful cause and comes back to life to fulfill his purpose. However, the story didn't quite take that route. For those who usually claims a plot to be very much predictable, this movie is not like those.
The first part of the film was quite good, filled with dark comedy. We witness Mickey's suffering, understand why he chose his job, and see how indifferent everyone is to his recurring deaths. This tone persists through about two-thirds of the movie.
The expedition leaders were the most disappointing characters. They should have been more responsible and sensible, but the story chose to depict them as foolish jesters. The ending and climax was not very satisfying and was quite unpredictable, with numerous plot points, such as communication with the planet's inhabitants, that felt chaotic.
As for the acting, Robert Pattinson delivered an excellent performance, showcasing distinct personality shifts between his versions of Mickey. The other actors also did a commendable job, but the story itself was the primary letdown.
Spoilers:
I am left with two major questions after watching the movie:
First - How did the leader of the planet's inhabitants know Mickey's name?
Second - How was Mickey confident that detonating himself wouldn't also destroy the other Mickey?

author: Jithindurden
title: Reminded of Okja
text:
This movie reminded me a little bit of Bong Joon Ho's previous Hollywood movie Okja. Both go to the satirical critique of different sides of capitalism a bit too much, along with showing some cute and powerful sci-fi animals. But overall, I preferred Mickey 17 to Okja, probably a lot more because of how I feel about the exact message that is being conveyed. It's funny and dark, but a lot of the stuff that is shown to be caricature that would be usually perceived as almost slapstick doesn't really feel like that anymore. This exact kind of behavior seems pretty normal in today's world. The megalomaniac idiots who hold all the power purely by exploitation are so real that it doesn't feel funny or serious in this presentation. There are too many aspects of this movie that could've been explored a lot more, but even with such heavy themes, it doesn't strive for greatness and is content in being able to convey its heavy themes lightheartedly, which feels like a shame after the humongous success of Parasite.
Overall, it was pretty good. Even though it was pretty predictable, the comedy being mostly okay and not fully exploiting the potential, I'd always want to watch such exposes of capitalistic evil that also shows how people will fall for it and won't stop the bootlicking even when they see that their egoistical master is a bumbling idiot.

author: cutie7
title: A Trump Biopic We All Deserve
text:
'Mickey 17' is a bleak, vicious sci-fi comedy set in a world where human life has long since lost its value, reduced to nothing more than a tool for the elite. Cloaked in religious rhetoric, the ruling class cynically exploits cloning and disposable workers for colonial missions.
To escape his debts on Earth, Mickey Barnes (Robert Pattinson) signs up as an "expendable" on a deep-space mission, meaning he's tasked with endless high-risk, often fatal jobs. Each time he dies-often in horrific ways-he's resurrected via 3D bioprinting, forced to remember every gruesome end.
The film is sharp, satirical, and completely unhinged. Mark Ruffalo plays a corporate dictator so exaggerated he feels like he binge-watched Trump speeches for inspiration. While 'Mickey 17' isn't 'Parasite', its scathing critique of social and political issues hits just as hard-if not harder. Instead of the usual rallying cries for resistance, the film paints a bleak picture of a world where everything has already been bought, sold, and repackaged as cheap entertainment. The result? A chaotic, at times absurd, yet disturbingly accurate commentary on a society where people are worth little more than a piece of plastic.
And yet, for all its bleakness, 'Mickey 17' is still a comedy-albeit one fuelled by nervous, borderline hysterical laughter, the kind that comes when you realise there's no way out. It's a film that reminds us progress isn't always a good thing, and the future might not be the utopia we once hoped for. Ironically, the most human character in the film is the one designed purely to die.
This film won't be for everyone, but if you're drawn to dark humour, razor-sharp satire, and Robert Pattinson teetering on the edge of madness, 'Mickey 17' is absolutely worth your time.

author: Tom_Hofman
title: Robert Pattinson Shines in This Gripping Sci-Fi
text:
Mickey 17 is an impressive and gripping film that keeps you engaged from start to finish. The story is not only original and interesting but also full of surprises. The sci-fi setting is immersive, and the themes of identity and survival are well explored.
Lately, I've been getting annoyed by the trend of movies exceeding the two-hour mark. This film is no exception-especially the lengthy explanation of how Mickey had to complete his tasks. A tighter introduction would have made the film even stronger.
That being said, the acting is fantastic. Robert Pattinson once again proves why he is one of the best actors of his generation. His portrayal of both Mickey 17 and Mickey 18 is layered and distinct, making each character feel truly unique. The rest of the cast also delivers strong performances, adding to the overall quality of the film.
In short, a great and captivating movie with outstanding acting, though it would have benefited from a more concise opening.

author: akoaytao1234
title: Falls behind his Masterpiece, but totally serviceable

author: bpirwin
title: An interesting premise marked by ham-fisted polemic
text: Minor spoilers follow. The basic premise of the film envisions of world in which a certain class of humans, "expendables" perform dangerous tasks, resulting in death, but are "reborn" via a process of biological "reprinting." What happens when two of the same expendable coexist? This is a premise that was worth exploring. This never fully happens as the film takes a turn and goes down a path of ham-fisted, political polemic. Mark Ruffalo's character is an amalgam of a buffoonish Elon Musk and Donald Trump who leads a church/corporation with plans to populate another planet with a pure white civilization. In one shot, Ruffalo's profile intentionally mimics a Mussolini poster. The church's logo mimics a swastika. Everyone involved in the church/corporation is portrayed as technically inept, stupid, and hypocritical. Even in their moments of religious expression, they can't even be allowed to sing on-key. As a social critique, it is ham-fisted and unrelenting to the point of being tiresome. District 9, this is not. In its self-righteous distain for much of America it is a window on the soul of Hollywood. This is sad because the basic premise of the film was quite promising.

author: fadrique247
title: I felt sorry for Robert Pattinson
text:
Robert Pattinson is the one redeeming aspect of this film. He is great in every scene, but, gosh, the rest of the actors were horrible-especially Mark. The movie itself is unfunny, and the third act drags on forever in the most boring way possible. The script is painfully weak, filled with awkward dialogue and lifeless humor that never lands. The pacing is a mess, with scenes that feel completely unnecessary and characters who add nothing to the story. The direction is uninspired, and visually, it lacks any creativity.
Bong Joon-ho has proven himself to be a great director, but Mickey 17 feels like a real misfire. The film struggles to maintain a consistent tone, jumping between dark comedy and sci-fi thriller in a way that feels jarring rather than engaging. Even the world-building, which had the potential to be fascinating (the first 20 minutes) is underdeveloped and fails to make the story feel immersive.
Mark Ruffalo's performance, in particular, is grating-his delivery feels exaggerated and out of place, making it difficult to take his character seriously. The third act, which should be the film's most gripping moment, instead feels like an endurance test, dragging on without any real payoff. The film attempts to be thought-provoking but lacks the depth or emotional weight to leave a lasting impression.
Overall, Mickey 17 is a frustrating watch, wasting its intriguing premise with weak execution. Despite Pattinson's solid performance, everything else falls flat. 1/10.

author: filipkowalik
title: A confusing writing choice derails the entire movie
text:
Mickey is an "expendable", a human that upon death can be reprinted, which means that he can perform the most dangerous tasks without needing to fear death.

This was the unique concept that the movie is based on and that was showcased on trailers in order to sell the film.

That is why I was shocked when I saw that this concept gets completely thrown out of the window in the middle of the movie.

From the moment when there are two "mickeys" we almost never hear or see anything related to human printing until the end of the movie. When you think that the movie is going to become most interesting, it devolves into an extremely generic and unoriginal colonizer vs colonized plot, with characters and concepts painfully similar to those in "Okja" (a movie written and directed by the same person as Mickey 17).

It is very strange to see such an experienced director completely throw away the concept that makes the movie unique. It is still an okay watch, as Robert Pattinson delivers once again and the decors are of high quality, but it really feels to me like a lot of potential was wasted because of the decision to stray away from the concept of human re-printing halfway through the film.

author: pranayjalvi
title: A mixture of Joon Ho's earlier movies
text:
Mickey 17 sometimes wobbles balancing its different tones and it is not the director's best work, but still was a good outcome. What holds Bong's eighth feature together is his palpable rage at humanity's cruelty mixed with his compassion for a protagonist who cannot die - and, therefore, cannot truly live. The movie offers a timely escape where empathy can overcome cruelty on the other side of the galaxy. The film, in short, exhilarates and exhausts in equal measure, abundant in ambition and arduous, at points, in execution, although for some it may be slow paced. Comparisons aside, Mickey 17 is a remarkably solid and compelling sci-fi flick, with an absurdist flair and a great performance from Robert Pattinson.
My Rating : 7/10.

author: movieman6-413-929510
title: After his Oscar win, Bong Joon Ho could have been a bit more creative with his new directorial work.
text:
Mickey 17 is a new Sci-Fi comedy directed, written and partly produced by Bong Joon Ho, director of Parasite and Snowpiercer.
Mickey Barnes (Robert Pattinson) has signed up as a disposable crew member for a space mission. This way he can be used to explore or try things out. If this is fatal, he dies, but his body is recreated.
When they think the 17th version of Mickey has died again, they have already made an 18th version. The 17th Mickey is still alive, however, and when he comes home, Mickey 17 and Mickey 18 have to fight out which one gets to stay, because multiple versions of the same person are not allowed.
Bong Joon Ho based this film on the book Mickey 7. However, he made it Mickey 17, so that he could have Mickey die more often in the film. For a Sci-Fi comedy, it would have been more fun to see Mickey die in different, creative ways. Unfortunately, he has kept it more to the same death scenes, which can make it seem a bit repetitive and time-wasting. If they had just kept it to seven, the film would have been a bit less long-winded.
You don't really get to know most of the different Mickey variants and the focus is mainly on the battle and the relationship between Mickey 17 and Mickey 18. Both are somewhat different from each other, but how the differences between the variants exactly arise is not really explained clearly. He also tries to be funny with how the different variants die, but this remains a somewhat repetitive joke. He also tries to make jokes about certain current affairs, such as politics and a certain president.
Bong Joon Ho knows how to creatively portray the other world, but with the creatures that live on this world, you can often see that they have been placed in the film with CGI.
Robert Pattinson does get some space to portray the two different Mickey versions in different ways, but if he had been given space for this with the other fifteen, he would have had more playful opportunities to portray the roles in different ways. Other cast members do know how to handle the different versions of Mickey in a fun way. Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette play more exaggerated versions of a certain president and his wife.

author: cellapie
title: Too Close For Comfort
text:
In a near distant future, Mickey Barnes (an astounding Robert Pattinson) boards a spaceship to help settle a frozen planet since he and his shady pal Timo (Steven Yeun) need to escape from merciless loan sharks after their macaroon business fails.

Our Mickey signs up to be an "expendable," which means he keeps getting reproduced via a 3D printer each time he dies. We meet him in his 17th iteration right before he is to be eaten by a massive beast. Or is he? He is not, but first we go back to how it all started and his life on the spaceship with his sweet but aggressive girlfriend, Nasha (Naomi Ackie, a boss) who are all under the command of a loud, loutish failed politician Kenneth Marshall (Mark Ruffalo, gleefully gnawing away at the scenery) and his dingbat, power-hungry wife Ylfa (Toni Collette, always a scream).

Back to the beginning. Mickey 17 lives but nobody knows that yet so out pops Mickey 18! That's where the fun begin as the two are at odds at first (you know 18 tries to kill 17) but then Nasha finds out and kinda digs it. It's not long before they all get caught up in one of Marshall's schemes and everything comes to a head.

Director Bong Joon Ho does an excellent job at space exploration and keeps the action flowing in a 2+ hour running time to the point that not only do you care for our Mickey but you start to become invested in his -- or rather, their -- lives/survival! The movie is quite the statement about power and the haves and have nots that it's a little TOO relevant for our current times. Also, just give the Oscar to Pattinson now. It's easy to forget what a phenomenal actor he is -- just watch 2017's "Good Time" for more proof -- but he absolutely owns this movie. B+

author: mhafen
title: Very disappointing
text:
I loved Edward Ashton's "Mickey 7" novels, and had high hopes for this film. I wondered how they would create a screen adaptation of those books. Well, they didn't, honestly. And I would definitely not recommend this film, even if you're not familiar with the books.

If you are a fan of the original stories I don't know how you can't be disappointed in this film. It lacks the humour and creativity of "Mickey 7" and "Antimatter Blues." It doesn't even qualify as a "dark comedy" if there isn't any comedy. And I mean, the CGI "creepers" are nothing more than gigantic tardigrades. No creativity.

Mark Ruffalo and Toni Collette are over-the-top in their roles (which were not in the original books), bordering on annoying. Robert Pattinson was forced to play two wildly different Mickeys, which he did well, but shoudn't have had to, as each "reprint" is the same as the last with some updated memories.

And on that subject: unless Mickey's memories are uploaded at the time of his death, he cannot remember dying. This is a detail not overlooked in the original stories, but missed in this film. Kind of a gigantic plot hole.

Save your money and wait until it appears on some streaming service you already subscribe to.

title: Mickey 18 is the Man!
text: I was very captivated from start to finish, mostly with Pattinson's unreal performance! Naomi Ackie and Toni Collette were also fantastic in their roles, however the biggest problem for me with this film was Mark Ruffalo's god awful Trump wishy washy impersonation. I really love Ruffalo's other work, minus the avengers stuff, but with this one I felt myself disliking him as an actor through his character. This film is very good and could've been great had Ruffalo's role been better casted with someone less obsessed with the current political climate and more inclined to leave a lasting philosophical effect/impact on us in a more clever way. author: JTReviewsPlus
title: Bong Joon Ho does it again
text:
Writer and Director Bong Joon Ho doesn't seem to miss when it comes to delivering memorable movie-viewing experiences with films like Parasite, The Host, and Snow Piercer. Mickey 17 is no exception.
The film follows expendable Mickey Barnes during a voyage to colonize the faraway ice planet Nifelheim. Expendables are exactly what you would expect only after said expendable dies, they are cloned with the memories of their past lives intact. However, chaos ensues when Mickey 17 unexpectedly survives a mission where he was presumed dead.
Mickey 17 is narrated by Mickey himself jumping from past to present in creative ways. It can get confusing at times but the time jumps add context to this fascinating sci-fi world that's worth exploring.
Every cast member nails their respective roles but Robert Pattinson is on a whole other level as two different versions of Mickey. His ability to play both a shy pushover and unorthodox tough guy is fun to watch.
Many sci-fi movies in recent years are seemingly super serious or doom and gloom but Mickey 17 has a more optimistic feel to it. The sci-fi concepts aren't anything new but its comedic execution is what makes it standout.
Aside from the at-times confusing time jumps and slow start, Mickey 17 is a wild thrill ride.

title: Too familiar. Good bits but some let downs.
text:
Mickey 17 is a movie that's not bad but not always good.
Robert Pattinson nails an American accent, which to be honest is totally unnecessary given the amount of different nationalities involved!
British features strongly.
But anyway he does well. And he's always great in the role of all Mickey's.
The supporting cast are fine except for in my opinion a terrible character in Mark Ruffalo's Kenneth Mars and yes I know what he was going for. It's just pretty bad.
The story isn't bad, it's decent enough for a sci fi movie. But it doesn't nail any political or social matters like Parasite or Okja, both of which are absolutely brilliant films.
And therefore a straight sci fi actioner could've been better here.
Although admittedly there's some pretty funny moments.
I sound disappointed which is probably the right emotion. I was expecting something really good but this had too much of Okja and Snowpiercer type action and acting to be unique.
I don't want Bong Joon-Ho to become a parody of himself like Wes Anderson. I believe he's capable of much more.
I have absolutely loved all of his past efforts even Barking Dogs Never Bite, which I think is hilarious.
So that's 3 American made movies all very similar in tone. Definitely time for something more.
Anyway it's worth a watch but this is not a classic.

author: ta-98251
title: A fun thought provoking journey that blends sci-fi and comedy
text:
Mickey 17 - An enjoyable journey from Bong June Ho, director of Parasite and Snowpiercer. In cinemas March 7th.
Set in 2054, Mickey 17 is a Sci-Fi based on the Mickey7, the 2022 novel written by Edward Ashton. Mickey is part of a crew sent to colonize planet Nilfheim where they're at liberty to use practices banned on earth, namely cloning. But how exactly does this work and who will they meet on the Nilfheim?
Bong June Ho's stamp is apparent as he seamlessly blends Sci-Fi, dread and comedy into a package that asks profound social questions concerning humanity, colonisation, cloning, science, religion and more. The world we're introduced to is somehow believable for the most part despite some excentric characters and even more excentric moments.
The story and visuals are backed by excellent performances from the cast. Robert Pattison is on top form and the script affords him the chance to show off his versatility. Similarly, Mark Ruffalo once again reminds us that he can deliver comedic performances as well his more grounded performances whilst Naomi Ackie, Steven Yeun and Toni Collette were all a lot of fun.
Mickey 17 is a fun watch, that delivers strong performances and poses some worthwhile questions. Whilst some of these may be familiar the overall package feels like a unique one.

title: I don't understand the positive reviews
text:
Whereas Parasite was a phenomenal movie by Bong Joon-ho, Mickey17 felt completely flat and unoriginal.

For a comedy, it was not that funny and it failed to meaningfully engage with the main theme. Overall, I believe it is possible to make a dark comedy about the value of human life, but this version felt very superficial.

Mark Ruffalo's performance is a too obvious reference to Trump, taking away from the movie. The idea of a "superior race" is just briefly mentioned but not explained nor shown in any specific manner.

The threesome could have been done differently, I missed a bit of a freakout about the whole situation (also this was directly after Pattison almost died from poisoning). The scene where Kai came onto him after the whole Jennifer situation made zero sense.

How can Pattison remember anything about his previous deaths if the clone contains only the memories from when they were copied (before the death)? Why don't they make sure that one body is dead before cloning the next?

Also in general I don't understand why Mickey 18th character is so different from Mickey17th, 18 should have reacted very differently when he first saw 17.

The character of Yeun felt flat, Naomi Ackie played very well but was given little to work with to be fair. She just played "the girlfriend" for most of the movie and then suddenly at the and she is on the council?

Overall, there were many moments in the movie that annoyed me and if I watched this at home I would not have finished it. Quite crazy that this is the same director who made Parasite.

author: Lizyeliz
title: Thrilling, Thought-Provoking, and Fun
text:
Mickey 17 delivers strong social messages. It explores themes of colonization, greed, and the belief in superiority over another species (population)-taking what isn't yours without understanding those who were there first.

Being Mickey feels like living through a never-ending nightmare-one where you die painfully, actually feel it, then wake up and somehow have to move on. But unlike a bad dream, he never truly gets a break. I really felt sorry for him, constantly being thrown back into a cycle of suffering.

Robert Pattinson once again proves his versatility, seamlessly portraying different facets of his character. His performance is captivating, and the film balances intense moments with humor-some scenes genuinely cracked me up! The storyline keeps you engaged from start to finish; not once did I feel bored. I loved the plot, the characters, and the way everything unfolded. Definitely a must-watch!

author: constheo
title: Bong Joon-ho set the bar so high - even for himself
text:
Let's start with the obvious-while "Mickey 17" offers plenty of social commentary, it falls short of the sharp satire and intelligent (class) critique that made "Parasite" a modern masterpiece. Instead, what we get is a sci-fi parody that explores humanity's vanity and self-destruction, yet for some reason, it never truly feels like it takes place in a distant future.
***
Robert Pattinson delivers another strong performance, continuing his streak of unique and compelling roles. He has successfully reshaped his career, moving far beyond his early days, and frankly, we prefer him this way. His unexpected comedic side is a revelation, adding a fresh layer to his performance. Mark Ruffalo also shines, delivering a performance reminiscent of his role in Poor Things, with certain expressions and mannerisms subtly evoking Trump.
***
The production is undeniably grand and expensive, evident in its visually striking yet occasionally excessive scenes. The film often gives off a sense of familiarity-as if we've seen these themes before. The idea for example that we are the real aliens and "monsters" is hardly new, and at times, the script leans too heavily on familiar concepts explored already by many movies.
***
While Mickey 17 is a solid film, it's far from a masterpiece. Perhaps the biggest challenge is that Bong Joon-ho has set the bar so high that anything less than exceptional feels like a slight let-down. There's a lingering sense that something is missing-a sharper edge, a deeper impact, or a more innovative twist.

author: kevin_robbins
title: While Mickey 17 doesn't quite reach the heights of Parasite, it's a strong addition to the sci-fi genre.
text:
My wife and I caught an advanced screening of Mickey 17 (2025) in theaters this evening. The story follows Earth's decline and a colonization mission to inhabit a new planet. To determine if the habitat is livable, certain volunteers become "expendables," meaning they can die and be regenerated as a copy of themselves a day later. When one expendable begins exploring, he quickly realizes the aliens might be the good guys-and the humans, the villains. But what can he do about it?

Directed by Korean 🇰🇷 icon Bong Joon-Ho (Parasite, Snowpiercer, The Host), the film stars Robert Pattinson (Twilight), Naomi Ackie (Blink Twice), Steven Yeun (The Walking Dead), Mark Ruffalo (The Avengers), and Toni Collette (Hereditary).

There's a lot to like about this movie. The writing is smarter than expected, with subtle jabs at American politics and a strong message about entitlement. The sci-fi elements are top-tier and executed exceptionally well, making for a unique and engaging concept.

The characters, their backgrounds, the love story, and their evolution all unfold naturally within the plot. The acting is outstanding-everyone delivers, but Pattinson especially shines. His narration is excellent, and the way he differentiates his two characters, even in stature and body language, is impressive. While CGI plays a role, his performance was elite.

That said, some sequences could have been trimmed, and a few moments felt repetitive-intentionally so, but slightly overdone. Still, the film's full-circle storytelling works well, making for an entertaining and thought-provoking experience.

While Mickey 17 doesn't quite reach the heights of Parasite, it's a strong addition to the sci-fi genre. I'd rate it 7.5-8/10 and recommend seeing it once.

author: diluvian-failure
title: Mickey 17: A Superficial Exploration of Big Ideas
text:
Bong Joon-ho's Mickey 17, screened at Berlinale's Urania cinema, arrives with considerable anticipation, especially given the director's previous success with films like Parasite. However, this sci-fi offering, based on Edward Ashton's novel Mickey7, ultimately falls short, bogged down by superficial explorations of complex themes and a frustrating lack of cinematic storytelling.
The film's initial setup, depicting a near-future reality of dehumanization and casual cruelty, feels intentionally off-putting. While this world-building aims for a visceral impact, it quickly becomes tiresome. The narrative then shifts into a series of lengthy speeches, where the film's supposed ideas about colonization, human identity, governance, and corruption are laid bare in a manner akin to amateur middle-school debates. This reliance on dialogue rather than visual storytelling significantly weakens the film's impact.
Robert Pattinson, a talented actor, is unfortunately underutilized. While his performance is solid, it lacks the space to truly shine. Mark Ruffalo, on the other hand, comes across as pretentious and artificial, his presence more annoying than engaging. The female characters are relegated to mere mannequins, their potential completely wasted.
The central conflict between human personality and technological advancement concludes with a simplistic, Luddite-esque resolution, offering no genuine exploration or insight. Similarly, the secondary theme of colonization is reduced to a simplistic good-versus-evil narrative, flattening the complexities of the issue.
Mickey 17 ultimately suffers from a pervasive superficiality. It raises intriguing questions but fails to provide meaningful answers or even stimulate productive discussion. While fans of Korean cinema and Robert Pattinson may feel compelled to see it, others can safely skip this one.
